Fayette County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Fayette County, Kentucky?

A Fayette County bill touches three public offices. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values each parcel, the Sheriff collects the current year's payment, and the County Clerk picks up bills that run late. Because Lexington and Fayette County merged their governments on January 1, 1974, the sheriff states there is no separate city bill: one statement covers every taxing district.

The PVA works from 101 East Vine Street, Suite 600, in Lexington (phone 859-246-2722, fax 859-246-2729) and says in plain terms that it neither sets tax rates nor takes payments. The sheriff's Property Tax Division is in Room 236 of the Fayette District Courthouse at 150 North Limestone, reachable at 859-252-1771. Its counter is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays and stays open until 6:00 p.m. through October. The sheriff reports collecting over 110,000 bills worth nearly $260 million a year.

The bill pays for the Commonwealth, Fayette County Public Schools, the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government (LFUCG), the county extension and soil conservation districts, the health department, Lextran and a park fund. Property in the Downtown Lexington Management District carries a further charge.

How is a Fayette County property tax bill calculated?

The bill equals the assessed value, minus any exemption, times the rate for the property's tax district, per $100 of value. Every parcel is valued as of January 1 at what the PVA calls fair cash value: the most probable price in an open sale between a willing buyer and a willing seller.

Rates depend on which city services a parcel receives. The seven residential districts on the PVA's chart share the same state, school, general services, extension, conservation, health, Lextran and park fund lines, and differ only in refuse, street light, street cleaning or full-service charges.

Real property rates in Fayette County for 2026, in dollars per $100 of assessed value, by tax district
DistrictServices billed on top of the base rateTotal rate
1Full services1.2598
2General services only1.0868
3Refuse1.2238
4Street lights1.1138
5Refuse and street lights1.2508
6Street lights and street cleaning1.1228
7Refuse and street cleaning1.2328

As an illustration only, a home assessed at $293,500 (the Census median value for owner-occupied homes in the county) in District 1 would owe about $3,698, since 2,935 hundreds times 1.2598 is roughly that figure. The same value in District 2 comes to about $3,190. Properties certified as abandoned and blighted by the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission pay an extra $1 per $100, and Downtown Lexington Management District parcels pay an extra $0.10 per $100.

When are Fayette County property tax bills due?

Payment is due by the end of December, and early payers get a discount. For 2026, statements were mailed in the last week of September and were due in mailboxes by October 1. Anyone still without a bill by about October 10 can call 859-252-1771 for a duplicate, because an unreceived bill does not excuse payment.

  • October 1 to November 1: pay the face amount less 2 percent.
  • November 2 to December 31: pay the face amount. The sheriff's online portal warns that payments after December 31, 2026 draw a late fee.
  • January 1 to January 31: 5 percent penalty.
  • February 1 to April 15: a 10 percent penalty with a further 10 percent add-on.
  • After April 15: the bill is delinquent at 21 percent and moves to the County Clerk.

Payment options include the sheriff's counter (cash, check or money order), any Lexington Republic Bank lobby through January 31 with the bill coupon, the online portal (card or bank debit, with a convenience fee the sheriff does not receive) and mail to PO Box 34148, Lexington, KY 40588-4148. A mailed payment counts at the amount due on its postmark date, and a postage meter stamp is not accepted as proof. The sheriff cannot take installments or grant extensions, and a returned check adds a $35 fee.

How do I challenge a Fayette County assessment?

Speak with a PVA assessor first, and only then file an appeal with the County Clerk. The PVA reviews each of its roughly 300 assessment areas every three to four years under a state quadrennial plan, and neighborhood sales drive most reassessments. Many owners receive a notice in April that includes a map of recent sales close to the property.

In 2026 the PVA wanted conferences finished by Monday, May 18, and the clerk had to receive the appeal to the Local Board of Tax Appeals by Wednesday, May 20. Kentucky's statewide calendar places the tax roll inspection in the 13 days beginning on the first Monday of each May, so the same window recurs yearly. The clerk's page adds that postmarks do not count for the appeal form.

  • Bring comparable sales, a recent appraisal, photographs, insurance policies, construction costs, listings or sale contracts.
  • A paid representative must attach a letter of authorization from the owner.
  • Hearings take place at the LFUCG Phoenix Building, 101 East Vine Street, in a first-floor conference room, and the clerk mails each appellant a time.
  • After the roll is finalized, the PVA still accepts a request for review, though it cannot change the bill already issued for that year.

The appeals office at the clerk can be reached at 859-253-3344.

Does Fayette County offer a homestead exemption?

Yes. A qualifying home loses $49,100 of assessed value under the exemption, a figure the state set for 2025 and 2026. An owner qualifies by turning 65 at any point in the calendar year or by being classified as totally disabled, and the house must be the primary residence.

The disability route needs total disability status under a public or private retirement system, payments across the calendar year, and a yearly confirmation to the PVA. A copy of the system's disability letter serves as proof. Age can be shown with a driver's license, birth certificate or registration, passport, school record or marriage record.

Each residence gets one exemption and each person gets one. Applications go by mail to the Fayette PVA at 101 East Vine Street, Suite 600, by fax to 859-246-2729 or by scan to the PVA's email.

What happens to Fayette County property taxes when I sell my house?

Because the bill is issued to whoever owned the property on January 1, a seller may receive a statement for a year in which the buyer takes title. After a sale, the PVA tries to mail the bill in care of the new owner, though a closing near printing time can outrun the update. Questions about the prorated share go to the closing agent or attorney, because the sheriff does not issue prorated bills or accept prorated payments.

A bill still open after April 15 moves to the County Clerk. The clerk takes only cash, money order or cashier's or certified check payable to the Fayette County Clerk, refuses partial payments and adds interest every month. The County Attorney's Office, at 859-254-4941, handles payment arrangements for owners who cannot pay in full.

Each summer the clerk offers eligible delinquent bills to third-party buyers, somewhere from day 90 to day 135 after the handover. The 2026 sale was July 24. In the Department of Revenue's sample, a $1,000 bill stands at $1,254 on the day it transfers, counting the penalty, the sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission. Clerk and attorney charges come later. A sale ordered by a court, including for delinquent taxes, goes through the Master Commissioner. The clerk also offers a free alert service: register a name or address and an email arrives whenever a document is recorded against it.

How does Fayette County's market look to a seller?

Fayette County is a 286 square mile urban county in the central Bluegrass region, formed by the Virginia General Assembly in 1780 and joined to Lexington as a single government since 1974. Scott, Bourbon, Clark, Madison, Jessamine and Woodford counties surround it, and Lexington is its seat and only city. Census QuickFacts describes a county unlike most in Kentucky:

  • Population: 329,751 in 2025, up 2.2 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Homes: 152,488 housing units, with 53.8 percent owner-occupied.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $293,500, with median gross rent of $1,164.
  • Median household income: $69,479.
  • Building permits in 2025: 1,052.
  • Mean travel time to work: 20.9 minutes.

With nearly half of homes rented and steady permit activity, a house needing repairs or carrying a tax balance still draws buyers. If a sale has to close without repairs or a listing period, a cash buyer who takes the house as-is can pay off the tax from the proceeds.

More questions about Fayette County, KY Property Tax Guide

When is the 2% discount deadline in Fayette County?

The discount ends on November 1 of the assessment year. In 2026 it ran from October 1 to November 1 and cut the bill by 2 percent. After that the bill is due at face value through December 31.

Where do I pay Fayette County property tax in person?

Pay at the Sheriff's Property Tax Division, Room 236 of the Fayette District Courthouse, 150 North Limestone. The counter takes cash, checks and money orders. Any Lexington Republic Bank lobby also takes payments through January 31 if you bring the bill coupon.

How much is the Fayette County homestead exemption?

For 2026 the deduction is $49,100, taken from the fair cash value of a qualifying primary residence. The owner must be 65 during the calendar year or totally disabled, and the PVA at 859-246-2722 processes applications.

Can I appeal my Fayette County assessment after the window closes?

Not for the current bill. The PVA conference and the clerk's appeal filing both fall inside the May inspection period, and the 2026 deadlines were May 18 and May 20. After that you can still request a review through the PVA, but a finalized assessment cannot change the bill for that year.

What if Fayette County taxes stay unpaid?

On April 15 the bill becomes delinquent at 21 percent and passes to the County Clerk, who adds monthly interest and fees. The clerk may then sell the bill to an outside buyer at the summer sale, held on July 24 in 2026.

What we could not confirm

Jefferson County by the numbers

Which Louisville offices value and bill a Jefferson County house?

Valuation belongs to the PVA, and billing belongs to the Sheriff. The Sheriff's own description says it gathers about $1 billion a year from over 300,000 taxpayers for 13 taxing jurisdictions, among them the state, Louisville Metro, the school board and several fire districts.

The PVA works from the Glassworks Building, 815 W. Market St., Suite 400, Louisville, KY 40202, phone (502) 574-6380. The Sheriff's Property Tax Department is inside the Fiscal Court Building at 700 W. Liberty St., phone (502) 574-5479, which serves walk-in payers from 8 AM until 4 PM on business days.

The PVA measures fair cash value as of each January 1. Whoever the records name as owner on that date, or when the roll is printed, receives the bill.

When must Louisville homeowners pay each year?

Mailing is due by November 1. The early-pay discount of 2 percent lasts until December 1 here, a month past the date in the state statute, and then the stages step up on the Sheriff's calendar.

Payment stages posted by the Jefferson County Sheriff for the current-year tax bill (source: Jefferson County Sheriff's Office)
DatesAmount owed
November 1 to December 1Bill less 2 percent
December 2 to January 4Bill at face value
January 5 to February 5Face value plus 5 percent
February 6 to April 15Face value plus a 10 percent penalty and a 10 percent Sheriff's add-on fee

When the last day of a stage lands on a Saturday, Sunday or office holiday, it rolls forward to the next open day. A missing bill still carries the late charges, so ring the department if yours has not come by mid-November.

  • In person: cash, check or money order, with the stub from your bill.
  • Mail: make the check out to Jefferson County Sheriff and send it to PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570.
  • Web portal: eChecks run $2, and cards run 2.25 percent, or a flat $1.95 when the payment is $86 or less.
  • Dropboxes sit at the downtown office and at County Clerk branches such as Dixie, Fairdale, Highview, East and Westport.

Installment-style payments toward a current bill are also taken between November 1 and April 15.

How do Louisville owners challenge a PVA valuation?

The route starts with a PVA conference rather than a board hearing. KRS 133.120 sets that order, the conference falls in the yearly open inspection period, and Jefferson County runs it through an online form.

  • File one conference per parcel ID.
  • Attach an appraisal, photographs, an insurance policy, repair quotes, construction costs or a listing agreement.
  • Pick comparable sales from about the last two years, matched on size and type. The PVA opens its sales search to the public free for the appeal window.
  • Results come back in writing within roughly one to two weeks, according to the PVA.

When the conference result stands, complete the lower section of that form and deliver it to the Jefferson County Clerk. State law sets the filing deadline at one workday after the inspection period ends. The Local Board of Assessment Appeals hears the case, and skipping that board forecloses the Board of Tax Appeals. Paid representatives need written authorization and must fit a listed profession.

An appeal never pauses collection. Pay tax on your own claimed figure now; a higher number from the board brings a supplemental bill with interest.

How much can the homestead exemption cut a Jefferson County bill?

Revenue's figure for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years is $49,100, subtracted from an eligible home's assessment. Eligible means 65 or older, or totally disabled, and living in the house.

Apply it to the Census typical value of $248,400 and the taxable base drops to $199,300. A bill shrinks but never disappears unless the assessment is smaller than the deduction. Bring proof of age to the PVA, such as a passport, birth certificate or license. Disability claims need proof of benefits from a federal or retirement-system program.

West End homeowners may have another option. LHOME and the West End Opportunity Partnership offer a grant or 0 percent loan toward the residential bill in nine neighborhoods: Algonquin, California, Chickasaw, Park DuValle, Parkhill, Parkland, Portland, Russell and Shawnee. LHOME's number is (502) 882-8091.

Does a small city inside Jefferson County send its own bill?

Frequently. The Sheriff's bill funds the state, Metro, schools and fire districts, while many smaller cities inside the county bill their own residents on top.

The PVA tallies 83 incorporated taxing jurisdictions among roughly 60,000 properties. Those cities offer services such as police, sanitation and parks, with rates posted by each city. State law has recognized just two city classes since 2015: first class, which is Louisville, and home rule cities, which are all the rest.

A seller in a place like St. Matthews or Jeffersontown should call city hall for a balance and a payoff letter. Looking only at the Sheriff's account can miss a separate city liability.

Does Jefferson County tax debt follow the house to a new owner?

It does. The debt sticks to the owner and the land alike. KRS 134.015 calls it the taxpayer's personal obligation from the assessment date, and the KRS 134.420 lien can run 11 years no matter who holds title.

Anything unpaid at the April 15 cutoff goes to the Clerk, where monthly interest of 1 percent and extra fees start. An outside investor may buy the certificate at the summer sale, and the County Attorney's page estimates the added cost near 40 percent.

A County Attorney payment plan keeps a bill out of that sale, though plans for a given year open only after the Sheriff's collection period closes. Requests to waive certain penalties go in writing to the same office.

The Sheriff's FAQ explains the usual closing split: the seller pays a prorated share for the months owned, and the buyer settles the whole bill when it arrives. Read your settlement statement for how the closing agent divided it.

How big is the Jefferson County housing market?

Kentucky's most populous county counted 795,222 people in the 2025 Census estimate, inside borders it shares with Louisville Metro. Land area is 380.8 square miles, which worked out to about 2,056 residents per square mile in 2020.

  • Owned homes had a middle value of $248,400 in the 2020 to 2024 survey.
  • Owners live in 62.1 percent of homes.
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,593 with a mortgage and $608 without.
  • Median household income: $69,866.
  • Housing units in 2025: 366,702.

Children attend Jefferson County Public Schools, or the Anchorage Independent district through eighth grade. Deed recording questions go to the County Clerk's Legal Records Division.

More questions about Jefferson County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where can I hand in a Jefferson County tax payment?

Walk-in payments are taken downtown at 700 W. Liberty St. between 8 AM and 4 PM Monday to Friday, cash, checks and money orders only. You can also pay online, drop an envelope in a dropbox or mail PO Box 34570.

How long does the 2 percent early discount last?

The 2 percent discount covers payments received between November 1 and December 1 inclusive. Face value applies until January 4, and a 5 percent charge starts January 5.

Will the Sheriff take part of a bill now and the rest later?

Yes. Part payments on a current-year bill are accepted while collection runs, and once the bill moves to the Clerk the County Attorney decides who qualifies for a plan.

How early must I act to lower my assessment?

Act during the yearly inspection period, because a tax bill arrives too late to contest. File the PVA's online conference first. Only a failed conference opens the door to a petition at the Clerk.

Does closing on the sale wipe out a tax lien?

No. A lien outlives a sale, and the title company will insist on clearing it out of your proceeds. Obtain a current-year figure from the Sheriff and earlier-year figures from the Clerk.

Selling in Campbell County?

What we could not confirm

  • 2026 Campbell discount/penalty dates (page showed 2025)

Campbell County by the numbers

Which Campbell County offices touch a Northern Kentucky tax bill?

Three offices share a Campbell bill. The Property Valuation Administrator sets the value, the Sheriff's Office mails and collects, and the County Clerk inherits what goes delinquent. Rates come from neither the PVA nor the sheriff: the PVA's page explains that every taxing district's board figures its rate from the assessments inside that district.

The county runs along the Ohio and Licking Rivers and has two seats, Newport and Alexandria, with sheriff's windows in each. At 93,076 residents in 2020 and 615 people per square mile, Campbell is the densest county in this group by a wide margin, and it has the highest home values.

By law the PVA assesses at 100 percent of fair market value, meaning the price a willing buyer and seller would agree on. Field staff look at every parcel in person at least every four years, and new construction is reviewed when it appears.

History explains the two offices. Campbell was formed on December 17, 1794 as Kentucky's 19th county, and an 1883 law let Newport keep a separate court house district while Alexandria remained the legal seat until a 2010 ruling gave Newport equal status. The county is the fourth-smallest in Kentucky by land and has six school districts, so which district serves a house changes the school line on the bill.

Rates move each year under House Bill 44. A district can adopt the compensating rate, which keeps revenue from existing property flat as values rise, or a rate that raises up to 4 percent more, which needs a public hearing. A rate above that can be put to a recall vote. A rise in your assessed value therefore does not automatically mean a bigger bill.

What is the Campbell County payment calendar?

The PVA's calendar has finished bills reaching the sheriff by September 15, and mailing usually follows around November 1. For 2025 the sheriff ran the discount phase from November 1 through November 30, which the PVA's calendar phrases as payment with discount before December 1.

  • All of December: face amount, no discount.
  • All of January: delinquent, plus 5 percent.
  • From February 1: plus 10 percent and a 10 percent sheriff's add-on fee.
  • Older years: settled at the County Clerk, never the sheriff.

One line item surprises owners: the 911 fee printed on the bill is exempt from the 2% discount and stays at full price. The sheriff mails only to the listed owner and cannot redirect a bill to a lender, so anyone with escrow should pass the bill along at once.

Which payment options does the Campbell sheriff offer?

Owners can pay online, by mail, or at either sheriff's location. Newport's office sits in the County Administration Building at 1098 Monmouth Street, and Alexandria's is at 8330 West Main Street. The sheriff's tax page lists weekday hours from 8 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon at both.

The web option goes through an outside vendor. A card payment adds a 3 percent charge to the cardholder, an e-check adds $3, and e-checks above $30,000 are refused. The sheriff keeps none of those fees. A mailed check should name the sheriff and show the bill number, and the canceled check is your receipt.

A returned check puts the bill back to unpaid on the sheriff's and PVA's records, and the repayment must follow the schedule printed on the bill. That matters in a closing week, when a bounced check can leave a lien open.

How does a Campbell County appeal work?

A PVA conference has to happen before the 13-day inspection period ends, and the appeal itself is filed with the county. Inspection starts the first Monday in May, per the PVA's calendar, and the Board of Assessment Appeals then meets for five days starting 25 to 35 days after it closes.

The state calendar sets the filing deadline at the workday after inspection ends, while the county PVA's calendar lists six work days. With the two sources differing, read the dates on your notice and get the exact last day from the PVA before filing. Anyone paid to represent you must be an attorney, appraiser, accountant, licensed broker or similar professional under KRS 133.120.

Good evidence for a Newport or Alexandria house includes recent sales of similar homes, photos of damage and repair estimates. The state revenue guide adds that the PVA should be able to hand over the sales used to value your home, so request that list first.

Which exemptions and corrections can Campbell County owners request?

Owners who reach 65, or who are totally disabled, can apply for a homestead or disability exemption through the PVA, which can state the filing cutoff for the year. The state wants disability verification before December 31. The sheriff's page advises owners turning 65 to contact the PVA before paying.

The PVA at 1098 Monmouth Street, (859) 292-3871, also fixes a wrong property address, mailing address or owner name. Corrections can be written on the return stub, which the sheriff forwards. An assessment or exemption can be changed only by the PVA.

  • PVA, 1098 Monmouth Street: value, address, name and exemption questions.
  • Sheriff, Newport or Alexandria: bill lookup and payment.
  • County Clerk, (859) 292-3845: any year that has gone delinquent.

Farm acreage is valued at its agricultural value, which the state's assessment guide says can sit far below the market price per acre in urban areas. A seller with a few acres at the edge of Alexandria should ask the PVA how the parcel is classed.

What happens to Campbell County taxes when I sell?

The debt travels with the parcel, so the title company will want a payoff of the current bill and any delinquent certificate before closing. KRS 134.015 makes the tax a personal debt of the owner on the January 1 assessment date, and the delinquency lien continues under KRS 134.420 no matter who owns the house afterward.

A bill that outlasts the sheriff's season moves to the County Clerk carrying a 10 percent penalty, the sheriff's fee and 1 percent monthly interest. Clerk, county attorney and third-party purchaser fees pile on from there, and the state's collection page works five examples, running from about $1,388 to $1,704 on a $1,000 bill. The clerk at (859) 292-3845 gives the live figure.

An owner who has fallen behind can still sell as-is, with the payoff deducted from proceeds. Early numbers from the clerk show what remains.

How strong is the Campbell County housing market?

Home values here lead this group: $252,000 is the 2020 to 2024 median for owner-occupied homes, and 182 building permits were issued in 2025. The county belongs to the Cincinnati metropolitan area, and Northern Kentucky University is in Highland Heights.

Campbell County housing profile from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page
ItemValue
Residents (2025 estimate)95,441
Homes counted in mid-202543,090
Share lived in by owners71.1%
Typical home value$252,000
Typical monthly rent$1,145
Typical monthly owner cost, mortgaged$1,627

Only 86.1 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, the lowest of the four counties, which points to more moves and more rentals. Owners of older Newport homes, duplexes or inherited houses can sell directly for cash when repairs or tenants slow a standard listing.

More questions about Campbell County, KY Property Tax Guide

When do Campbell County tax bills go out?

Mailing typically happens around November 1. In 2025 the 2% discount lasted through November 30, December was face value, January added 5%, and after January 31 a 10% penalty and sheriff's fee applied.

Where do I take a Campbell County payment?

Visit the Sheriff's Office in Newport (1098 Monmouth Street) or Alexandria (8330 West Main Street), mail it, or use the vendor link on the sheriff's tax page.

Is the 911 fee discounted?

No. The sheriff states that the 911 line on a bill is outside the 2% discount.

Who handles questions about my Campbell value?

The PVA, at (859) 292-3871. The sheriff only collects, and cannot alter an assessment, address or exemption.

Can a house with unpaid Campbell taxes still sell?

Yes. Delinquent bills sit with the County Clerk, and closing pays them from the proceeds. Ask the clerk, at (859) 292-3845, for the amount before fixing a date.

Pulaski County by the numbers

Who values and who bills a Pulaski County property?

Two Somerset offices split the job. The Property Valuation Administrator places a value on each parcel and answers at (606) 679-1812. The Pulaski County Sheriff's tax office prints the bill and collects it, with staff on duty weekdays from 8:00 AM until 4:00 PM and a tax mailbox at taxes@pulaskisheriff.com.

Neither office votes on rates. Each taxing district sets its own levy, from the fiscal court to the school board. Three public school systems serve the county, namely Pulaski County, Somerset Independent and Science Hill Independent, so the school share of a bill follows the district lines.

The sheriff handles more than houses. Its FAQ lists real estate with school taxes, tangible property, franchise and gas taxes, undeveloped land, oil, and limestone, sand and gravel.

What does the Pulaski County sheriff's calendar look like?

The sheriff's own FAQ says bills begin to be mailed during early October. The steps below follow that page, and the 5 percent January step agrees with KRS 134.015.

Pulaski County sheriff: amount owed by payment date
When paidAmount
October 1 to November 1Bill less a 2 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Base amount
January 1 to January 31Base amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Base amount plus 21 percent
April 16 onwardPay the County Clerk, (606) 679-2042

Counter payments can be cash, check or card, and card users pay a small added fee. The office refuses part payments and wants the full bill at once. A mailed check comes back with a receipt if you enclose a stamped return envelope. A lost bill is replaced at no charge.

What would a median Pulaski County home owe the state?

Kentucky's rate for 2025 is 10.6 cents on every hundred dollars of assessment. With Census QuickFacts listing a median value of $166,900 for Pulaski County homes, the state portion works out to about $176.91. Local districts stack their rates above that figure.

The older or disabled owner deduction changes the base. At $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, it leaves $117,800 taxable on that median house and brings the state portion to about $124.87. The sheriff's FAQ still quotes an older deduction amount, so use the Department of Revenue figure and confirm it with the PVA when applying.

Paying inside the October 1 to November 1 window earns the 2 percent discount on the whole bill.

How do I dispute a Pulaski County valuation?

Every Kentucky appeal opens with a meeting at the PVA office, whether the parcel is a Lake Cumberland cottage or a farm near Eubank. The roll can be inspected for thirteen days from May's first Monday. At the meeting the PVA must explain how the number came about and record your claimed value, anything agreed and the result.

  • The appeal reaches the clerk on the first workday after the roll closes.
  • A local board of property owners hears cases about a month later, in a session of up to five days.
  • Supporting papers are required: land and building descriptions, insurance policies, construction cost and sales listings. A file without them is rejected.
  • Anyone you hire to speak for you must come from the statutory list and hold your signed authorization.

If bills print before the board rules and the final value exceeds your claim, a supplemental bill follows for the gap.

Who owes the tax when a Pulaski County house sells mid year?

The sheriff's FAQ is direct: whoever held the parcel at the start of the year owes the fall bill, though a closing may prorate it. Your closing attorney can explain how the contract divides the year, and the tax office can tell you whether the parcel shows paid or open.

State law agrees. Under KRS 134.015 the tax is the owner's personal debt as of the assessment date, and a lien described in KRS 134.420 stays on the land for eleven years. Lenders that escrow often pay the bills they hold. The sheriff still stresses that the bill is the homeowner's duty, so give your lender a copy if your mailing address changed.

A seller moving away should also tell the PVA, because the older owner deduction follows the person and the buyer must apply separately.

What follows after April 15 in Pulaski County?

On April 16 the sheriff passes unpaid bills to the County Clerk. Each turns into a certificate of delinquency backed by a lien. A buyer of a delinquent bill collects the tax plus 12 percent a year and costs such as attorney and filing fees, according to the sheriff's FAQ. The house itself is not auctioned at that stage.

The clerk adds interest of 1 percent monthly. A Department of Revenue example shows a $1,000 bill reaching $1,254 on transfer and about $1,387.79 within five business days, with the county attorney's commission and postage added after notices go out. Notices go out before a sale, which the law places between 90 and 135 days after transfer.

Paying the clerk before the sale day keeps an investor from acquiring the bill.

What stands out about Pulaski County for someone selling?

Pulaski County dates to December 1798, when land from Lincoln and Green counties was combined and named after Count Casimir Pulaski. Somerset is the seat, joined by Burnside, Eubank, Ferguson and Science Hill. The county covers about 658 square miles of land, third largest in Kentucky, with Lake Cumberland and its houseboat trade in the south. The county's own figures list an average elevation of 974 feet, 58.9 degrees as the yearly mean temperature, 47.29 inches of rain and 12.6 inches of snow. Alcohol sales are limited to Somerset and Burnside.

Roads are a strength. US 27 runs north and south, Kentucky 80 east and west, the Cumberland Expressway reaches US 27 north of Somerset, and Kentucky 914 loops the city. Interstate 75 lies about 28 miles east, and Lexington is 76 miles north. Somerset Community College keeps a campus on Monticello Street, and Lake Cumberland Regional Airport serves general aviation at the south end of town.

  • July 2025 population estimate: 67,384, a 3.6 percent rise over 2020.
  • Housing: 26,210 households, 72.5 percent of homes lived in by owners.
  • Typical home value $166,900; typical gross rent $803.
  • Midpoint household income of $51,898, with 20.1 percent below the poverty line.
  • 129 building permits in 2025.

Visitors come for Lake Cumberland, the Mill Spring Battlefield, Somersplash Water Park, the Master Musicians Festival in July and the Somernites Cruise on the fourth Saturday of each month from April to October. Rail service on the Norfolk Southern line and the airport round out the access, and Somerset sits 129 miles northwest of Knoxville and 128 miles southeast of Louisville. A house with roof, septic or shoreline trouble can still go to a direct cash buyer, with any tax owed settled at closing.

More questions about Pulaski County, KY Property Tax Guide

Can I pay a Pulaski County tax bill by card?

Yes, at the counter of the sheriff's tax office, with a small fee added for cards. Cash, checks and mailed checks also work, but the full bill must be paid at once because part payments are refused.

What are the extra charges after January in Pulaski County?

The sheriff lists 5 percent for January and 21 percent for February 1 through April 15. After that the County Clerk takes payment.

When does the Pulaski County early discount apply?

From October 1 through November 1, a 2 percent discount comes off the bill. The base amount is due November 2 through December 31.

Where do I claim the older owner deduction in Pulaski County?

Call the PVA at (606) 679-1812. The state set it at $49,100 for owners 65 and up or totally disabled, for 2025 and 2026.

Will the sheriff auction my house over unpaid Pulaski County tax?

Not at the sheriff stage. After April 15 the bill goes to the County Clerk and can be sold to an investor, who then holds a lien with 12 percent yearly interest and costs.

Who to contact in Boone County

What we confirmed on official pages

Selling in Boone County?
We buy Boone County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Boone County by the numbers

How does property tax work in Boone County, Kentucky?

Boone County property is valued by the county Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), billed by the Boone County Sheriff, and taxed by several overlapping districts. The PVA sets the assessment as of January 1, and the sheriff mails and collects the bill in the fall.

Boone sits at the top of Kentucky, 256 square miles along the Ohio River across from Cincinnati. Burlington is the county seat, Florence is the largest city, and Union and Walton are the other cities. Your bill adds a state rate, a county rate, a city rate where one applies, and separate rates for the library, health department, extension office, fire district and school district. Neighbors can therefore owe different totals if their parcels fall in different districts.

Sellers should ask which year they owe. Kentucky taxes follow the January 1 owner, so a bill that shows up in September or October may carry the name of whoever held the house in January.

What is the Boone County collection schedule and what are the penalties?

The sheriff's 2026 notice sets four stages, shown below. KRS 134.015 supplies the pattern, so the same calendar repeats every year unless the state approves a delayed schedule.

Boone County Sheriff collection schedule posted for 2026 bills
StageDatesWhat you pay
Discount10/01/26 to 11/01/26Bill minus 2 percent
Face amount11/02/26 to 12/31/26The printed amount
First penalty01/01/27 to 01/31/27Printed amount plus 5 percent
Second penalty02/01/27 to 04/15/27Penalty of 10 percent, plus the sheriff's 10 percent add-on

Source: Boone County Sheriff property tax notice.

Partial payments are refused, so each bill is settled in one payment. Card payments online add a vendor charge, and e-checks add a smaller flat charge. The sheriff's office is on Conrad Lane in Burlington, with Saturday hours in October, and bills go in the mail before the end of September.

What happens when a Boone County bill is still open in April?

A bill still open when business closes on April 15 passes from the sheriff to the County Clerk, who records a lien. The sheriff's notice lists what the clerk then adds: a 20 percent attorney fee, a 10 percent fee for the clerk, and interest of 1 percent a month. It also warns that the debt can be sold to a private buyer the following summer. For 2026 bills that transfer date is April 15, 2027.

  • KRS 134.015 keeps the lien attached to the parcel for up to 11 years, whoever buys the house.
  • Warnings go to the owner of record, so a stale mailing address can hide them.
  • Revenue's own guidance says the county attorney can arrange an installment plan.

A parcel with an open certificate can still be sold. The seller's share covers the payoff, and the clerk quotes it, not the sheriff.

What is the route to a Boone County assessment appeal?

Begin with the PVA. A formal appeal cannot be filed until you have met with that office, and Boone's online request form is open from October 1 to May 1. You can also email appeals@boonecountyky.org to book the meeting.

The legal window is short. Under state law the tax roll sits open for inspection for two weeks beginning in the first week of May. If the meeting does not settle the value, you file with the County Clerk by the next business day after that window ends. The Boone PVA points out that a bill itself cannot be appealed, because values must be final before rates are calculated.

  • Bring sale prices of comparable homes close to yours, the evidence the PVA's own model uses.
  • Add photos or repair estimates if the house is in worse shape than the county record shows.
  • Ask to see the sales the PVA relied on for your parcel.

The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after inspection closes, under KRS 133.030. If you still disagree, its decision letter explains the next appeal step.

Why did my Boone County assessment go up?

Sales drive most increases. The Boone PVA values homes from nearby arm's length transactions through a computer assisted system, and every parcel gets a physical look within four years, so a jump often means several years of price growth arriving at once.

The office also points to House Bill 44, which caps growth in countywide tax revenue at 4 percent a year. That law acts on the tax rate, not the assessed value, so a rising valuation can come alongside a falling rate. Kentucky requires the PVA's values to land within 90 to 110 percent of sales prices, and a yearly ratio study tests it.

Census data shows the pressure. Boone had 135,968 residents in 2020 and an estimated 145,316 by July 2025, up 6.9 percent, across 56,021 housing units. The survey's middle owned home sits at $277,300 for 2020 to 2024, and household income of $99,414 is more than triple the figure reported for Bell County in southeast Kentucky.

Who gets the Boone County homestead or disability exemption?

A Boone homeowner who turns 65 in the tax year, or who is totally disabled, gets a flat deduction from assessed value. The PVA lists $49,100 for 2026, and the sheriff says it should print on the face of your bill once the PVA holds your form.

  • Own the house and live in it on January 1.
  • One deduction per household, even if both spouses meet the age test.
  • Disabled owners under 65 renew every year, unless the disability is a veteran's service connected rating or a permanent finding by Social Security or a state retirement system.
  • The deduction belongs to the owner. After a sale the PVA lifts it from the old address, and the buyer applies on their own.

If the amount is missing, call the PVA before you pay. KRS 132.810 allows a refund for late approval, though fixing it first is simpler. Forms go in by mail, fax, email or the PVA's online form.

What should a Boone County seller expect at closing?

Closing agents commonly settle the year's tax out of the seller's funds and split it by days of ownership. The PVA notes that a bill for a house bought after January 1 may still arrive in the former owner's name, so the settlement statement is where the split gets recorded.

Three checks help. Find out whether this year's bill is paid, and ask the sheriff for a duplicate if yours never came, since that office cannot see new deeds. Make sure a recorded deed or other document updates the owner name at the PVA, because name changes happen there. For an inherited house, the PVA accepts a death certificate to update the record.

Owners with a delinquent bill, a missing exemption or deferred repairs sometimes pick a direct sale to a cash buyer, who purchases the house in its present condition, with the tax payoff deducted at closing.

Where are the Boone County offices?

Four offices cover the cycle. The PVA in Burlington values property and takes exemption forms and appeal requests at 859-334-2181. The sheriff collects bills at 859-334-2175, with an online portal at boonecountytax.com. The County Clerk files deeds, receives appeals and holds the bills that go delinquent in April. For 2026, the sheriff also listed Heritage Bank branches as places to pay.

Most of the county belongs to Boone County Schools, and a portion lies in the Walton-Verona Independent district, so the school share of your bill depends on the parcel. Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport is inside the county, and Census figures put 2022 transportation and warehousing receipts at about $1.87 billion.

More questions about Boone County, KY Property Tax Guide

What dates matter for the 2026 Boone County bill?

Four stages apply to 2026 bills, and the sheriff's table above lists each one. Paying by November 1, 2026 earned the discount, and bills still unpaid at the end of January 2027 moved to the larger penalty stage.

Can a Boone County assessment be appealed after the bill arrives?

No. Appeals belong to the May inspection period. Meet with the PVA first, then file with the county clerk by the next business day after the period closes.

How large is the Boone County homestead exemption?

The Boone PVA lists $49,100 for 2026. It comes off the assessment, not the bill, and applies to owners turning 65 in the tax year or totally disabled.

Who receives the bill if I sold my Boone County house during the year?

The bill goes to whoever owned on January 1. The buyer should forward it or call the sheriff for a copy, and the settlement statement divides the cost.

Is a Boone County home with back taxes still sellable?

Yes. A lien attaches to the parcel, so the unpaid amount and any clerk and attorney fees come out of what the seller receives. Request an exact payoff from the sheriff or clerk before choosing an asking price.

Daviess County by the numbers

What kind of housing market does Daviess County have?

Daviess County is western Kentucky's river-city market. Owensboro anchors it, and the Census Bureau places the county in the Owensboro metropolitan area on the Ohio River. Kentucky cut it from Ohio County on January 14, 1815. The name carries an old typo: the man it honors, Joseph Hamilton Daveiss, was entered with the wrong spelling in the state clerk's records, and the error stuck.

The county spans 477 square miles, 18 of them water. Land along the river in the north is mostly level, while the south rolls into hills and valleys that once supplied coal near Panther Creek. Residents numbered 103,312 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate of 104,898 is 1.5 percent higher.

What do Census figures say about Daviess County homes?

QuickFacts for the 2020 to 2024 period and 2025 show a market with real depth:

  • 45,155 housing units across 41,639 households
  • 68.1 percent of households own, so close to a third rent
  • Typical home value: $199,900
  • Typical rent: $918 a month
  • Typical monthly owner cost: $1,387 with a mortgage, $512 without
  • 253 building permits in 2025

Apply the Fiscal Court's real property rate of 12.2 cents per $100 to a $199,900 house and the county's own share comes to roughly $244 a year. School, city and special district rates sit on top of that.

Who sends and collects the Daviess County bill?

The Sheriff's Office tax division handles both, at 212 St. Ann Street, Room 103, in Owensboro. The counter takes questions at 270-685-6133 on weekdays until 4:30. It closes for Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, Black Friday, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year's Eve and New Year's Day.

Mailing happens during the first week of November. A homeowner whose lender pays from escrow may still receive a bill, because the servicer sometimes intends to pay without asking the sheriff to hold a copy. If you expect a bill and see none, allow a couple of days for postal delays, then look the parcel up on the sheriff's website, since the mailing address on file may be wrong. Call or email the tax counter with the parcel numbers to correct an address. Property inside Owensboro also owes city tax through the City of Owensboro Tax Office at 270-687-8537.

What did Daviess County set as its tax rates for 2025?

In August 2025 the Fiscal Court adopted the compensating rate for real property, dropping the county's figure from 12.9 cents to 12.2 cents per $100 of assessed value. Tangible personal property stayed at 13.8 cents, and motor vehicles and watercraft at 17 cents. The county called it its biggest tax cut in at least twenty years.

These are the county's rates alone. School districts and other taxing bodies add their own, which makes a parcel's full rate higher than 12.2 cents. Ask the tax counter for a parcel-level bill, or search the parcel on the sheriff's website, before telling a buyer what the house will cost to carry.

What are the Daviess County payment windows?

The Department of Revenue approved a calendar that repeats each year. A payment inside the first window saves 2 percent, and each later window costs more.

Daviess County collection periods (source: Daviess County Sheriff's Office, Tax Collection page)
WindowEffect
November 10 to December 102 percent discount
December 11 to January 10Base amount
January 11 to February 105 percent penalty
February 11 to April 2521 percent penalty

Under KRS 134.119, a mailed payment with a U.S. Postal Service postmark inside the window is on time. A returned check costs $25, and the bill goes back to unpaid.

How can I pay a Daviess County property tax bill?

Three channels work. Online, go to dcsoky.gov and use Pay Taxes Online. Several bills can share a cart, the options are card or electronic check, and the fee appears before you confirm. The office warns that payments sent through any other website will not be honored.

  • At the counter: cash, card, check, cashier's check or money order, with checks for the exact amount
  • By mail: checks payable to the Daviess County Sheriff's Office, drawn on U.S. banks only
  • Online: card or e-check on the sheriff's own site

Two bills for one parcel usually mean an exemption was added after the first printing. Read both and look up the balance online.

How do I challenge a Daviess County assessment?

Call the PVA at 270-685-8474 first. A conference with the PVA or a deputy is required before any appeal, and it must happen inside the May inspection window, which opens the first Monday of May and lasts thirteen days. The value being tested is the January 1 fair cash value.

When the conference settles nothing, file at the County Clerk's office, 270-685-8434, by the close of the following workday. The local board of assessment appeals sits 25 to 35 days after the window ends and rules on evidence, so bring comparable sales, an appraisal or repair quotes. A board ruling you dispute can go to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

Can a Daviess County homeowner lower the taxable value?

People at least 65, or classified as totally disabled, can claim the homestead exemption on the home they occupy. For 2025 and 2026 it is worth $49,100. A house assessed at $199,900 would be taxed on $150,800.

The application goes to the Daviess County PVA. A driver's license, birth certificate or passport proves age. A disability claim needs proof that a federal agency or a retirement system classified you as totally disabled.

What if I sell a Daviess County house after bills are printed?

The sheriff's office tells anyone who sold or bought after January 1 and thinks a bill came in error to ask the closing title company. Valuation fixes on January 1 under KRS 132.220, so paperwork can trail a sale. Your settlement statement should split the year's tax between seller and buyer.

A delinquent notice goes out on February 11. When business closes on April 25, unpaid bills pass to the County Clerk, carrying heavy fees and exposure to the tax sale. A delinquency can be paid off from the sale proceeds at closing.

What does a delinquent Daviess County bill turn into?

After April 25 the bill becomes a certificate of delinquency held by the County Clerk, with a lien on the parcel. The state process adds interest at 1 percent a month, a 10 percent clerk fee and a 20 percent county attorney fee. The county attorney mails notices by mid-May and mid-June, and installments may be possible.

From mid-July to late October the clerk may sell certificates to private buyers, after advertising the list in the local paper and on the clerk's website at least 30 days ahead. Once a buyer holds the certificate, the owner pays that buyer, who adds charges. Anyone planning a sale with a delinquency should settle it before the summer sale dates.

More questions about Daviess County, KY Property Tax Guide

When does the Daviess County 2 percent discount end?

December 10 every year. The window opens November 10, and bills are mailed in the first week of November.

What is the final day to pay a Daviess County bill before it goes to the clerk?

April 25, at close of business. After that the bill moves to the County Clerk with added fees and can be offered at the tax sale.

Can I pay Daviess County property tax online?

Yes, through the Pay Taxes Online link on the Daviess County Sheriff's Office site, dcsoky.gov. Card and e-check payments carry a fee that shows before you confirm.

Who do I phone when my Daviess County value looks too high?

The PVA at 270-685-8474, to book the conference that Kentucky requires before an appeal can be filed with the County Clerk.

Does Owensboro bill its own property tax?

Yes. The City of Owensboro Tax Office, 270-687-8537, bills city tax separately from the county bill the sheriff sends.

Selling in Jessamine County?

Get My Cash Offer →

Jessamine County by the numbers

Which Jessamine County office does what with property tax?

The county splits the work in two. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a value on each parcel, and the sheriff sends the bills and banks the payments.

The PVA's own duties page lists what the office will not do: set rates, mail bills or take a payment. What it does is value property at full fair cash value on January 1, log deed transfers, update parcel maps and handle exemptions. The sheriff's office at 201 North Main Street in Nicholasville, staffed weekdays from 8 to 4, collects the state, county, school and district levies on real and tangible property and hands each share to the right body.

The PVA also lists tangible personal property, with returns due May 15, and logs building permits that the city and county planning offices send in each month. Call the PVA when your value looks wrong. Call the sheriff at (859) 885-4139 when you need a payoff or a receipt.

How fast has the Jessamine County tax roll grown?

The assessment roll has grown every year since 2013, and the 2026 total of about $6.71 billion is up 9.00 percent. Residential property is the biggest piece at roughly $5.22 billion, commercial adds about $1.04 billion and agricultural about $444 million.

Jessamine County assessment roll by year, as posted by the PVA
YearResidentialTotalChange
2026$5,223,249,119$6,710,234,7399.00%
2025$4,786,456,183$6,157,159,0837.60%
2024$4,418,399,761$5,722,955,01010.80%

Source: Jessamine County PVA, Assessment History.

Residential value alone climbed from about $3.65 billion in 2022 to $5.22 billion in 2026. A house bought a few years back can therefore carry a far larger assessment than at purchase, and each property class is reassessed on a four-year cycle, so a single bump may bundle several years of price movement.

How does the PVA sort Jessamine County property?

Four classes cover everything taxable. Where a house falls depends on its location and its acreage.

  • Residential: homes inside Nicholasville or Wilmore, whether single-family, duplex, townhouse or an empty lot.
  • County Residential: homes or land outside those cities on under 10 acres, sometimes with trailers, barns or sheds.
  • Farms: tracts of 10 acres or more, where agricultural value is set.
  • Commercial and Industrial: businesses on commercial or industrial ground, plus golf courses, apartments and trailer park land.

A farm owner who wants use-value pricing files by March 1 of the year in question, and horticultural land qualifies from 5 acres. The PVA describes the program as a way to keep farms operating and preserve farmland through tax relief.

When does a Jessamine County tax bill come due?

Bills reach the sheriff by September 15. Pay by November 1 and the bill drops 2 percent under KRS 134.020, then it sits at face value through December. January adds 5 percent, and from February the add-ons are 10 percent plus a 10 percent sheriff's fee.

After the close of business on April 15, whatever is left moves to the county clerk as a certificate of delinquency, secured by a lien on the parcel. The state revenue department describes monthly interest of 1 percent and attorney and clerk commissions from there, with a summer sale where an outside investor can purchase the bill. The clerk's website carries a delinquent tax search.

Check dates with the sheriff each fall, since Kentucky permits a delayed schedule in some counties.

What is the path for contesting a Jessamine County value?

First comes a talk with the PVA. Assessment notices usually go out in April, and the roll opens for inspection on the first Monday of May for 13 days, Saturdays included. The PVA office takes conferences by phone or in person at (859) 885-4931, and the notice and the Jessamine Journal carry the dates.

Bring something that backs a lower figure: an appraisal, photos, an insurance declaration, active listings or nearby sales.

  • Conference with the PVA during the open window.
  • If it fails, an appeal form goes to the County Clerk within one workday after the window closes, and a three-member Board of Assessment Appeals hears the case.
  • The last stop is the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals, whose members the Governor appoints.

Revenue officials add that the local board meets 25 to 35 days after inspection ends and turns away appeals that lack evidence. Because every step falls in spring, fall bills cannot be contested this way.

Which relief programs help a Jessamine County owner?

Owners 65 and over, and owners ruled totally disabled, can deduct a fixed sum from assessed value. The PVA's announcement for 2025 to 2026 lists that sum as $49,100.

One exemption per household is the cap. The age exemption stays on the books while the first applicant owns and occupies the home, and it leaves with them at a sale. The disability version needs a fresh application every year, per the PVA. File at the PVA office or mail P.O. Box 530, Nicholasville, KY 40340, marked "Homestead Exemption" or "Disability Exemption", with a driver's license or birth certificate copy and, for disability, a Social Security award letter or similar proof.

Churches and charities use Revenue Form 62A023. Owners of business equipment file tangible personal property returns by May 15, and late returns draw 10 percent or 20 percent penalties.

What do past Jessamine County assessment swings tell a seller?

The PVA's history table runs back to 1969, and it shows that the roll does not always rise. Looking at the longer record puts the recent run in perspective.

  • 2007 added 12.66 percent, the largest jump of the 2000s, and 2006 added 9.92 percent.
  • 2011 and 2012 each slipped by about 1 percent, the only back-to-back declines in the table since 2000.
  • From 2013 through 2020 gains stayed between about 1 and 7 percent a year.
  • 2024 added 10.80 percent, the biggest single-year gain since 2007.

Sellers who bought near a peak should not assume the next year's roll will match the last one. If a new notice looks out of line with sales on your street, the May conference is the place to say so.

What tax steps should a Jessamine County seller take before listing?

Start by asking the sheriff for a payoff on the current bill. The name on a September bill can still be the prior owner's, so agree on the split with the buyer in writing.

Then look the address up in the clerk's delinquent search for older years. If you hold the age exemption, tell the PVA about the sale so it can move to your next home.

Census numbers show why buyers keep arriving: 57,147 people in the July 2025 estimate, up 7.8 percent from 2020, with 22,061 housing units, a $268,100 median home value for 2020 to 2024 and two thirds of homes owner-occupied.

More questions about Jessamine County, KY Property Tax Guide

Does the PVA mail the Jessamine County tax bill?

No. The PVA only sets assessed value. The sheriff mails and collects the bill, and the PVA's duties page says its office sets no rates and collects nothing.

What is the discount deadline in Jessamine County?

November 1. KRS 134.020 gives 2 percent off for payment on or before that date, and the face amount is due through December 31.

Where does an unpaid Jessamine County bill end up?

With the county clerk after April 15, as a certificate of delinquency with a recorded lien and interest of 1 percent per month.

What does the Jessamine County age 65 exemption deduct?

The PVA lists $49,100 for 2025 to 2026. It applies to owners who live in the home, and the state adjusts the amount every two years.

Can I contest my Jessamine County value in the fall?

Not through the standard process. The PVA conference and the clerk filing both take place in May, before bills are delivered.

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky

Scott County by the numbers

Where does a Scott County, Kentucky tax bill come from?

Two offices split the work. The PVA fixes what a Scott County parcel is worth. The sheriff mails the bill and takes payment, and its own page insists the office never sets a value. It collects for 28 districts, among them the state, the county, school systems, fire and library districts and, by contract, some cities. Mailing normally happens on November 1. For a value you dispute, call the PVA at (502) 863-7885. For payment questions, call the sheriff at (502) 863-7855.

Georgetown adds its own levy. City hall's Clerk's Office takes payment over the counter, by post or by phone, and lookup and online payment run through the city's OpenGov portal. Bills from before 2025 are found through the city's Tax Master service. A house inside Georgetown carries a city bill in addition to the county one.

How is Scott County laid out, and what shaped it?

Scott County lies north of Lexington in the Bluegrass and is counted in the Lexington-Fayette metro. Lawmakers split it from Woodford County in 1792 and honored Gen. Charles Scott. Its 285 square miles include only 3.7 of water, and seven counties touch it: Grant, Harrison, Bourbon, Fayette, Woodford, Franklin and Owen. Georgetown holds both the courthouse and the largest population, while Sadieville and Stamping Ground are the two smaller cities.

The county grew quickly: 33,061 residents in 2000, 47,173 in 2010 and 57,155 in 2020. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 62,262, an increase of 8.9 percent since 2020.

  • Georgetown began as Lebanon, the name Elijah Craig gave his 1782 settlement, and was renamed for George Washington in 1790.
  • Elijah Craig, who led that settlement, is credited with early mills and possibly the area's first bourbon.
  • The Choctaw Nation operated the Choctaw Academy at Blue Spring in the county from 1825 until 1842.
  • Voters approved countywide alcohol sales in 2019.

Four interchanges on I-75 (exits 125, 126, 127 and 129) feed Georgetown from the east, putting Lexington roughly 16 miles south and Cincinnati about 69 miles north. US 25 crosses town and US 62 works as a bypass. Georgetown College is downtown.

How much does Toyota shape the Scott County market?

The 1988 opening of Toyota's Georgetown assembly plant, the company's first fully owned U.S. factory, set off the city's biggest growth spurt. Camry, Lexus ES and RAV4 models roll out of it. The city's 2018 annual financial report listed it as the top employer with 10,019 workers, well ahead of Scott County Schools at 1,219. The Census Bureau counts 26,711 jobs at county employers in 2023.

One district, Scott County Schools, serves the whole county: nine elementary schools, three middle schools and two high schools. Great Crossing High School and a new elementary school opened in 2019 as enrollment climbed. Relocating families ask about zones, so look yours up before you list.

How does Scott County housing compare statewide?

Prices here sit well above the Kentucky norm. QuickFacts shows a typical owner-occupied home at $288,500 and a typical household income of $85,158 for 2020 to 2024. Builders took out 393 permits in 2025, so a resale competes with new construction.

  • Households: 22,642, with an estimated 25,010 housing units by July 1, 2025.
  • Homeowners hold 71.7 percent of occupied units, and rent in the middle is $1,247.
  • Owner costs with a mortgage run $1,637 a month, against $514 without one.
  • Commutes average 22.2 minutes, and 34.7 percent of adults finished a four-year degree.
  • Poverty touches 8.8 percent of residents.

In 2020 the median resident was 36.2 years old, about two in three residents lived in urban areas and just 6.2 percent of housing units stood vacant.

Which Georgetown landmarks and conditions affect a sale?

After the Civil War Georgetown turned into a railroad hub, with lines tied to Cincinnati, Louisville and Frankfort, and Confederate General John Hunt Morgan raided the town on July 15, 1862 and again on July 10, 1864. Downtown falls within the Oxford Historic District, a National Register listing. Ward Hall, a Greek Revival mansion beyond the city line, has its own listing.

Near the old downtown, call the city before you plan any exterior work to prepare for a sale. Annual rainfall averages about 45 inches, and May is the wettest month at 5.26 inches, so gutters and grading deserve a look before showings.

Which dates and charges govern a Scott County bill?

The calendar comes from KRS 134.015. A 2 percent discount rewards full payment by November 1, the face amount applies through December 31, January adds 5 percent, and later payment costs 10 percent.

Whoever held title on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a delinquent bill leaves a lien on the land itself. Spell out the split in your sales contract so the closing agent knows what to deduct from your proceeds.

What happens when a Scott County bill goes unpaid?

Around April 15 the sheriff's unpaid bills move to the County Clerk. The county attorney writes in May, offering payment agreements to eligible owners, and again in June. The clerk's site lays out the path to the annual sale.

Scott County Clerk delinquent tax calendar
DateStep
April 15Unpaid bills transfer to the clerk
May and JuneCounty Attorney mails notices and offers payment agreements
June 30Deadline to sign a payment agreement
July 1Advertising costs attach to remaining bills
August 21, 4:30 pmLast chance to pay and stay out of the sale
August 24, 8:30 amSale in the third-floor Fiscal Court Room

Those dates belong to the 2026 sale, which has passed, and the sequence repeats yearly with the dates shifted. The clerk takes cash, cashier's checks, money orders and cards, and a 2.75 percent vendor fee applies to cards. For payoff figures call the clerk at (502) 863-7875, extension 2260, or the County Attorney at (502) 863-7870 about agreements.

Where do I go in person for Scott County tax business?

  • Sheriff (current-year bills): 240 Caleb Conley Way and 120 N Hamilton St, Georgetown, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm.
  • County Clerk (delinquent bills, deeds, motor vehicles): 101 E Main Street, Georgetown, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm.
  • County Attorney: 198 E Washington St, Georgetown.
  • Georgetown-Scott County Revenue Commission (occupational and business tax): (502) 603-5860.

The county Treasurer's page states that vehicle and property taxes are not collected in that office.

How do I contest a Scott County valuation or claim an exemption?

Kentucky makes a PVA conference the first step, and only after it can you petition the local appeals board, which wants comparable sales, repair bids or similar proof. An appeal does not suspend the bill, so pay on the value you claim while it runs.

The homestead exemption is open to owners past 65 and to those totally disabled, through the PVA. The state's deduction of $49,100 for 2025 and 2026 turns a $320,000 assessment into a $270,900 taxable base. The PVA can confirm the figure for the current year.

More questions about Scott County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which office takes Scott County property tax payments?

For the current year, the Scott County Sheriff's Office at (502) 863-7855. Around April 15 unpaid bills go to the County Clerk, and Georgetown's own city bill is paid through the city.

When was the 2026 Scott County tax sale?

August 24, 2026 at 8:30 am in the third-floor Fiscal Court Room. Payment by 4:30 pm on August 21 kept a bill out of it, and later years follow the same pattern with new dates.

Is there a payment plan for delinquent Scott County tax?

Possibly. The County Attorney mails a May notice describing agreements for eligible owners, and June 30 is the cutoff to sign one. The office answers at (502) 863-7870.

Does turning 65 give a Scott County owner the homestead exemption automatically?

No. File at the PVA, (502) 863-7885, with proof of age. The state deduction for 2025 and 2026 was $49,100.

Does Georgetown bill property tax separately from the county?

Yes, the city bills its own property tax. You can search and pay through the city's OpenGov portal or at the City Clerk's Office.

Kenton County by the numbers

Which Kenton County offices touch your tax bill?

Three offices share the job here. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) assigns value, the Kenton County Sheriff mails and collects, and the Kenton County Clerk inherits any bill still open after April 15.

The PVA says plainly that it neither sets rates nor creates taxing districts nor takes payments. Escrow questions and bill questions go to the sheriff, while the summer sale and delinquent lists belong to the clerk. The rate itself comes from the school district, city, county and fire district named on the bill.

The county has two seats, Covington and Independence, and the offices mirror that. The PVA's Covington office is at 1840 Simon Kenton Way, Suite 3300, weekdays 8:15 to 4:15. Its Independence office is at 5272 Madison Pike, weekdays 8 to 4 and shut from 1 to 2. One number, 859-392-1750, serves both.

What is the Kenton County tax collection schedule?

Collection runs from October 1 to April 15. The best price is the first window, which ends November 1 and trims 2 percent off the face amount, and penalties begin in January.

Kenton County Sheriff collection schedule
Payment windowAmount due
October 1 to November 1Face amount less 2 percent
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to January 31Face amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Face amount plus 10 percent plus 10 percent

Source: Kenton County Sheriff, Frequently Asked Questions. A weekend or holiday on April 15 pushes the close to the next business day.

Payment options include the sheriff's Covington counter (1840 Simon Kenton Way, Suite 1200), the Independence courthouse, Heritage Bank branches for cash or checks, the mail, and card or e-check payment online for a convenience fee. Mortgage escrow works too. Bounced checks cost $50. No bill in hand by October 15? Phone 859-392-1800.

How low is the Kenton County rate, and what does a bill include?

The county's slice is thin. In August 2025 the Fiscal Court voted to lower its real property rate from 12.5 to 11.5 cents per $100 of valuation, a fifth straight annual cut and the lowest since 1983.

The county's example makes the point: a home valued at $275,000 pays $316.25 to the county. The rest of the bill comes from bodies the Fiscal Court does not control. The county names school districts, the health department, the library and fire protection districts.

Cities add their own taxes. The sheriff's property tax page offers a phone list for city tax collections and notes that Morning View has no city taxes. Ask the sheriff for a line-by-line breakdown on any specific address.

For scale, the Census survey for 2020 to 2024 shows a $244,400 median value, and 70.7 percent of households own.

What is the review and appeal path in Kenton County?

Open with a review request to the PVA. The office accepts them any time after January 1, and that request doubles as the mandatory conference that precedes a formal appeal.

Conferences run by email or in person by appointment, and the Review Request Form can be filed online, in person or by phone. Proof is the owner's job, and the PVA's supporting documentation list shows what counts. Sales dashboards and a comparable sales map for houses and condominiums are posted on its site. Nothing is accepted after the inspection period closes.

  • The formal inspection period starts the first Monday in May and lasts 13 days.
  • For 2026 the PVA posted May 18 at 4:15 PM as the end of the conference period and May 20 at 4 PM as the filing deadline with the clerk.
  • A conference record, Form 62A307, must accompany any filing with the clerk.

The Board of Assessment Appeals is separate from the PVA and runs through the County Clerk's office. A loss there can go to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals, which answers to neither the PVA nor any taxing authority.

Which Kenton County areas has the PVA been reviewing?

The PVA's published Quadrennial Review Plan covers 2023 through 2026, so field inspections have moved through the county in stages. Each parcel gets a physical look at least every four years.

The PVA's home page carries a notice for owners in Elsmere, Erlanger, Fort Mitchell, Lakeside Park and Park Hills that inspectors are working their areas, and it lists the sales behind the 2026 re-evaluation for Bromley, Covington and Ludlow. The office also values about 5,000 commercial and industrial properties and prices motor vehicles at January 1 using NADA figures.

Anyone turning 65 in 2026 may qualify for a homestead reduction, and applications go in online. The exemption belongs to the owner and not the house, so a buyer applies separately after a sale. Totally disabled owners can apply as well. Business personal property returns are due May 15, with no relief from a tax filing extension.

What if a Kenton County bill is not paid by April 15?

Once April 15 passes, the sheriff stops and the Kenton County Clerk picks up the file. The bill turns into a certificate of delinquency with a lien, and fees plus 1 percent monthly interest pile on.

The clerk's yearly sale is held in July. A bill still open then can be sold to an outside buyer, and redeeming it costs substantially more. State revenue officials show the climb with a $1,000 example: $1,254 on transfer and roughly $1,388 if paid at the clerk's counter within five business days, before the county attorney's fee applies.

  • The county attorney's first notice goes out in the month after transfer.
  • A newspaper ad and a website list name the delinquent parcels ahead of the sale.
  • The sale is set 90 to 135 days after the clerk receives the bill.

For a seller, the practical point is simple: clear any old certificate before listing so the payoff does not surprise you at closing.

What should a Kenton County seller expect at closing?

A bill that arrives after a sale may still show the former owner, or both owners. The sheriff explains that the seller credits their share to the buyer or escrow agent at closing, and the owner of record then pays the whole bill.

Kenton ranks third in Kentucky by population, at 169,064 in 2020 and an estimated 175,779 in July 2025. Its 160 land square miles lie where the Licking meets the Ohio, and I-71, I-75 and I-275 all cross it. The county counts 74,593 housing units and a median household income of $80,548.

Median gross rent is $1,069 and 681 building permits were issued in 2025. Five school districts serve the county, from dense northern cities to rural southern areas. Thomas More University is the only college wholly inside the county, and Gateway Community and Technical College holds classes at sites in Covington and Park Hills among other places.

Industrial growth also feeds the tax base. Wikipedia reports that in October 2026 Niagara Bottling announced a $141 million beverage plant in Elsmere, on 52 acres at the C5 Airport East Logistics Center, with 60 full-time jobs.

More questions about Kenton County, KY Property Tax Guide

When are Kenton County property tax bills due?

Pay by November 1 for the 2 percent discount. Face amount is due through December 31, penalties begin January 1 and the sheriff stops on April 15.

Where do I pay my Kenton County property tax?

At the sheriff's Covington or Independence counters, a Heritage Bank branch, by mail to P.O. Box 188070 in Erlanger, online, or through mortgage escrow.

Who do I call if my Kenton County tax bill is wrong?

The PVA at 859-392-1750 handles value and exemptions. The sheriff handles the bill itself, and the PVA neither collects nor sets rates.

What is the Kenton County appeal deadline?

A PVA conference must happen inside the 13-day May inspection window, and the clerk filing is due one working day after the window closes.

What is the Kenton County property tax rate?

The Fiscal Court lowered its real property rate to 11.5 cents per $100 in August 2025. School, city, library, health and fire levies are billed on top.

What we could not confirm
