Who sets the value and who sends the bill in Clark County, Kentucky?

Two offices do the bulk of the work. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) assigns each parcel its assessed value, and the sheriff mails and collects the bill starting around October 1. The county clerk steps in after April 15 for anything left unpaid. The sheriff's own page says the office never puts a value on property: your bill is the PVA's value multiplied by the rate for each taxing body covering the parcel, such as the state, the county, a school district or a special district.

The county sits next to Lexington and belongs to its metropolitan area. It covers 255 square miles, and Winchester serves as both seat and sole city. If your house is inside Winchester, ask the city whether it bills a separate city tax and when. The 2020 census counted 36,972 residents, which gives Clark a bigger and more urban tax base than the mountain counties to its east.

Where can I pay a Clark County property tax bill?

The Clark County Sheriff's Office takes payment by several routes, and its 2025 taxpayer notice laid them out. The sheriff's office is in the basement of the Governor James Clark Judicial Building in Winchester, and the phone number for questions is (859) 744-4390.

Ways to pay the Clark County sheriff, from the 2025 County Taxpayer's Notice
MethodDetails in the notice
By mailCheck or money order to 17 Cleveland Avenue, Winchester, KY 40391; the USPS postmark counts, private meters do not
Drop boxCheck or money order in the box off West Broadway, with the bill number, map number or address written on it
OnlineDebit, credit or Google Pay through the sheriff's website, with merchant fees
In personCheck, money order or cash; cards with fees; weekday hours of 8:00 am to 4:00 pm
Bank counterA downtown bank branch on West Broadway takes checks and money orders for the exact amount, with the bill, and no cash

If a bill has not reached you by October 15, call the sheriff. A buyer or mortgage company that should pay it needs the bill forwarded right away.

What are the Clark County due dates and penalties?

They are the same dates every year, set by KRS 134.015 and printed in the sheriff's notice. Use them as a recurring calendar rather than a one-time list.

  • Through November 1: pay in full and take a 2 percent discount.
  • Late autumn through year end (November 2 to December 31): the bill as printed.
  • Every day in January: 5 percent is added.
  • February 1 to April 15: a 10 percent penalty plus a 10 percent add-on.

The county clerk takes over whatever is still unpaid when business closes on April 15. The sheriff's notice warns that payments at the clerk's office carry a 20 percent county attorney fee, a 10 percent clerk fee and monthly interest of 1 percent, and that delinquent bills can be sold to a third party. The county's own FAQ says the same: bills go out October 1, the face amount ends December 31, and collection passes to the clerk after April 15.

What do sellers find in Clark County?

An old settlement with in-town houses and working farms side by side. Records show settlers here as early as 1753, and the county was cut from Bourbon and Fayette in 1792. Railroads arrived in 1873 and the early 1880s, and once I-64 met the Mountain Parkway near Winchester in the 1960s, manufacturing moved in around the city.

The 2020 census found 14,917 households and 16,116 housing units. About 65.6 percent of occupied homes were owned and 34.4 percent rented, with 7.4 percent of units vacant and a median age of 41.5. The census counted about 71 percent of residents in urban areas, and the rest in rural parts of the county, where acreage and farm parcels change hands.

  • The Kentucky River, Red River, Lulbegrud Creek and Boone's Creek cross the county, so parcels near the water deserve a look at flood risk before you list.
  • Tobacco and livestock remain farm products across the rolling terrain.
  • Beer cheese began here, and Winchester hosts a yearly festival for it.

How can I challenge a Clark County assessed value?

Phone the Clark County PVA at (859) 745-0250 and ask for a conference before the public review of the roll ends. The review lasts thirteen days from the first Monday of May, and a conference is the required first step. You may hold it by phone.

Still unhappy afterward? Put a written petition in the clerk's hands by the next workday after the review closes, naming the parcel, your reasons and your estimate of fair cash value. A hearing follows roughly a month later. The board expects facts, such as sale listings, construction costs or loan papers.

Officials can also start a review. The county judge/executive, a mayor or a school superintendent may ask the board in writing to look at specific parcels, which is how some values rise without the owner filing anything. The plain plan: confer, file, bring comparable sales and pay on the figure you claim.

How does the homestead exemption apply in Clark County?

An owner who has reached 65, or who is totally disabled, can have a set sum removed from the home's assessed value. The state figure was $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, and a fresh amount is published every second year. A home assessed at $210,000 would be taxed as though it were worth $160,900.

File with the Clark County PVA. A birth certificate, driver's license or passport shows age. Disability claims require a federal or retirement system classification, and most renew yearly.

What if I sell a Clark County house with unpaid tax?

Title companies pay the balance at the closing table out of your price. Ask the sheriff what the current bill stands at, and ask the clerk whether an earlier bill turned into a certificate of delinquency. Under KRS 134.015 the lien from an unpaid year stays with the land for eleven years whoever owns it, so a buyer's title search will turn it up.

Clearing the balance before April 15 is cheapest, because the sheriff holds the bill and extras stop at the penalty and add-on. Afterward the clerk's percentages stack up, and an outside investor can buy the claim. An empty, inherited or run-down house can still sell to an investor who accepts it unrepaired and pays the tax out of the price. Ask for that payoff to be shown as its own line on the settlement statement.

At closing, ask the agent to divide the current year by the date the deed transfers, so each side covers its own months.

More questions about Clark County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which Clark County phone numbers cover tax bills and values?

Call the sheriff's office at (859) 744-4390 for bill and payment questions. For value questions call the Clark County PVA at (859) 745-0250.

When do Clark County bills get mailed?

Around October 1 each year. The 2025 notice said bills would go out September 30 and appear online, and that owners without a printed bill by October 15 should call.

Does the Clark County sheriff accept cash?

Yes, at the sheriff's office counter in Winchester. The downtown bank location listed in the 2025 notice does not accept cash.

Who sets the value of my Clark County home for tax?

The Clark County PVA, not the sheriff. The sheriff only collects the bill that results from the PVA's assessment and the local tax rates.

What if I miss the April 15 date in Clark County?

The unpaid bill transfers to the county clerk. There a 20 percent county attorney fee, a 10 percent clerk fee and 1 percent interest per month apply, and the bill can be sold to a third party.

What is Nelson County like for a house sale?

Nelson County became the fourth Kentucky county in 1784, carved from Jefferson County. It spans about 418 square miles of land. Bardstown, the seat, ranks among the state's oldest cities and counted 13,567 people in 2020. The area calls itself the Bourbon Capital of the World, and Heaven Hill, Barton 1792, Willett and Lux Row operate in and near town.

The sheriff's patrol area runs through Bardstown, Bloomfield, New Haven, Fairfield, Boston, Chaplin and New Hope, so one county holds several distinct town markets. Bardstown grows around the crossing of U.S. 31E, U.S. 62 and U.S. 150, with the Bluegrass Parkway just to the south. Wikipedia places the county in the Louisville combined statistical area.

Bardstown City Schools and Nelson County Schools both operate here, and the Archdiocese of Louisville runs Catholic schools. Nelson County High School stands within the boundaries of the Bardstown district, so buyers should check which district an address falls in. Summers in Bardstown run hot and humid and winters mild to cool, and a typical year brings about 52 inches of precipitation and 12 inches of snow.

What does Census data say about Nelson County housing?

The population estimate for July 2025 is 49,036, up 4.9% from the 2020 base. Of residents 16 and older, 63.0% are in the labor force.

Around 90.3% of residents had not moved in the past year, and 23.8% of adults 25 and over hold a four-year degree. With 222 permits, resale listings compete with newly built homes.

Which Nelson County and Bardstown features draw buyers?

The bourbon industry shows in the economy. The Census Bureau counts 1,023 employer establishments for 2023 with total employment of 17,214 and a payroll of $926,774 thousand, and employment grew 3.8% from 2022. Retail sales for 2022 reached $836,642 thousand, about $17,666 per resident, and medical and social service providers took in $202,154 thousand.

Bardstown adds history to the draw. Its Old Talbott Tavern dates to 1779 and is described as the oldest western stagecoach stop still operating. A Bardstown historic district carries a federal historic register listing, and the Civil War Museum is described as the fourth largest in the country. My Old Kentucky Home State Park hosts The Stephen Foster Story each summer. The Basilica of St. Joseph Proto-Cathedral recalls the 1808 founding of the Diocese of Bardstown, the first Catholic diocese west of the Appalachians. Residents travel an average of 26.6 minutes to work, and the Kentucky Bourbon Festival, designated the state's official bourbon festival in 2000, draws visitors to town each year.

How do Nelson County penalties stack up over the season?

KRS 134.015 gives the pattern, and the sheriff's page confirms the dates.

Nelson County Sheriff, what each payment date costs
If paidEffect on the bill
Up to November 1Two percent knocked off
Between November 2 and December 31Bill stands as printed
During JanuaryFive percent extra
February 1 through April 15Twenty-one percent extra

On a $2,500 bill the totals are $2,450, $2,500, $2,625 and $3,025, so a latecomer pays $575 more than an early payer. Anything unpaid at the sheriff by April 15 passes to the County Clerk.

The sheriff returns any check that differs from the bill by even a dollar, as well as late or partial ones, because audit rules demand exact accounting. If a lender escrows your tax, send the bill to the lender. The first proper payment received gets processed, and no refund goes to an owner who pays ahead of the lender.

How does a Nelson County owner challenge an assessment?

Begin at the PVA, which holds a conference with the owner or a representative. KRS 133.120 requires it before any formal appeal, and a phone call can count. The tax roll is displayed for 13 days beginning the opening Monday in May under KRS 133.045, and the conference must fall before or during that stretch.

A disagreement that survives the conference becomes a written petition at the County Clerk. It lists the parcel, the reasons and the owner's estimate, and it is due the workday after inspection closes. Hearings are public, and the owner supplies the facts: sales listings, insurance policies, construction costs or loan papers. The bill itself is not delayed, and an increase is billed with interest from the original due date.

Who qualifies for Kentucky's homestead exemption in Nelson County?

Owners aged 65 and up, and owners classified as totally disabled, are eligible. The state figure of $49,100 applies to the 2025 and 2026 years. On a home assessed at the county midpoint of $238,000, taxes would be figured on $188,900. The Nelson County PVA takes the filing, and a passport, birth certificate or license shows age. Disability claims renew each year, except for service-connected veterans and for owners ruled permanently and totally disabled by federal Social Security or the state retirement system.

What tax tasks should a Nelson County seller finish before closing?

The tax is a personal debt of the January 1 owner, and delinquent property carries a lien for eleven years under KRS 134.420. A buyer's title company searches for it.

  • Collect every bill for the parcel, including city and independent school lines for a Bardstown address.
  • Ask the sheriff for the exact payoff on the planned closing date.
  • Write the buyer's mailing address for tax bills into the deed, per KRS 382.135.
  • For an inherited house, the executor files an affidavit with the County Clerk naming recipients and values.

A New Haven or Bardstown city bill is separate from the county bill, so a payoff quoting only the county number leaves a gap.

On a bill of $2,500, a one-year gap in payment can mean hundreds of dollars in penalties, so confirm the payoff in writing and keep the receipt with the closing file.

More questions about Nelson County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which office handles a Nelson County valuation complaint?

The PVA, at (502) 348-1810. The sheriff does not assess property.

Does the Nelson County Sheriff take inexact payments?

No. A check that does not match the bill exactly, along with any late or partial payment, is returned.

What becomes of a Nelson County bill still open after April 15?

It moves from the sheriff to the Nelson County Clerk.

Do bills differ across Nelson County?

Yes. Districts 1, 7, 8, 11, 12 and 13 get one county bill, while districts 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9 also receive New Haven, Bardstown, Bardstown Independent School or Fairfield bills.

What deduction does a senior get on a Nelson County home?

The state subtracts $49,100 from assessed value for 2025 and 2026, after an owner who is 65 or over, or totally disabled, applies at the PVA.

Whom do Woodford County, Kentucky owners call about a tax matter?

Questions about what a property is worth go to the Property Valuation Administrator. Questions about what you owe go to the sheriff. The valuation office is in the courthouse at 103 S. Main Street, Room 108, Versailles, and the county directory shows it open from 8 each morning, closing at 4 Monday to Thursday and 5:30 on Friday. For the sheriff, the website gives 859-873-3119 and 859-873-3126 and has bill search with online payment.

A notice stating each property's value reaches owners in spring. Bills leave the sheriff's office in the last week of September, and overdue notices follow in February. The sheriff warns that the office never mails threatening demands for property tax, so a letter from an unfamiliar "unit" with an 800 number should be reported, and the demand ignored.

What should a seller of a Woodford County house know?

Woodford covers 192 square miles of the Bluegrass and sits inside the Lexington metro area. Versailles holds the courthouse and the most people, while Midway is the lone second city. Neighbors are Fayette, Franklin, Scott, Jessamine, Mercer and Anderson. Lawmakers created the county in 1788 out of Fayette County, Virginia, naming it for General William Woodford, and it was the last of Kentucky's nine original counties. Scott and Franklin later took slices of it.

Labrot and Graham, the 1812 distillery behind Woodford Reserve, is here, along with Midway University, the Kentucky Castle and a youth outdoor program called the Life Adventure Center. A royal guest stayed at Lane's End Farm in 2007. Public schools include Woodford County High and Middle plus Huntertown, Northside, Southside and Simmons elementaries.

The 2020 through 2024 survey paints an affluent market:

  • The middle owned home is worth $299,700.
  • A typical household earns $83,788, and 9.7 percent of residents live in poverty.
  • Seven in ten households own (71.7 percent), and 40.7 percent of adults finished a bachelor's degree.
  • Rent runs $1,138. Owners pay $1,571 with a mortgage and $577 without.
  • There are 11,917 housing units, and builders pulled 95 permits in 2025.

How has the Woodford County population changed?

Growth here has been gradual. Headcounts of 14,434 in 1970, 23,208 in 2000, 24,939 in 2010 and 26,871 in 2020 lead to a 2025 estimate of 27,883, a 3.8 percent gain. In 2020 the median resident was 42.9 years old, and a fifth of the county (19.4 percent) had reached 65. There were 10,736 households in 11,487 housing units, with 6.5 percent of units empty, and 62.8 percent of people lived in urban areas. The latest survey lifts the 65 and over share to 22.5 percent and puts Hispanic or Latino residents at 9.4 percent.

Commuters average 24 minutes. The 2023 business census listed 618 employer establishments, 7,913 jobs and $340.1 million in payroll, and 2022 retail sales reached $321.5 million.

What is a Woodford County owner's tax year?

It follows the statewide calendar kept by the Department of Revenue and set out in KRS 134.015.

Yearly property tax steps for a Woodford County owner
WhenStep
January 1Values are set, and the owner of record on that day carries the tax
Opening Monday of May, 13 daysRoll on public display

Source: Kentucky Department of Revenue, The Property Tax Calendar, and KRS 134.015.

If you list in spring, last year's bill is still yours when your name was on the January 1 roll. Ask the sheriff for a written balance so the title company can pay it off.

How does a Woodford County owner challenge a value?

First, sit down with the PVA office. The state demands that conference, and the office has to walk you through how it reached your number and write down what each side claims. Then take the appeal to the County Clerk before business closes on the workday after the display period ends. With a May 3 to May 17 display, for example, the last day is May 18.

  • Bring proof: building and lot details, insurance papers, what the house cost to build, and listings of sales. An appeal without it is denied.
  • A professional you pay to speak for you must be an attorney, accountant, broker, appraiser or someone similarly recognized, and must carry your written permission.
  • Audio recording of the hearing is allowed, and the board must put any change in writing.

If you skip the local board, the Kentucky Claims Commission is closed to you. Where bills print before a case ends, and the final value tops your claim, you receive a supplemental bill for the gap.

Why are some Woodford County parcels valued differently?

The method depends on the property. Houses are compared to nearby sales, with adjustments for things like a basement. Barns and other farm structures are priced as replacement cost minus depreciation, and income property is valued from its earnings. Farmland is assessed on its agricultural worth under Section 172A of the state constitution, which can cut the tax on open pasture sharply. Anyone planning to divide a farm should ask both the PVA and the clerk what changes when the use changes.

Any parcel can be revalued yearly, and each must be inspected at least every fourth year. If your figure looks too high, ask the PVA which sales it relied on.

What does the Woodford County homestead exemption cover?

Owners who reach 65, and the totally disabled, can have a fixed sum subtracted from the assessed value of the home they live in, one per household. File Form 62A350 at the PVA office. The exemption carries on while the same applicant stays. A veteran with a service connected disability rating, or anyone with a permanent Social Security disability finding, files once. A buyer applies fresh, and the PVA can quote the current sum, which the state revisits every two years.

What if a Woodford County bill is unpaid after April 15?

Once the clerk records the lien, interest of 1 percent a month starts. A clerk commission of 10 percent comes next, and a 20 percent attorney commission after that. The attorney sends two notices, one at 30 days and one later, ahead of a sale 90 to 135 days after the transfer. Under KRS 134.420 the lien can last 11 years and travels with the parcel. At a sale it is paid out of your proceeds, and a private buyer who purchases the certificate may add fees.

More questions about Woodford County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who sends out Woodford County tax bills each year?

The sheriff mails them during the last week of September. The sheriff's website lists 859-873-3119 and 859-873-3126 and provides bill search plus online payment.

How can a Woodford County owner push back on a valuation?

Schedule the PVA conference, then lodge the appeal with the County Clerk the next workday after public display ends. The PVA is at 103 S. Main Street, Room 108, in Versailles.

When does the 2 percent Woodford County discount stop?

It ends November 1. The printed amount is due until December 31, then 5 percent is added for January and 10 percent after that.

If a Woodford County house sells in spring, who owes that year's tax?

The January 1 owner is taxed and appears on the bill. The sale contract and title company decide who pays at closing, so get a written sheriff balance first.

What are good questions for the Woodford County PVA?

Ask which recent sales back your value and when staff last inspected the house. The answers tell you if an appeal is worth the effort before May.

Which Allen County, KY offices handle my tax bill?

Two offices share the work in Allen County. The Property Valuation Administrator appraises every parcel. The Allen County Sheriff is the one who gets paid. The PVA neither sets your tax nor takes payment: the bill comes from the assessed value times rates adopted by the county government, the school board and special districts such as the library and health department.

State law picks January 1 as the day property is valued and also as the day ownership is fixed for tax purposes. A house bought later in the year is billed to the prior owner for that year, though the PVA tries to mail the new owner a copy based on the recorded deed. The PVA's county web page says the certified tax roll and ownership information are posted online for anyone to check.

What does an unpaid Allen County tax bill grow into?

Costs rise in stages once the sheriff passes a bill to the county clerk. Revenue's worked example starts from a $1,000 bill. By the time the sheriff transfers it, a 10 percent penalty, an add-on fee and an assumed 4 percent commission have lifted it to $1,254.00. What are the tax payment windows in Allen County?

KRS 134.015 sets the calendar. A bill paid in full on or before November 1 is reduced by 2 percent. The printed amount applies through December, January brings a 5 percent penalty, and from February the penalty is 10 percent.

The sheriff keeps collecting until April 15. At day's end, every bill still unpaid is turned over to the county clerk and recorded as a lien against its parcel, which makes it a certificate of delinquency. A sale cannot happen sooner than 90 days later and must be held within 135. In between, the county attorney mails notices and the clerk advertises the list a month or more before the sale date.

An overdue bill leaves a lien that stays with the land. The statute keeps it alive until it is paid or eleven years run out, whoever holds title. Buyers end up with the problem, so a seller owing money should pay it or have it paid out of the sale price.

How do I contest an Allen County assessment?

Start at the PVA, because the state insists on a conference with the PVA or a deputy before an appeal is accepted. The real property roll is open for viewing for 13 days from the opening Monday of May, announced by the PVA in the paper with the biggest circulation.

Following the meeting, file with the county clerk no later than the next workday after viewing ends. A panel of local property owners then hears the case, between 25 and 35 days after viewing ends. Bring condition photos, repair estimates, insurance records and nearby sales. Evidence counts only if it is presented with you and the PVA's representative both present, and any change in value needs a written explanation.

You may make an audio recording of the hearing. If bills are printed while the case is pending, they use the value you gave. Should the board decide on a higher number, a supplemental bill makes up the difference.

How much tax does a typical Allen County house carry?

Kentucky's state real property rate for 2025 is 10.6 cents on each $100 of assessed value, lowered from 10.9 cents in 2024. For a house valued at the county's $192,300 Census median, the state's cut is about $203.84. Local levies sit on top of that figure, and the sheriff's tax bill search shows the full amount for any parcel.

An owner with the homestead exemption pays on $143,200 instead, which puts the state portion near $151.79. Neither number includes the 2 percent early-payment discount, which applies to the whole bill.

Who qualifies for the Kentucky homestead exemption in Allen County?

Send the application to the Allen County PVA, (270) 237-3711. Disability-based claims need yearly renewal. Two groups skip that step: veterans with a service-connected disability, and owners found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

What should I know about Allen County, Kentucky, before selling?

Allen County touches Tennessee and was carved out in 1815 from Barren and Warren counties. Scottsville is the seat and the only city. The Bowling Green metropolitan area includes the county, and bordering it are Warren, Barren, Monroe and Simpson counties in Kentucky plus Macon and Sumner counties in Tennessee. A fire at the courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records, which can make very old title research harder. Land area is 344 square miles, and 77.5 percent of residents live in rural areas.

US 231, a four-lane parkway, links Scottsville to Interstate 65 about 30 miles away, and the county's own business page puts Nashville roughly 60 miles and Louisville 120 miles from town.

The population has been climbing. The 2020 census counted 20,588 residents and the latest federal estimate, for July 2025, is 22,536, a rise of 9.5 percent.

  • Housing units: 9,390 as of 2025.
  • Owner-occupied share: 74.5 percent.
  • Midpoint home value: $192,300.
  • Midpoint household income: $61,403, with 14.3 percent of people below the poverty line.
  • Mean commute: 27.3 minutes, against 23.8 minutes in neighboring Adair County.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 17.

Households number 8,035, averaging 2.63 people, and 90.9 percent of residents stayed put over the previous year. The sheriff's office does more than collect: its county web page also lists enforcement of foreclosures, repossessions and tax delinquencies among its duties. Owner costs at the midpoint are $1,231 a month with a mortgage and $424 without, and gross rent at the midpoint is $844.

Permits totaled just 17 against more than 9,000 housing units, so resales dominate. A seller who has the tax account paid up and a clean deed of record faces fewer questions at closing.

Which Allen County office takes tax payments?

The sheriff does, as KRS 134.140 and 160.500 provide. The office at 194 W Wood St in Scottsville answers at (270) 237-3210. The PVA's role ends with valuation.

What is the penalty for paying Allen County taxes late?

Late payment costs 5 percent more in January and 10 percent more afterward. Once the bill reaches the clerk after April 15, monthly interest of 1 percent, commissions and fees join in, as the state's worked examples show.

Is the Allen County homestead exemption automatic at age 65?

No, you have to apply at the Allen County PVA. The state sets the figure at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. Qualifying owners must be 65 or over, or totally disabled.

I bought a house in Allen County after January 1. Who gets the tax bill?

The seller's name appears on that year's bill, since ownership for tax purposes is fixed as of January 1. The PVA attempts to mail a copy to the buyer. If nothing comes, call the sheriff.

It can slow one down. The lien stays on the parcel until the debt is paid or eleven years elapse under KRS 134.420, and a change of owner does not remove it. Obtain a payoff from the sheriff and clear it at or before closing.

Alton, McBrayer and the other crossroads places in this 202-square-mile county use the same two offices as Lawrenceburg, the only city.

Bills leave the Sheriff's Office in the final days of September and money is accepted starting October 1. Lenders are no longer mailed copies, meaning a borrower paying through escrow ought to ask the servicer in October if it holds a copy.

Richard Clough Anderson Jr., a legislator and later U.S. minister to Colombia, gave the county its name. A General Assembly act of January 28, 1854 changed the line between Anderson and Franklin counties, so owners near that edge can ask the PVA to confirm which county bills the parcel.

How fast does an unpaid Anderson County bill grow?

On its tax page the Sheriff publishes the statewide schedule from KRS 134.015. The accepted forms are cash, check and money order. Installments are refused, and a postmark earns nothing because the office needs the funds in hand by the date.

Anderson County Sheriff tax bill stages with the effect on the amount owed (andersoncountysheriff.com)
StageDatesEffect on the amount

Consider a made-up $2,000 bill. It costs $1,960 in the discount month, $2,000 in November and December, and $2,100 in January. From February the state's own sample shows the add-on being figured on the tax plus penalty, so the bill becomes $2,000 plus $200 plus $220, or $2,420. From best month to worst the gap is $460.

After that last day the bill is no longer the Sheriff's problem. At the County Clerk it turns into a certificate of delinquency. The Sheriff's page lists the extras: 20 percent for the County Attorney, 10 percent for the Clerk, and 1 percent interest each month. Summer can bring a sale to an outside buyer.

What does a $1,000 bill turn into at the clerk's counter?

Kentucky's revenue agency offers a model. A $1,000 bill, once the 10 percent penalty, the Sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission are included, reaches the clerk at $1,254. Paid in five business days it comes to $1,387.79, and after the county attorney's first notice, $1,611.30. Commission rates differ by county, so get a real payoff figure from the clerk.

The first letter goes out within a month of the handoff. KRS 134.128 puts the tax sale between 90 and 135 days after the transfer, with advertising in print and online.

The Sheriff handles everything until April 15. Afterward the clerk's website has a lookup called DTax for delinquent taxes. Its page says the data is informational and the clerk alone decides the actual dollar amount for each bill at the time of any sale. An owner with an old balance should obtain a written payoff from the office and not rely on a screen.

Is it worth contesting a valuation in Anderson County?

The order is fixed. Assessments speak as of January 1. The roll is open for 13 days from the first Monday of May. A meeting with the PVA or a deputy must happen first, and the County Clerk accepts the appeal through the next day after inspection ends.

About a month after inspection closes (25 to 35 days) the local appeals board meets, for five days at most. It expects paper: proof of the land and structures, insurance coverage, building costs and comparable listings. A bare filing loses. Staying home from the hearing ends the appeal, and a final value over your claim means an extra bill.

Does an Anderson County senior pay less?

The PVA takes homestead applications from owners who have turned 65 and from owners classified as totally disabled. For 2025 and 2026 the state subtracts $49,100 from assessed value, a figure reset every other year. On a house assessed at $225,100 it would leave $176,000 to tax.

Age is shown with a birth certificate, license or passport. A disability claim is renewed yearly unless the owner is a service-connected disabled veteran or has been found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

What has population growth done to Anderson County housing?

Anderson County had 4,520 residents in 1830, fell from 7,404 in 1860 to 5,449 in 1870, then rose to 14,571 in 1990 and 23,852 in 2020. An estimate for mid-2025 reads 25,225. Wikipedia calls it the ninth fastest-growing and 48th most populated of Kentucky's counties. Residents had a median age of 42.0 in 2020, and just over half (56.8 percent) lived in areas the Census counts as urban.

Houses follow people: the county held 10,652 housing units in July 2025, and builders took out 147 permits in 2025. Owners can compare their assessments with recent neighborhood sales before the roll opens.

About 90.4 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, and 94.5 percent of households have a computer, so most owners can look up a parcel online or call the PVA without much trouble.

  • Half of owner-occupied homes were valued above $225,100 (2020 to 2024 survey).
  • Households that own: 77.6 percent of 9,653.
  • Midpoint household income: $74,488; midpoint gross rent: $927.
  • Owners paid a median $1,391 a month with a mortgage and $411 without one.

Someone who bought last year can list the deed price as next January's value if the home is unchanged.

Who employs Anderson County homeowners?

In 2023 the county held 352 employer establishments with 4,175 jobs and $189.3 million in payroll. Shops sold $338.8 million in 2022. Some 60.2 percent of residents over 16 work or look for work, and the average trip to work takes 30.4 minutes.

Among adults, 90.5 percent have a high school diploma and 26.2 percent a bachelor's degree or higher. Broadband reaches 88.7 percent of households, 1,350 residents are veterans, and 22.0 percent are children.

The 2020 count found 9,369 households and 10,044 housing units, of which 6.7 percent stood vacant. Rental vacancy was 3.8 percent against 1.3 percent for owned homes, and 22.4 percent of households were headed by a woman with no partner present.

Alongside the 352 employer establishments, the county had 1,788 nonemployer businesses in 2024 and 427 employer firms in 2023, 99 of them owned by women. Households average 2.51 people. Building permits fell from the 192 Wikipedia lists for 2022 to 147 in 2025.

How do I clear back taxes before selling?

  • The Sheriff can quote the live balance, earlier years included. After April 15 ask the Clerk.
  • Have the closing agent clear arrears out of your share and record the release.
  • The deed must show where the buyer's tax bill goes (KRS 382.135).
  • Anyone with a homestead exemption should tell the PVA about the sale.

Behind on taxes and unwilling to make repairs? Request a written cash offer. Taxes and clerk charges are taken from the price at closing.

More questions about Anderson County, KY Property Tax Guide

Until what date does the discount last?

Through November 1. KRS 134.015 gives 2 percent off to a taxpayer paying in full by then. Between November 2 and year end the printed amount applies.

What happens if I wait until February?

Between February 1 and April 15 the Sheriff adds a 10 percent penalty and another 10 percent as an add-on fee.

Can I pay in two halves?

No. Partial payments are not taken, and a check that arrives after the cutoff counts as late whatever its postmark.

Where does an objection to my value begin?

Ask the PVA's office for a conference. The County Clerk cannot accept an appeal without one, and the filing deadline falls on the workday after inspection ends.

How big is the homestead break?

For the 2025 and 2026 years it removes $49,100 from the assessed value. Applications go to the PVA.

Who does what in Boyle County's tax system?

Three desks touch a Boyle County bill. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), at 859-238-1104, decides what the property is worth for tax purposes and processes exemptions. The Sheriff's Office, at 321 W. Main Street, Room 103 in Danville (859-238-1123), mails the bills and takes the money. The county clerk inherits any bill still open after the spring cutoff.

The clerk's delinquent-tax page spells out that the sheriff never puts a value on anything. A bill that looks too large is a PVA conversation, and the call is easiest before the check goes out.

  • Value, exemptions, name or mailing address on the bill: PVA.
  • Paying this year's bill or looking it up: Sheriff's Office.
  • Bills from prior years: County Clerk.

What does Boyle County look like to a seller?

Boyle County fills 183 square miles of central Kentucky around Danville, the county seat. Junction City and Perryville are the other two cities. The county dates to 1842, carved from Lincoln and Mercer counties, and Perryville was the site of the October 8, 1862 battle. Centre College stands in Danville. Neighbors are Mercer, Garrard, Lincoln, Casey, Marion and Washington counties. Business figures for 2022 give the county economy some scale: $725.7 million in retail sales and $471.6 million in healthcare receipts.

Census Bureau numbers for July 2025 put the population at 31,632, a 3.3 percent rise over the 2020 count of 30,614. For the 2020 to 2024 period, QuickFacts shows what a seller is up against:

  • Owner-occupied houses are valued around $209,900 at the midpoint, and 68.0 percent of units are owner-occupied.
  • Typical rent is $778, spread over 12,045 households.
  • The typical household earns $61,159, and workers spend 21.3 minutes getting to work on average.
  • The county logged 94 building permits during 2025.

When are Boyle County tax bills due?

The sheriff publishes a ladder of five cutoffs for each tax year. The 2026 version is below, and a postmark on or before the date counts.

Boyle County Sheriff's Office schedule for the 2026 bills (source: boylecountyky.gov)
Paid or postmarked byAmount owed
November 30, 2026Face amount less a 2% discount
December 31, 2026Face amount
January 31, 2027Face amount plus a 5% penalty
April 15, 2027Face amount plus a 21% penalty
After April 15, 2027Handed to the County Clerk as delinquent

Each year repeats this pattern with the calendar moved forward. The sheriff's Tax Bill Web Portal searches by bill number, map number, owner or address. Owner searches sometimes fail on reversed names, so try Doe John as well as John Doe.

Which school district bills Danville properties?

Street by street. Boyle County has two districts: Danville Schools inside the city and Boyle County Schools everywhere else. A handful of parcels inside the Danville limits still sit in the county district, so a Danville mailing address proves nothing.

Danville's property tax page explains the effect. A parcel in the Danville Independent district receives its school bill straight from the school system (859-936-8507). A parcel in the county district has school tax included on the sheriff's bill. Library, health, fire and similar special districts show up as extra lines where they apply.

What is the Danville city tax rate per $100?

Danville's 2025 real property rate is 11.9 cents on each $100 of assessed value, compared with 14.4 cents in 2017. Kentucky's own rate was 10.6 cents in 2025. The city reports taking the compensating rate every year since 2017, so the rate slid while assessments grew.

  • Real property: 0.1190 in 2025, 0.1220 in 2024, 0.1440 in 2017.
  • Tangible personal property: 0.1595 in 2025.
  • Cars, trucks and boats: 0.2000 in 2025.

House Bill 44 lets a city hold revenue level with the compensating rate or raise it by up to 4 percent after a hearing. Beyond 4 percent, voters can petition to recall the increase. A dollar total can still climb when the PVA lifts the assessed value under a lower rate.

Can I contest my Boyle County assessment?

A conference at the PVA's office comes first, and Kentucky offers no way around it. Values are fixed as of January 1. The roll lies open to the public for thirteen days in early May. After a conference you file the appeal with the county clerk by the close of the workday that follows the last open day.

The local board of assessment appeals sits roughly a month later, for up to five days. It wants evidence: nearby sales, an appraisal, repair quotes, insurance values or listings. Without it the appeal fails. An owner who never files locally cannot move on to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

Where bills are printed before the dispute ends, they use your own claimed value, with a supplemental bill if the board lands higher.

Who gets the Kentucky homestead exemption?

An owner aged 65 and up, or classed as totally disabled by a public or private retirement system, can knock a set dollar amount off the assessment of the home where they live. The state's ceiling is $49,100 through the 2026 tax year. Ownership and residence must both hold on January 1.

Applications go to the Boyle County PVA, which Danville names as the office for senior homestead questions. Send yours in before December 31. When your bill shows no exemption and you qualify, call the PVA before paying.

What happens when a Boyle County bill goes unpaid?

After April 15 the bill becomes a certificate of delinquency at the clerk's office and a lien attaches to the property. Interest accrues monthly at one percent, and clerk and county attorney commissions, postage and advertising pile on. The state's sample turns a $1,000 bill into $1,254 when it leaves the sheriff and roughly $1,388 within the first week at the clerk.

County attorney letters follow at about 30 and 60 days, and a sale of unpaid certificates to outside buyers can be set between 90 and 135 days after the handoff. A seller with old tax outstanding should ask the clerk for a payoff so the closing agent settles it from proceeds.

What happens to the tax bill when a Boyle County house sells?

Kentucky bills whoever holds title on January 1. A house that changes hands in March still produces that year's bill in the seller's name. Closing agents normally split the year between buyer and seller on the settlement statement, then either pay the sheriff or give a credit to the party who will. A lender with an escrow account does not get a bill automatically, so owners should forward it.

Houses that arrive through an estate, carry back taxes, or need repairs a retail buyer would balk at can sell directly to a cash buyer and clear the tax at the same table. Get the current figure from the sheriff and the older figure from the clerk before the closing date.

More questions about Boyle County, KY Property Tax Guide

Whom should I phone if my Boyle County assessment looks too high?

The PVA at 859-238-1104. The sheriff collects only, and the clerk handles appeal filings.

Is the Boyle County 2% discount still available after November?

No. On the 2026 bills the discount ran through November 30, 2026. December brings the face amount and January adds a 5 percent penalty.

Do Danville homeowners get one tax bill or two?

It varies. Parcels in the Danville Independent district get a separate school bill, while everything else, including Boyle County school tax, comes on the sheriff's bill.

What is the Kentucky homestead exemption worth?

The ceiling is $49,100 through the 2026 tax year, for owner-occupants aged 65 and up or totally disabled.

Can I sell a Boyle County house that has unpaid property tax?

Yes. Ask the clerk for a payoff on past-due bills and the sheriff for the current figure, then have the closing agent pay both from proceeds.

Which offices handle property tax in Grant County, KY?

A Grant County tax bill passes through three counters. The PVA decides what each parcel is worth. The sheriff takes payment on the current year. The county clerk takes over whatever bills remain after mid-April. Rates come from the levying bodies themselves: the fiscal court, the school system, and any city or special district that taxes the parcel.

The PVA keeps an office in the Williamstown courthouse, 101 North Main Street, and the phone is (859) 824-6511. The sheriff works from 212 Barnes Road, Suite A, weekdays from 8 to 4, and answers at (859) 824-3333. Checks can be mailed to PO Box 235, Dry Ridge, KY 41035. The county directory sends delinquent-bill questions to the clerk at (859) 824-3321.

City tax bills never go through the sheriff. Williamstown, Dry Ridge, Corinth and Crittenden each bill their own, so a municipal charge on a closing statement is a question for that city hall.

What is the payment calendar for a Grant County tax bill?

The sheriff mails bills and posts them online on October 1, then takes payment until April 15. Splitting a bill into two installments is not allowed. Cards work, with a processing charge from the card company, and a mail-in payer who wants a receipt encloses a stamped return envelope.

Grant County Sheriff's posted schedule for current-year bills (source: Grant County Sheriff's Office, tax collection page)
Payment madeResult
Oct. 1 through Nov. 1Two percent off the bill
Nov. 2 through Dec. 31Bill at face value
All of JanuaryFive percent added
Feb. 1 through Apr. 15Twenty-one percent added, as posted

The state law behind this calendar, KRS 134.015, sets a 10 percent penalty for anything paid after January. The sheriff's 21 percent for February through April 15 runs higher than that, so request an itemized payoff in writing if a contract depends on the number.

Why did my Grant County tax bill arrive in the seller's name?

The sheriff bills whoever was listed as owner on January 1. Buy in spring and the year's first bill still carries the previous owner's name. Deed transfers never reach the sheriff, which leaves the seller to pass the bill on.

  • Write the split of that year's bill into the purchase agreement, since the county does not apportion it.
  • Have the deed carry a c/o address for the buyer, as KRS 382.135 demands.
  • After recording, call the PVA and confirm the mailing address now on file.

If the closing agent pays the open bill from the seller's proceeds, the settlement statement should show it on a line of its own.

How do I appeal a Grant County assessment?

Nobody can file an appeal without first sitting down with the PVA or a deputy, which makes that office your first stop. Then comes a 13-day public viewing of the roll, starting the first Monday of May.

  • At the conference, the PVA walks through the method behind your value and keeps a written record.
  • Hand the written appeal to the Clerk before the office closes on the workday after the viewing period ends.
  • Collect proof: nearby sales, contractor bids, photos of damage, insurance papers, cost of construction.
  • Attend the board hearing, which falls within five weeks of the window closing. A no-show forfeits further review by the state Claims Commission.

An appeal without documents is denied by the board. Should bills go out before the board decides, your own figure is billed for now. A higher final value brings a second bill for the difference.

Is there a homestead exemption in Grant County?

Yes. For 2025-2026, owners who have reached 65 or are totally disabled may deduct $49,100 from the assessment. A Grant County house assessed at $250,000 would be taxed on $200,900.

Applications are made at the PVA, and the sheriff's office refers anyone asking about it there. A birth certificate, driver's license or passport proves age. Disability filers renew yearly, with two groups spared that chore: veterans rated service-connected, and anyone holding a permanent-disability finding from Social Security or the state retirement system.

Notify the PVA at sale so the deduction leaves your old address, and a qualifying buyer can apply separately.

What happens to unpaid Grant County taxes when I sell?

Back taxes ride with the parcel. The sheriff deals only with the current year, so a bill that crosses April 15 lands with the Clerk, and a lien is recorded against the property. A buyer inherits the lien, which can last 11 years (KRS 134.420).

Costs climb in steps. The state's worked example begins with a $1,000 bill. It arrives at the Clerk as a $1,254 certificate, and by the time the county attorney's first notice has gone out the payoff reads $1,611.30, after monthly interest, two commissions, postage and a $10 lien fee.

An auction of the certificate can happen from day 90 to day 135 after transfer, and the winning bidder may tack on charges. Get a Clerk's quote on the payoff before the sign goes up. With a cash buyer, the lien is paid at closing out of the price.

What else should a Grant County seller know about the area?

Grant County lies in northern Kentucky inside the Cincinnati metropolitan area. It was carved from Pendleton County in 1820 and has 258 square miles of land. Williamstown holds the courthouse, while Dry Ridge, Corinth and Crittenden complete the list of cities. Families here send children to Grant County Schools, with campuses such as Dry Ridge Elementary, Sherman Elementary, Mason Corinth Elementary, Crittenden Mt Zion, Grant County Middle and Grant County High, or to Williamstown Independent Schools, and the Ark Encounter in Williamstown brings in visitors from across the region. Seven counties border it: Boone, Kenton, Pendleton, Harrison, Scott, Owen and Gallatin. Public transit is limited to demand-response service from Senior Services of Northern Kentucky, and county voters approved full alcohol sales in a December 2015 special election.

Growth is the main story here. The census counted 9,999 residents in 1970, 22,384 in 2000 and 24,941 in 2020, and the 1939 courthouse in Williamstown has since been joined by a judicial center that opened in April 2010. Census QuickFacts reports:

  • A 2025 population of 26,181, which is 5.0 percent above the 2020 base.
  • Homeowners make up 75.1 percent of households, and the median home value is $209,500.
  • Median household income of $69,178 and a mean commute of 26.9 minutes.
  • Median gross rent of $862 and 110 building permits in 2025, with 96.7 people per square mile.

A cash purchase closes as-is, which can suit an owner with repairs waiting or a balance outstanding.

More questions about Grant County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who takes property tax payments in Grant County, KY?

The sheriff's office handles it, either at 212 Barnes Road, Suite A in Williamstown or through the mail to PO Box 235, Dry Ridge. After April 15, the County Clerk collects.

When does the Grant County early-payment discount end?

On November 1. Paying the whole bill from October 1 through that day takes two percent off, and face value applies from November 2.

Can a Grant County tax bill be paid in two installments?

No. The sheriff requires full payment of each bill, so pick a payment window you can cover in one go.

What does the homestead deduction take off a Grant County house?

It removes $49,100 from the assessment for 2025-2026. Filing is with the PVA at (859) 824-6511, and the owner must be 65 or older or totally disabled.

Must back taxes be settled before I list a Grant County house?

They can wait. The lien follows the parcel and is settled from the sale proceeds. Call the Clerk at (859) 824-3321 for the amount so your title agent can plan.

Which Grayson County offices deal with a tax bill?

Grayson's sheriff takes the money, and the PVA sets the value. The sheriff works from 117 S. Main Street in Leitchfield, KY 42754, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Central Time, phone (270) 259-3024. For assessed values and exemption papers the sheriff's FAQ points callers to the PVA at (270) 259-4838.

A third office enters once a real property bill is transferred. The Grayson County Clerk, at (270) 259-5295, quotes payoffs on those older bills. A buyer's title company will want to know which of the three offices holds each year, so keep the numbers handy before listing.

  • Current bills can be paid on the sheriff's online portal, by mail or at the counter. Cards are accepted in both places, with a processing fee.

  • No bill by November 10? Call the sheriff for a copy and give the property address and owner name.
  • With an escrow account, hand the bill to your lender and confirm later that the payment went out.

What should a seller know about Grayson County itself?

Rural west central Kentucky describes most of Grayson County, with Leitchfield serving as seat and largest city. Settlers got a county of their own in 1810, cut from Hardin and Ohio, and it now spans roughly 497 square miles of land. Caneyville and Clarkson are the other two cities, and Big Clifty is a census-designated place.

Two Army Corps of Engineers lakes shape the local market. Rough River Lake lies along the northern border and Nolin River Lake along the southeast edge, which is why businesses use the label "Twin Lakes." The Western Kentucky Parkway and US 62 carry most traffic, and the county runs its own airport. The 2020 census counted 13,275 housing units here, 21.4 percent of them vacant.

Fire has shaped the county seat's story: three courthouses burned, in 1864, 1896 and 1936. The county sits in Kentucky's Western Coal Field region, though only its western third holds coal, and it borders six counties: Breckinridge, Hardin, Hart, Edmonson, Butler and Ohio. Leitchfield voted to allow alcohol sales in 2016 after limited sales began in 2010.

The Census Bureau's county table for Grayson gives this picture:

  • Population: 27,406 in July 2025, a 3.7 percent rise since April 2020.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 74.6 percent, across 10,129 households.
  • Median owner-occupied home value, 2020 to 2024: $164,600.
  • Median owner costs: $1,274 a month with a mortgage, $416 without. Persons per household: 2.58.
  • Median gross rent: $658. Median household income: $50,757. Persons in poverty: 22.4 percent.

Someone dealing with a roof leak, a cracked foundation or a lien can sell a Grayson County house as-is to a cash buyer.

What are the 2026 Grayson County payment windows?

The sheriff's 2026 schedule opens the discount on November 1 and closes it on November 30. Face amount is due all of December, and 2027 brings the penalties. Kentucky's own default under KRS 134.015 is a discount through November 1, so follow the sheriff's published windows.

Grayson County 2026 bill windows and the fire dues amount deducted when opting out (source: Grayson County Sheriff's 2026 opt-out form)
Pay betweenStatus of the billFire dues deducted if opting out
Nov 1 to Nov 30, 20262% discount$40.00
Dec 1 to Dec 31, 2026Face amount$40.00
Jan 1 to Jan 31, 20275% penalty$42.00
Feb 1 to Apr 15, 202721% added$48.40

Whatever is still open after April 15, 2027 goes to the County Clerk. The sheriff's property tax page carries the schedule for each tax year.

What are fire and rescue dues on a Grayson County bill?

Many bills here carry a fire and rescue membership charge for the county's fire districts. An owner can drop it for one year by signing an opt-out form and sending the form in with the payment. The sheriff asks owners to call before paying online if they plan to opt out.

The form carries a warning for anyone who sells or leaves a house empty. Under KRS 75.450, an owner who opts out can be billed by the fire district for at least $500 or $1,000, depending on the type of facility, after a fire or other non-medical incident at the property. A new form is needed every year.

If you are listing, settle the dues question before paying the bill and tell the closing agent which way you went.

How can a Grayson County owner contest a value?

Book a conference with the Grayson County PVA first, since Kentucky closes the appeal door to owners who skip it. Call (270) 259-4838. Roll inspection lasts 13 days from the first Monday in May.

  • Expect the PVA to walk through how the number was built and to write down your claimed value and any agreed change.
  • No later than the next business day after inspection ends, take the appeal to the county clerk.
  • A local board hears cases roughly four to five weeks later. Come with repair estimates, insurance records, photos and nearby sale listings, because an appeal with no paper behind it is denied.
  • Missing the hearing forfeits the later route to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

A paid representative must come from the state's approved professions, such as attorneys, CPAs and appraisers, and needs your written authority. When bills were printed before the case ended and the board lands above your claim, the clerk sends a supplemental bill for the gap.

Can Grayson County owners get a homestead break?

Grayson County owners aged 65 or up, or totally disabled, can claim the break on the house where they live. For the 2025 and 2026 assessment years the state sets it at $49,100 off assessed value. At Grayson's Census median of $164,600, taxable value would fall to $115,500.

Take proof of age (birth certificate, license or passport) to the PVA. For a disability claim, ask the PVA which papers prove the classification and how often to renew.

After a sale, ask the PVA what to file so the break comes off the house you sold and can be claimed at your next home.

Who pays Grayson County back taxes when a house sells?

The parcel keeps the debt, so a buyer's title search will turn it up. Taxes are the owner's debt from January 1, and the lien on an unpaid bill can last 11 years whoever owns the house, per KRS 134.420.

At the clerk, interest accrues at 1 percent per month and commissions are layered on. The county attorney mails notices at the 30-day and 60-day marks. The clerk can hold a sale of the certificates 90 to 135 days after the transfer, and the buyer at that sale may tack on charges of its own.

Get two payoff figures before listing: the current year from the sheriff and any transferred bills from the clerk. Both can be settled at the closing table from what the buyer pays.

More questions about Grayson County, KY Property Tax Guide

When does the 2026 discount end in Grayson County?

On November 30, 2026. The sheriff's schedule starts the discount November 1, then shows face amount for December and a 5 percent penalty in January 2027.

Does the Grayson County Sheriff accept installments?

No. The office wants the whole bill at once and refuses partial payments. If a lender escrows your taxes, it can send the full amount for you.

My Grayson County bill never came. What now?

Phone the sheriff at (270) 259-3024 after November 10 and ask for a duplicate. Give the property address and the owner's name.

Where do I settle a Grayson County bill after April 15?

With the County Clerk at (270) 259-5295. Real property bills still open on that date move to the clerk, who quotes the payoff including interest and commissions.

Who takes homestead applications in Grayson County?

The PVA, at (270) 259-4838. Bring proof of age or disability. The 2025 and 2026 exemption takes $49,100 off assessed value.

What should a seller know about Hart County's land and people?

Hart County is cave country in south central Kentucky, and nearly nine in ten residents (88.3 percent) were counted as rural in 2020. Hardin and Barren counties gave up land to form it in 1819. It spans 418 square miles and has two cities: Munfordville, the seat, and Horse Cave, the biggest.

Underground features define the west side. Part of Mammoth Cave National Park sits there, and the Fisher Ridge Cave System, charted at roughly 125 miles in 2018, passes beneath Hart County farms. Amish families began settling between Munfordville and Horse Cave in 1989, and 2,486 people, about 12.9 percent of the county, belonged to that community in 2020.

History left a mark on paperwork. The Battle of Munfordville took place in 1862, and a January 1928 courthouse fire consumed some county records. A seller of an older farm who finds holes in the title paperwork can ask the clerk what survives for that parcel.

The 2020 census recorded 7,418 households, of which 27.4 percent were single people living alone. Of 8,816 housing units, 15.9 percent stood vacant. Wikipedia's county profile labels the northern borders with Hardin and LaRue counties as the Eastern time boundary, while Hart County itself keeps Central time, so confirm which clock your closing office follows.

Which counties border Hart County, and how fast has it grown?

Seven counties touch Hart County: Hardin and LaRue to the north, Green to the east, Metcalfe to the southeast, Barren to the south, Edmonson to the southwest and Grayson to the northwest. Each neighbor runs its own PVA and sheriff, so a seller comparing listings across a county line deals with a different office.

Hart County's population climbed from 18,199 in 2010 to 19,288 in 2020, a gain of 6.0 percent, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of 20,117 continues the trend. With 412.56 square miles of land, density works out to 46.8 people per square mile, up from 44.2 in 2010.

How affordable is housing in Hart County?

Census estimates covering 2020 through 2024 depict modest prices and a strong owner base. Owners occupy about 72 percent of homes, and the middle value sits at $146,000.

Hart County in figures, drawn from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts table
ItemHart County
Residents, July 2025 estimate20,117
Housing units, 20259,192
Homes occupied by their owners72.4%
Middle owner home value$146,000
Middle monthly owner cost, mortgaged$1,140
Middle gross rent$693
Middle household income$52,285
New building permits, 2025272

The population rose 4.3 percent from the April 2020 base to the July 2025 estimate. A Hart County household averages 2.62 people, and 89.9 percent of residents stayed in one house through the previous year. Among adults 25 and over, 81.2 percent finished high school and 12.2 percent hold a bachelor's degree. Broadband reaches 83.7 percent of households.

Employers numbered 276 in 2023 and supplied 4,073 jobs. Retail sales came to about $244.8 million in 2022, or $12,492 for every resident, and the average commute runs 28.7 minutes. The poverty rate is 18.0 percent, and 1,002 residents are veterans.

When is a Hart County tax bill late?

Everything is due by the last day of the assessment year, and KRS 134.015 adds a reward for early payers and a surcharge for late ones.

  • On or before Nov. 1: the bill shrinks 2 percent when paid whole.
  • Nov. 2 through Dec. 31: face value.
  • January: face value plus 5 percent.
  • Later: face value plus 10 percent.

The PVA can tell you who is listed as owner on January 1, since that date controls the name printed on the bill. Someone who closes in spring will probably see the first bill arrive addressed to the seller, so decide at the table who covers it.

What can I do if Hart County values my property too high?

Talk to the PVA, and if that fails, petition the county board of assessment appeals. The process sits in KRS 133.120, rewritten by the 2026 General Assembly with an effective date of July 15, 2026.

  1. Ask for a conference with the PVA or a deputy. Phone conferences are allowed on request.
  2. Still unhappy? Put the appeal in writing and deliver it to the clerk's office by the workday after inspection closes. Cover three points: your objections, the parcel's identity, and your own valuation.
  3. Show up at the hearing with documents: listings, comparable sales, insurance records, building cost or loan papers. A petition with no facts behind it is denied.

The board meets between 25 and 35 days after inspection ends (KRS 133.030) and visits the property when asked. Meanwhile you owe tax on the number you claimed, and the board's final number may bring a bill for the difference.

Can Hart County homeowners get a homestead exemption?

Yes, for a person over 65 or totally disabled who lives in the house. The Revenue Department's deduction for 2025 and 2026 is $49,100. Against the county's $146,000 Census median, taxable value would fall to $96,900. File with the Hart County PVA, and report a sale so the deduction ends at the old address.

What happens to unpaid taxes when a Hart County house sells?

Back taxes ride along with the land. A lien for delinquency under KRS 134.420 stays attached after a sale, which is why title searches find it.

Ask the sheriff for a payoff before listing. Once claims pass to the clerk, KRS 134.119 piles a collection fee on top (ten percent of the tax plus ten percent of the penalty), and an investor may buy the certificate and add interest. Closing offers the cleanest fix: the title company deducts the payoff from your proceeds.

How does transfer tax work when a Hart County house sells?

The seller pays a Kentucky levy of $0.50 on each $500 of price, or part of $500. The clerk takes the money first and records afterward (KRS 142.050). At $146,000 that is $146. The clerk's office on Main Street in Munfordville holds the county's land records, so call for the current recording charge.

More questions about Hart County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which office mails the Hart County tax bill?

The sheriff, at (270) 524-2341. The PVA supplies the value, and the clerk picks up claims the sheriff could not collect.

How large is the homestead deduction for Hart County owners?

$49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. It goes to owners over 65 or totally disabled who apply with the PVA at (270) 524-2321.

Does Hart County reward early payment?

Yes. Paying the whole bill by November 1 cuts it 2 percent. Missing December 31 adds 5 percent through January and 10 percent after that.

Do I stop paying while my Hart County appeal is pending?

No. Meanwhile you owe tax on the figure you claimed, and a higher ruling brings a second bill with interest.

Can a Hart County house with back taxes be sold?

Yes, with the debt settled at closing. Obtain a payoff from the sheriff and have the title company send it from your proceeds.

Where does an Ohio County, Kentucky owner pay the tax bill?

Property tax is paid in the sheriff's tax office, 301 South Main Street in Hartford. Checks sent by mail use PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347, and the phone is 270-298-4444.

The county's sheriff page lists weekday counter hours of 8 a.m.-4 p.m. and a half day (8 a.m.-noon) on each month's first and last Saturday. A drop box is mounted on the door for after-hours payments. Postmarks are honored on mailed checks, and cash should never go in an envelope. A card works at the counter, and the sheriff's website has an online payment link. Refund checks, for example after a corrected assessment, are mailed at the end of each month, and the tax office takes refund questions on the same phone line.

Values are set elsewhere. An assessment, address or exemption question goes to the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) at 270-298-4433.

How large is Ohio County, and who lives there?

Ohio County is big and sparsely settled. Its 587 square miles of land rank fifth among Kentucky's 120 counties, yet the 2020 density was only about 40 people per square mile. Hartford holds the courthouse and Beaver Dam is the biggest town. Centertown, Fordsville, McHenry and Rockport round out the cities, with Rosine as a census-designated place. Rough River runs through the middle, and Green River traces the southwest edge.

The legislature carved the county out of Hardin County in 1798, and its coal mines made it well known across the region. In January 1865 Confederate cavalry burned the Hartford courthouse, although the county records had been carried out beforehand.

The head count tells its own story. Ohio County had 1,223 people in 1800, peaked at 27,642 in 1910 and fell to 17,725 by 1960 as farms and mines shed workers. It climbed back to 21,765 in 1980 and has hovered near 24,000 since 2010 (23,842 in the 2010 census and 23,772 in 2020, with density holding at roughly 40.5 people per square mile). Census Bureau figures sketch the housing picture.

  • Population: 23,934 by the July 2025 estimate, a 0.7 percent gain over April 2020.
  • Value of a typical owned house: $121,400 (2020 to 2024 survey), with $1,105 in monthly costs for those who carry a mortgage.
  • Ownership: 77.2 percent of the 9,107 households.
  • Income: $57,798 for the median household, with 15.3 percent of residents in poverty.
  • Age: 20.6 percent of residents are 65 or older.
  • Supply: 10,377 housing units and just 3 building permits in 2025.

What are the Ohio County payment periods and penalties?

Bills become payable on October 1. The sheriff publishes the calendar below, and the assessment date behind every bill is January 1.

Ohio County collection calendar (Ohio County Sheriff's Office, property tax information page)
DatesAmount due
October 1 to November 1Bill less 2 percent
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to 31Face amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Face amount plus 21 percent
After April 15Bill transfers to the County Clerk

KRS 134.015 lists a flat 10 percent for that stretch, so ask the tax office to price your parcel exactly.

If October 10 passes with no bill, the sheriff asks owners to call and will send a duplicate by mail, fax or email. A copy sent elsewhere is a one-time courtesy. The PVA alone changes the standing mailing address.

What happens to Ohio County bills left unpaid on April 15?

Prior-year payments stop at the sheriff on April 15 and move to the Ohio County Clerk, at 301 S Main St, Suite 201 in Hartford (weekdays 8 a.m.-4:30 p.m.; recording desk 270-298-4423). The clerk's delinquent tax page announced a tax sale for October 23, 2025, which has passed, so ask for the next date.

  • The bill turns into a recorded lien, with 1 percent monthly interest added, according to the state revenue department.
  • Large-scale bidders (over three certificates here, five statewide or $10,000 in total) register with the state first.
  • A listed house with a certificate needs a written payoff from the clerk, since the balance grows each month.

Where does an Ohio County owner turn to contest a value?

Begin with the PVA at 270-298-4433, where a conference must happen while the spring inspection period is open. Bring comparable sales, repair estimates and photos. A failed conference leads to a form at the County Clerk, then a local three-person board, then the state Board of Tax Appeals. The PVA appeal guide spells out each deadline, including 30 days to reach the state board.

Which breaks reduce an Ohio County tax bill?

The homestead exemption is open to residents who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Per the sheriff's page, a 70 percent VA rating or a 100 percent Social Security disability finding can also qualify, and the PVA decides each claim. It takes a set dollar amount off the assessed value, revised on a two-year cycle, and the next owner starts a new application.

Working farmland is taxed on what the land earns from farming, not on market price, and that can matter a great deal where 76 percent of residents live in rural areas.

What does an Ohio County seller owe beyond the tax bill?

The seller carries the state transfer tax: 50 cents per $500 of declared value, rounded up (KRS 142.050). At the $121,400 county median that is 243 units and $121.50, due before the clerk accepts the deed.

  • Confirm with the sheriff who is paying this year's bill.
  • Ask the clerk about any recorded lien or certificate.
  • Put a tax-bill mailing address in the deed, as KRS 382.135 demands.

What do owners and renters pay in Ohio County?

Carrying costs are modest. Owners with no mortgage pay a median of $395 a month, and renters pay a median gross of $739. The average household has 2.58 people, and per capita income is $28,772.

The Census counts 10,377 housing units against 9,107 occupied households, so roughly 1,270 units are empty, seasonal or on the market. Self-employed owners are common as well: the county had 1,351 nonemployer businesses in 2024, against 371 employer establishments in 2023.

Which parts of Ohio County's economy affect home sales?

Retail, health care and transportation carry the local economy. Stores rang up $255.6 million in 2022, or $10,876 per resident, according to the Census. Health care and social assistance took in $111.7 million, transportation and warehousing $58.4 million, and lodging and restaurants $23.3 million.

Employers supplied 7,858 jobs in 2023, a 14.3 percent rise over 2022, and paid $265.2 million in wages. A one-way trip to work takes 28.1 minutes on average, and broadband reaches 85.1 percent of homes.

The people side matters to a buyer too. Nine in ten residents (91.8 percent) were in the same house a year earlier, so few homes turn over. Only 13.9 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, and 874 residents are veterans. Few homes change hands in any single small town, which makes pricing a house in Fordsville, Rockport or McHenry harder than in Beaver Dam.

More questions about Ohio County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Ohio County property tax?

The sheriff's tax office in Hartford, at 301 South Main Street. Mail checks to PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347.

When does a penalty begin on an Ohio County property tax bill?

On January 1. A 5 percent penalty covers that month, and any payment made from November 2 through the end of December costs just the face amount.

Can a house with an unpaid tax bill still be sold?

Yes. Payoff comes out of the proceeds, using a figure from the sheriff before April 15 or from the County Clerk after it.

Whom do I call to question my Ohio County valuation?

The PVA, 270-298-4433. Values are outside the sheriff's authority.

What transfer tax would a seller pay at the Ohio County median price?

$121.50 on a $121,400 sale, which counts as 243 units of $500.
