What do the PVA, clerk and sheriff each do in Marshall County?

Valuation and recording share one address, 1101 Main Street in Benton, where the PVA and the County Clerk keep offices. Collection of the bill belongs to the sheriff.

  • PVA: appraises property and takes exemption filings. The county directory shows 270-527-4767 as an alternate phone, with the office open on weekdays until 4:30.
  • Clerk: holds every land record in the county and, in the county's own description, collects delinquent property taxes. Call 270-527-4740.
  • Sheriff: collects county tax. A bill lookup and payment link sits on the sheriff's page at marshallcountyky.gov.

Tax collection is one job among several for the sheriff, whose deputies patrol about 300 square miles and more than 900 miles of road, work the lake with marine patrols, and provide court security.

A house inside Benton brings a second bill. City Hall, 1009 Main Street (270-527-8677), collects Benton's own property tax, and the city's website cautions residents against using its link for county taxes.

How did Kentucky Lake shape Marshall County real estate?

Water explains most of Marshall County's modern history. The Tennessee River and Kentucky Lake form its northeastern border. Of 340 square miles, 39 are water. It is the only Purchase-region county that does not touch another state.

The legislature split the county from the northern half of Calloway County in 1842. For its first century the economy was farming, and the population swung hard: 15,215 in 1920, 12,889 in 1930, 16,602 in 1940 and 13,387 in 1950. In the 1940s the Tennessee Valley Authority impounded Kentucky Lake. Fishing resorts followed, and low-cost power from Kentucky Dam brought chemical and manufacturing plants to Calvert City. The impoundment flooded Birmingham and Gilbertsville, and Gilbertsville was rebuilt west of its first site. The county then grew to 20,381 by 1970, 25,637 by 1980 and 30,125 by 2000.

Benton, the seat, is the biggest of the county's three cities, with Calvert City and Hardin the others. Gilbertsville is counted as a census-designated place, and Aurora, Draffenville, Fairdealing and Briensburg are unincorporated. A state marker near Benton commemorates a March 23, 1864 clash between Confederate and Union cavalry. Central time applies here, and part of the Clarks River National Wildlife Refuge lies within the county. Owners of lakeside or second-home parcels should ask the PVA for the property's classification and last inspection date.

Who lives in Marshall County, according to the Census?

Marshall County leans older: one resident in four is 65 or over. Owners live in more than four of every five homes.

Marshall County, Kentucky: Census Bureau QuickFacts figures behind this guide
ItemNumber
Residents, 2020 census31,659
Housing units, 202516,975
Households, 2020 to 202413,209
Share of homes owner-occupied81.6%
Median home value$173,800
Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage$1,248
Median gross rent$798
Median household income$65,831
Building permits, 202586

Housing units outnumber households by roughly 3,800, a gap that includes homes with no year-round household. Ask a local agent how many nearby listings are vacant or seasonal before you set a price.

The July 2025 estimate of 31,659 equals the 2020 count exactly. Poverty affects 10.7 percent of residents, and about 91 percent of adults finished high school. A bachelor's degree is held by 21.2 percent. Commutes average 23.7 minutes. In 2023 the county's 734 employer establishments employed 9,645 people, paid $600.5 million and added 6.3 percent more jobs than the year before. In 2022, stores sold $638.4 million of goods, health care and social assistance billed $77.9 million, and transportation and warehousing billed $62.8 million. A further 2,366 businesses have no employees. Veterans number 1,879, foreign-born residents are 0.9 percent of the total, and broadband reaches 85.5 percent of households. Density barely moved between 2010 and 2020, from 104.4 to 104.8 people per square mile.

Why were Marshall County's 2026 tax bills mailed late?

Rates had to be finalized before the bills could be printed, so the Sheriff's Office announced a collection start of November 1, as Marshall County Daily reported on October 9, 2026. The schedule it published:

  • November 1 to 30, 2026: two percent discount.
  • December 1 to 31, 2026: face amount due.
  • January 1 to 31, 2027: five percent penalty.
  • February 1 to April 15, 2027: ten percent penalty.

Such a shifted calendar is permitted by KRS 134.015(3), under which the Department of Revenue can swap in new dates when billing falls behind. In a normal year the two percent discount ends November 1, and the face amount is good through December.

Whatever the year, trust the dates printed on your own bill. When the cycle ends, open bills pass to the County Clerk, and the Department of Revenue says they then accrue one percent interest monthly.

Where does a Marshall County owner turn when a value looks too high?

Walk into the PVA's office and ask for a conference, the opening move in KRS 133.120. Still unconvinced? Put your reasons and your own fair-cash-value figure in a petition to the County Clerk no later than one workday after inspection ends, then prepare for the board hearing described in KRS 133.030.

  1. Gather neighborhood sales, an appraisal or construction costs.
  2. Attend yourself, or send someone with written authority.
  3. Keep paying on your own figure until the board decides.

An owner who bypasses the county board loses the later state appeal, so the petition deadline carries weight. Working farmland may qualify for agricultural-use valuation under Section 172A of the state constitution; ask the PVA about it.

Does Marshall County's older population qualify for the homestead exemption?

Many do. About one resident in four is 65 or older, so the exemption touches a large share of homes. The $49,100 deduction for 2025 and 2026 turns the median value of $173,800 into $124,700 of taxable assessment. File with the Marshall County PVA, attaching proof of age or a disability classification. The benefit follows the owner, so a qualifying buyer files again.

How do the lien and the deed get handled in a Marshall County sale?

A delinquency lien may remain for eleven years under KRS 134.015(5), so any unpaid year has to be cleared by closing. Because the Marshall County Clerk handles delinquent property tax, prior-year payoffs come from that office (270-527-4740) and the current bill from the sheriff.

Deeds are recorded with the same clerk, who first collects the grantor's transfer tax of fifty cents per $500 of value under KRS 142.050. On a sale at the county median that comes to $174. The clerk lists open hours of 8 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays, with 270-527-4741 as a second line and 270-527-4746 for the vault. The homepage also promotes protection against deed theft, which any seller should ask about after closing.

More questions about Marshall County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where can I look up my Marshall County tax bill?

Use the bill lookup and payment link on the Sheriff's page of the county website. For value or exemption questions, ask the PVA at 1101 Main Street in Benton.

Do Benton residents pay a separate city property tax?

Yes. The City of Benton collects it separately, at City Hall, 1009 Main Street (270-527-8677). The city's page says not to use its link for Marshall County taxes.

What was the Marshall County discount for 2026 bills?

Two percent on payments from November 1 through November 30, 2026, under the schedule the Sheriff's Office announced. Face amount applied through December 2026.

Which Marshall County office collects delinquent taxes?

The County Clerk, at 1101 Main Street in Benton. The Department of Revenue says interest of one percent a month starts once bills reach the clerk.

What is the Marshall County homestead exemption worth?

$49,100 off assessed value for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years, for owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who apply at the PVA.

Where and how do Muhlenberg County owners pay the Sheriff?

Payment happens at the Sheriff's Office inside the courthouse at 100 South Main Street, Greenville, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. The number is 270-338-3345, and the mailing address is PO Box 227, Greenville, KY 42345.

  • Bills normally go out October 30, and collection opens November 1.
  • Online payment is possible. Telephone payment is not.
  • A drop box behind the courthouse, near the elevator entrance, accepts payments outside office hours.
  • Only full payment is taken, so a part payment does not count.

Value is a different question and belongs to the county Property Valuation Administrator (PVA). The sheriff's own site says assessed values may change before they are final.

What shaped Muhlenberg County, and what does it mean for a sale?

The county covers 479 square miles of western Kentucky, 467 of them land. The Green River and Lake Malone are its two main waters. Greenville is the seat, and Central City is the largest community. Logan and Christian counties gave up the land in 1798.

Coal built the local economy. Kentucky's first commercial coal mine opened here in 1820 along the Green River at Paradise, and during most of the 1970s no other county in the country mined more. Surface coal has been stripped out, and what remains lies deep. The north is gentle hill country with river flats and bald cypress swamps along Cypress Creek. The south has higher relief, gorges and sandstone outcrops. Lake Malone State Park, with a 788-acre lake, sits near Dunmor.

Listings therefore range widely, from town lots in Greenville and Central City to ground near the lake and parcels in old mining country. One public school system operates under the Muhlenberg County Board of Education, and a single Muhlenberg County High School has served the county since June 2009.

How do Muhlenberg County Census figures read for housing?

The population estimate for July 2025 is 30,634, which is 1.0% below the 2020 base, and 21.3% of residents are past 65. Home prices are modest, and so are tax bills.

  • 13,640 housing units in 2025, with just 5 building permits that year.
  • Owners occupy 78.8% of homes during 2020 to 2024.
  • The Census midpoint for an owned house is $127,400.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,167 with a mortgage and $396 without.
  • Gross rent has a midpoint of $718.
  • Household income has a midpoint of $51,927, and 19.1% of people are in poverty.

About 88.7% of residents did not move in the prior year. With so few new permits, a buyer here mostly picks among houses that already exist.

Which Muhlenberg County economy details matter to buyers?

Buyers ask about jobs, schools and commuting. Coal mining in the county and its neighbors began to grow again as the 2000s opened. The Greater Muhlenberg Chamber of Commerce, created in January 2006 when the Central City and Greenville chambers merged, counted over 155 member businesses at the time.

The Census Bureau lists 537 employer establishments for 2023, and employment rose 6.7% between 2022 and 2023. Retail sales for 2022 were $374,858 thousand, or $12,212 per resident. Workers spend a mean of 27.0 minutes getting to their jobs. The schools consolidated in steps, from eight secondary schools to two high schools in 1990 and then to one. A sheriff's receipt showing the year's bill paid is the quickest answer to a buyer's first question about taxes.

What else about Muhlenberg County do buyers and heirs ask?

Many calls come from heirs, so some numbers help. The Census Bureau counts 1,758 veterans in the county, and 16.5% of residents under 65 live with a disability. Some 84.2% of households have a broadband subscription, and 14.7% of adults hold a bachelor's degree. Health care and social assistance brought in $144,467 thousand in 2022, and lodging and food service sales were $39,476 thousand.

Culture and services cluster in the two main towns. Central City has a convention center with an outdoor pool and spray park. Muhlenberg County Public Libraries runs the Thistle Cottage Genealogy and History Annex in Greenville, a useful stop for anyone tracing an old deed chain. The county lies at the southern edge of the Evansville, Indiana television market. John Prine's song 'Paradise' criticized strip mining here and refers to the community where the 1820 mine opened.

What are the Muhlenberg County payment windows?

The sheriff's posted dates follow KRS 134.015, with a discount first, the printed amount next and penalties after.

Muhlenberg County Sheriff, month-by-month bill totals
Month paidResult for the owner
Whole of NovemberSubtract 2 percent
Whole of DecemberPay the printed total
Whole of JanuaryAdd 5 percent
February 1 through April 15Add 21 percent

Whatever the month, the sheriff wants the entire bill in one payment. On a $1,200 bill the figures are $1,176 in November, $1,200 in December, $1,260 in January and $1,452 from February through April 15. Waiting the full season costs $276 more than paying early.

After April 15 the county clerk handles delinquent bills, so a seller with an old unpaid year should call the clerk for the payoff.

What is the route for contesting a Muhlenberg County valuation?

The PVA sets value as of January 1. Under KRS 133.120, the owner first meets the PVA or a deputy during the tax roll's 13-day public inspection in May, which KRS 133.045 schedules. Anyone still dissatisfied files a written petition with the County Clerk naming the parcel, the reasons and the value the owner proposes, within a workday after the inspection ends.

The appeals board will deny a case if the owner refuses to supply reasonable value information the PVA or board requests, so assemble sales comparisons, an appraisal or repair estimates early. Nothing about a filed appeal postpones the due date, because the bill stays payable on the normal schedule while the case proceeds. A taxpayer who never appears before the county board cannot reach the state Board of Tax Appeals afterward. Tax is paid on the owner's claimed value, with any increase billed later plus interest.

What exemption is available to older Muhlenberg County owners?

Owners 65 and up, and those totally disabled, can subtract $49,100 from assessed value for the 2025 and 2026 years. Applied to the county midpoint of $127,400, that leaves $78,300 subject to tax. The Muhlenberg County PVA takes the application along with proof of age: a birth certificate, driver's license or passport. Disability filers renew annually unless they are service-connected veterans or have been ruled permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

What should a Muhlenberg County seller settle before the deed is signed?

The tax is a personal obligation of whoever owned the property on January 1. A delinquent bill places a lien on the parcel for up to eleven years under KRS 134.420, regardless of owner.

  • Ask the sheriff whether this year's bill has been paid and in which window.
  • Put the proration in writing in the sales contract.
  • Enter the buyer's address for future bills on the deed, as KRS 382.135 requires.
  • When a deceased owner's heirs sell, the executor first files an affidavit with the county clerk naming recipients and values.

More questions about Muhlenberg County, KY Property Tax Guide

Is telephone payment accepted by the Muhlenberg County Sheriff?

No. The office takes payment online, by mail to PO Box 227, in person at 100 South Main Street, or in the courthouse drop box.

May an owner send part of a Muhlenberg County bill?

No. The sheriff's FAQ requires payment in full.

How long is the Muhlenberg County discount window?

All of November. The printed amount is due in December, and the penalty starts January 1.

What hours does the Muhlenberg County Sheriff keep?

Weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., at 100 South Main Street in Greenville. The phone is 270-338-3345.

What is the Muhlenberg County deduction for seniors?

The state subtracts $49,100 from assessed value for 2025 and 2026 once an owner 65 or older, or totally disabled, applies at the PVA.

Who does what with a tax bill in Russell County?

Four county offices share the job. The PVA, at (270) 343-4395, assigns each parcel its worth. The sheriff, at (270) 343-2191, takes the money. The clerk, at (270) 343-2125, picks up bills nobody paid in time. The county attorney, at (270) 343-2121, mails the warning letters that come before the clerk's auction of delinquent bills.

The fiscal court's page on the PVA says the office's valuations underpin the bills that finance local services. So a complaint about the number belongs with the PVA, while a question about where to send a check belongs with the sheriff.

What is Russell County like for a homeowner?

This is a lake-and-ridge county in south central Kentucky. The legislature carved it out on December 14, 1825 from parts of Adair, Cumberland and Wayne. It covers 283 square miles, with about 29 of them under water. The ground drops from 1,140 feet on Dickerson Ridge in the far north to 530 feet beside the Cumberland River. Jamestown has the courthouse. Russell Springs is the larger town, at 2,715 residents in 2020 versus 1,867. The 2020 census classed all of the county as rural.

Clocks here run on Central time, and the neighboring counties of Casey, Pulaski and Wayne to the east run on Eastern, so confirm the hour when a distant buyer or title office schedules your closing. The Cumberland Parkway passes through Russell Springs on the way to Columbia and Somerset, and US 127 ties the town to the lake and the Tennessee line.

  • Wolf Creek Dam, in the south, holds back the Cumberland River as Lake Cumberland. Water first rose behind it in 1952, and the shoreline stretches roughly 1,255 miles.
  • The Army Corps of Engineers began lowering the lake in 2007 because of seepage under the dam. A new concrete wall inside the structure was complete by early 2013, and normal pool returned in spring 2014.
  • Summer pool normally sits near 723 feet above sea level, with the tree line a little higher.
  • A January 19, 2016 referendum ended the county's dry status, 3,833 votes to 3,423.
  • A local telephone cooperative finished a fiber network in 2015 that made Jamestown and Russell Springs early gigabit towns in Kentucky.

Russell Springs began as a resort around a mineral spring and incorporated in 1936. Jamestown incorporated in 1826 and is named for a local landowner, James Wooldridge. Lakefront sellers should expect questions about the drawdown years. The county also elects a surveyor, a useful contact when a shoreline line is in doubt.

How do Russell County housing numbers compare with the rest of Kentucky?

Homes are modest in price and the stock is loose. The 2020 census listed 10,088 housing units, and 26.0 percent stood vacant. Only 5 building permits were issued in 2025, so you are not competing with new builds. Roughly 22.6 percent of residents are past 65, and a commute averages 19.8 minutes.

Russell County, Census Bureau QuickFacts (2020 to 2024 unless noted)
MeasureValue
Census count, April 202017,991

With a typical value near $163,200, the yearly bill itself is rarely the obstacle in a sale. Several unpaid years on an inherited house can still eat most of the equity.

Why do buyers come to Russell County?

Mostly for the water. Among the 383 lakes run by the Corps, Lake Cumberland ranks fourth for visitor hours, and over 1,500 houseboats float on it. Lake Cumberland State Resort Park and General Burnside State Park both sit on its shores, and the Wolf Creek National Fish Hatchery works just below the dam, inside Russell County.

  • County median age at the 2020 census: 43.8.
  • Share of occupied homes owned by their occupants in 2020: 71.8 percent.
  • Households made up of one person living alone: 29.4 percent.

Pair that audience with a clean paper trail: a current bill, a payoff letter if needed, and a plain answer on any back years.

When is Russell County tax due, and how much do late payers owe?

One statewide schedule, from KRS 134.015, governs. Full payment by November 1 earns 2 percent off. After that the printed figure stands through December 31. A 5 percent charge arrives in January, and 10 percent from February 1.

The clerk's page says bills reach mailboxes in October and the sheriff accepts payment until April 15 of the following year. By statute the tax is a personal debt of the person who owned the property on January 1, so your sales contract should say who reimburses whom.

What happens if a Russell County bill is still open on April 15?

The sheriff passes it to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency, and a lien goes on record against the parcel. That lien survives a change of ownership. The clerk's page commits to a sale before August ends, advertised in the paper and online. Private buyers who register with the state may buy the certificate and then chase the owner for payment.

  • Amounts on the clerk's delinquent list move monthly, so ask for a fresh payoff figure.
  • The state revenue department says interest of 1 percent per month runs on the certificate, with clerk and attorney commissions on top.
  • A title search will surface the lien, so settle it ahead of closing.

Can I challenge what the PVA says my Russell County home is worth?

Yes. Open with an informal conference at the PVA, which can be done by phone. If that fails, file a written petition with the clerk by the workday after the roll's inspection period ends. Bring listings, building costs or loan papers. The appeal does not freeze collection, so pay on your own claimed figure while it runs.

Who qualifies for the Russell County homestead exemption?

Owners 65 and over, and owners classified as totally disabled. The Department of Revenue set the deduction at $49,100 for assessment years 2025 and 2026, so a county home assessed at $175,000 is taxed as if it were $125,900. With about 22.6 percent of residents past 65, many local owners will want it.

Apply at the PVA. Disability claimants must show a federal or retirement-system classification and generally renew yearly. Ask what the figure is for the current assessment year, since the state revises it.

What changes at the closing table for a Russell County sale?

Closing agents usually pull the current bill and any delinquent payoff, so ask for both early. A bill open before April 15 sits with the sheriff, and after that date it sits with the clerk, plus extra charges.

Cabins used seasonally, inherited houses and homes several years behind deserve a written payoff from the clerk before you list. A buyer who spots a lien in the title search will demand its removal or leave.

More questions about Russell County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where does a Russell County tax payment go?

To the sheriff's office, at (270) 343-2191, through April 15 of the year after the bill. After that, unpaid bills sit with the county clerk at (270) 343-2125.

What does a late Russell County payment cost?

Five percent in January and ten percent from February 1, under KRS 134.015. Once the clerk holds the bill, 1 percent monthly interest plus clerk and county attorney fees are added.

Will a Russell County tax lien follow a house into a sale?

Yes. KRS 134.015 keeps the lien on the parcel until the tax is paid or the 11-year limit in KRS 134.420 runs out, whoever owns it. A title search flags it.

What month does the Russell County clerk hold the tax sale?

Before the end of August. Newspaper and website notices go out ahead of it, and the clerk's office can confirm the date at (270) 343-2125.

Is the Russell County homestead exemption automatic once I turn 65?

No. Take proof of your age or disability status to the PVA and apply. The 2025 and 2026 amount was $49,100, and most disability claims renew every year.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Spencer County

  • Spencer County Sheriff's Office

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Assessment questions go to Spencer PVA (502) 477-3207; sheriff office (502) 477-3200

Tax rate

Selling in Spencer County?
We buy Spencer County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Which Spencer County offices handle a property tax bill?

Three desks in Taylorsville share the work. The Property Valuation Administration (PVA) sets each parcel's value, the sheriff bills and takes payment, and the clerk's office picks up what is left after April 15. The sheriff's own website is blunt about the split: the sheriff never sets a value.

  • PVA, (502) 477-3207: assessments, exemption forms and questions about why a number changed.
  • Sheriff, (502) 477-3200: mails bills on October 1 and collects for the state, county and school districts, plus some cities and special districts such as fire protection and libraries when contracted to.
  • County attorney, (502) 477-3225: handles overdue bills from 7 West Main Street and sits with the PVA when an appeal reaches the local board.
  • County clerk, 2 West Main Street: keeps the certificates of delinquency and takes payment on any that remain unsold.

If the bill looks wrong, the PVA is the first call, and the sooner the better.

What should a Spencer County seller know about the area?

Spencer County covers 192 square miles, 187 of them land, and borders Jefferson County to the northwest. The legislature carved it from Bullitt, Shelby and Nelson counties in January 1824 and named it for Captain Spier Spencer, who died at Tippecanoe. Taylorsville became the seat in December 1824, and Confederate guerrillas burned its courthouse in January 1865, though the county records were saved. Elk Creek is the lone census-designated place, Kentucky 44 and Kentucky 55 are the main roads, and six schools make up Spencer County Public Schools, including Hillview Academy and Taylorsville Elementary.

The county sits in the Louisville metropolitan area, and Taylorsville Lake, mostly inside the county line, is a leading local economic resource. Few places in the country grew faster early this century: from 2000 to 2005 Spencer ranked 19th among all counties by percentage growth, at 33 percent. Headcounts tell the same story: 6,801 in 1990, 11,766 in 2000, 17,061 in 2010, 19,490 in 2020 and 20,998 estimated for July 2025.

Spencer County snapshot from Census QuickFacts, with 2020 to 2024 survey values unless a year is shown
MeasureSpencer County
Growth, April 2020 to July 20258.1%
Homes lived in by their owners87.9%
Typical value of those homes$330,000
Households7,308
Middle gross rent$987
Middle household income$102,618
Average trip to work32.7 minutes
Permits for new buildings, 202585

Those numbers describe a commuter county. Just 255 employer establishments operated here in 2023, with 1,345 jobs on their payrolls, while residents drive farther to work than in Taylor, Todd or Trigg counties. A seller is working with a bill built on a $330,000 typical value, the highest among those four.

What are Spencer County owners paying each month?

By Kentucky standards, this is a costly county to own in. Typical monthly outlay is $1,795 for owners carrying a mortgage and $532 for those who own free and clear. Households average 2.75 people, and nearly everyone (91.6 percent) stayed put during the last year.

  • Seniors account for 18.1 percent of the population, a group that can use the homestead break covered further down.
  • Minors are 22.6 percent, and the 2020 count put kids in the home at just over a third of households.
  • Roughly one adult in four has a four-year degree (23.6 percent), and the poverty rate is 7.5 percent.
  • Of the 7,430 housing units tallied in 2020, only 4.1 percent sat empty.

Shopping happens mostly elsewhere: 2022 retail sales were $79.0 million, about $3,910 per resident and the lowest rate of the four counties compared here. New construction runs the other way, with 85 building permits in 2025, the most of the four. Ask the sheriff for the exact figure on your parcel instead of estimating from the county median.

When is a Spencer County tax bill due, and what does paying late cost?

Bills carry a December 31 due date, and the sheriff's website says they go in the mail on October 1. The cost of timing is set by the collection statute:

  • Through November 1, pay 2 percent under the printed amount.
  • November 2 to December 31 is the printed amount, no more and no less.
  • January adds a 5 percent surcharge.
  • From February 1, the surcharge climbs to 10 percent and the sheriff's add-on fee joins it. The sheriff's page describes the February to April 15 stretch as a 21 percent penalty.

Escrow does not remove the need to look. The bill explains what to do when a mortgage company pays, and the sheriff's online lookup will show whether the lender actually sent the money before January begins.

What happens to a Spencer County bill that goes delinquent?

The county attorney lays the path out in order. Anything unpaid at the April 15 cutoff goes to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency, and KRS 134.122 puts a lien on the real estate. The county attorney notes the bill is also the personal obligation of the January 1 owner, with interest at 12 percent a year. Ninety days later, outside investors may buy it. The first offering is usually held in August or September.

Two things stop a sale: a payment agreement with the county attorney, or a foreclosure or bankruptcy case in which the county attorney is a party. The office also tries to reach the owner by regular mail ahead of any sale.

  • Still with the county: pay the full balance and accrued interest at the clerk's office, 2 West Main Street.
  • Already purchased: deal with the investor, who may tack on substantial administrative costs.
  • Payment plans: usually 4 to 8 months, and they must end before the next bill is due. Apply by the online form, by phone, or at 7 West Main Street, where an appointment shortens the wait. Sold certificates are not eligible.

How do I contest a Spencer County assessment?

Book a conference with the PVA first, because the process cannot begin anywhere else. After that meeting, the written appeal is filed at the clerk's office during the May window for viewing the roll, with a one-workday grace period at the end. A board of local owners then hears it about a month later.

The board wants paper: closed sales near you, an appraisal, a contractor's repair quote, an insurance declaration. If you bring none, it denies the appeal. A bill printed early uses your claimed figure, and a supplemental bill follows if the board lands higher. Ask the PVA which home sales it used for yours. That list is the fastest way to test the comparison, and parcels are physically reviewed at least every fourth year.

Who qualifies for the Spencer County homestead exemption?

Owners past their 65th birthday, along with owners on a total-disability classification, can knock a fixed amount off the assessed value of the house they live in. The Department of Revenue put that amount at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, so a $200,000 house is taxed as if it were worth $150,900. File Form 62A350 with the Spencer County PVA by December 31. An approved application carries forward while the applicant stays in the home, and a buyer must file a fresh one.

How are unpaid taxes handled when a Spencer County house sells?

Under KRS 134.015, a delinquent bill is the January 1 owner's own debt, and its lien can outlast a change of ownership for up to eleven years. Buyers and title companies look for zero balances. Ask the sheriff for this year's payoff, then ask the clerk if any certificate exists and whether an investor bought it.

When a payment agreement with the county attorney is active, say so up front so the closing agent can include the remaining balance.

More questions about Spencer County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who takes payment on a Spencer County bill?

The sheriff's office does, at (502) 477-3200. The county attorney's page points owners to the sheriff's website, Property Taxes tab, to look up the current bill.

What changes once the April 15 cutoff passes in Spencer County?

The clerk takes over, a lien is recorded, and interest begins at 12 percent a year. After 90 more days an investor may buy the certificate, so call the county attorney before that point.

Does the Spencer County attorney offer payment plans?

Yes, for certificates that have not been sold. Plans generally last 4 to 8 months and must finish before the next bill is due. Call (502) 477-3225.

How big is the Spencer County homestead exemption?

The deduction is $49,100 through the 2026 tax period. Owners file with the PVA before the calendar year ends.

Can I list a Spencer County house that has past-due tax?

Yes. The balance is settled out of the sale, since the lien does not lift until it is paid. Line up written figures from the sheriff and clerk first.

Which offices deal with a Whitley County, Kentucky tax bill?

Three offices share the work. The valuation administrator, known as the PVA, sets each parcel's value, the sheriff mails and collects the bill, and the county clerk handles whatever is still open in spring. The fiscal court's directory lists Property Valuation at (606) 549-6008 or 6009 and the sheriff at (606) 549-6006 or 6007. County offices share the courthouse at 200 Main Street, Williamsburg, and the sheriff's site has a bill lookup. The lookup opens your bill in a pop-up window, so switch off your browser's pop-up blocker before you search.

Whitley covers 445 square miles of the Cumberland Plateau, with elevations from 723 to 2,220 feet. The Laurel and Cumberland rivers cross it, roughly 38,000 acres of the west belong to the Daniel Boone National Forest, and Cumberland Falls, Kentucky's largest waterfall, drops inside its borders. Williamsburg is the seat and Corbin is the biggest city, reaching into Knox and Laurel counties. Williamsburg Independent runs a single K-12 school, Corbin Independent crosses county lines, and Whitley County Schools covers the rest.

What is the housing market like in Whitley County?

Prices are low. Five year American Community Survey numbers for 2020 through 2024 value the middle owned home at $131,800, while the typical household brings in $44,615 a year. Roughly two of every three households own where they live, and the county's 2025 estimate of 37,297 residents is 1.6 percent above 2020.

  • Housing units on the July 2025 count: 15,904.
  • Typical rent: $798 a month.
  • Monthly costs for owners: $1,156 with a mortgage, $346 without.
  • Permits for new homes in 2025: only 52.
  • Residents under the poverty line: 25.5 percent.

Coal and timber built the county's economy, and the 1883 railroad spur helped both grow. The 2022 business census counted $493.3 million of receipts in the health care sector, close to the $526.5 million of retail sales. The University of the Cumberlands is in Williamsburg, and Eastern Kentucky University runs a branch campus near Woodbine.

What is Whitley County's history and daily life like?

Whitley was carved out of Knox County on January 17, 1818, and named for pioneer William Whitley. McCreary County was split off in 1912, and the courthouse burned in 1931 before federal money paid for a new one. North Corbin has the cafe where KFC began in 1930. Corbin and Williamsburg are the two places with retail alcohol sales, and the county is otherwise classed as moist.

Population swings tell the story of coal and timber. The count reached 31,982 in 1910, slid to 24,145 by 1970, then jumped to 33,396 in 1980 and stood at 36,712 in 2020. The median age that year was 38.0, with 24.3 percent of residents under 18 and 17.0 percent at least 65. The census counted 13,794 households and 15,469 housing units, 10.8 percent of them vacant. Rural areas hold 63.7 percent of the population.

Newer survey figures show 83.3 percent of households with broadband, a bachelor's degree for 20.9 percent of adults, 1,124 veterans and a mean commute of 24.5 minutes. In 2023 the county had 629 employer establishments with 10,058 jobs and a payroll of $466.4 million. Williamsburg-Whitley County Airport (KBYL) serves the county.

How does a Whitley County bill grow when it goes unpaid?

The state schedule in KRS 134.015 runs from a 2 percent discount by November 1 to a 10 percent penalty after January. Whoever owned the house on January 1 owes that year's bill personally, so a spring closing does not erase it.

When the sheriff is still unpaid on April 15, the clerk receives the bill, records a lien and files it as a delinquency certificate. From then on 1 percent interest accrues monthly, the clerk adds 10 percent and the county attorney adds 20 percent. The lien follows the parcel for up to 11 years, whoever buys it.

Whitley's clerk then sells the debt to private buyers. Terms for the 2025 bills are in the table.

Whitley County Clerk terms for the 2025 tax bill sale
ItemRule
Sale dateSeptember 17, 2026, 9:00 a.m., courthouse Room 2
Registration closedSeptember 7, 2026
FormatLottery, up to three bills per buyer
Registration fee$10 per certificate, capped at $250 for 25 or more
Deposit25 percent of the certificates listed

Source: Whitley County Clerk, Delinquent Taxes. The clerk takes no payments on the morning of the sale. Whoever buys your certificate collects from you and may add fees.

Buyers with a stake in an earlier year can file a priority list, which needs a $5 fee per certificate and a deposit of the full price, and every certificate carries a $30 filing charge. A buyer who wants more than three certificates in the county, more than five statewide or more than $10,000 worth must also enroll with the state revenue department. A seller with a delinquent parcel should clear it with the clerk before the sale date, because paying off the lien is cheaper than paying a buyer who tacks on fees.

How do you contest a Whitley County assessment?

Meet the PVA first, since Kentucky bars an appeal without that meeting. Values are fixed as of January 1, the roll lies open to the public for 13 days starting with the first May Monday, and the meeting belongs inside that stretch.

Then file with the County Clerk no later than the following workday. A local board hears the case 25 to 35 days later and dismisses anything that comes without proof.

  • Recent sales of nearby houses like yours.
  • Photos and repair quotes where the house has defects the record misses.
  • Insurance or construction cost papers.

Before you file, ask which sales the PVA used on your parcel.

Who qualifies for the homestead exemption in Whitley County?

Homeowners at least 65 years old, and the totally disabled, subtract a fixed amount from the assessed value of the home they live in. A couple gets one deduction. File form 62A350 at the PVA office; an approved claim carries forward while the same owner stays. A buyer must apply again, and the PVA can quote the current deduction, which the state resets every two years.

What should a Whitley County seller confirm before closing?

Treat the tax like a payoff, alongside any mortgage. The title company asks the sheriff and the clerk for balances, and both come out of what you receive.

  • Match the name on the bill to the deed.
  • Look for a bill on a garage, mobile home or other addition missing from earlier rolls.
  • On an inherited house, check whether the bill was mailed to someone who has died.
  • Ask the clerk if an earlier year was sold to a private buyer.

Get each balance in writing so the payoff matches the closing statement.

More questions about Whitley County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where does a Whitley County owner send the tax payment?

To the sheriff, whose site offers an online lookup and whose office the fiscal court lists at (606) 549-6006 or 6007. After April 15 the bill sits with the County Clerk.

Is it too late to pay a Whitley County bill after January?

No, but the cost rises. A 10 percent penalty applies after January, and after April 15 monthly interest and commissions come on top.

Can a Whitley County owner sell with a delinquent bill?

Yes. The title company gets the figures from the sheriff and clerk, and the balance is subtracted from what you receive. The lien stays until it is cleared.

When must a Whitley County assessment appeal be filed?

No later than the workday after the roll inspection ends. The roll opens for 13 days beginning the first May Monday, and you must meet the PVA before filing.

Which Whitley County office answers valuation questions?

Property Valuation, listed at (606) 549-6008 or 6009. The sheriff covers the amount due, and the clerk covers delinquent bills.

Henderson County by the numbers

Which Henderson County, KY office does what with a tax bill?

Three county offices take turns with the same bill. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) fixes what a parcel is worth, the Sheriff's Office sends the bill and takes payment, and the County Clerk's Office keeps whatever is left unpaid.

The county attorney's tax collection FAQ gives the timeline. Real estate notices are mailed in late October or early November, and the sheriff accepts payment from November 1. A bill turns delinquent on January 1 after its due date. The sheriff holds the file until uncollected bills are turned over to the clerk, and from that point the clerk's office maintains them.

The county's own wording ties delinquency to two conditions: the due date has passed and any appeal rights have expired. A seller with an unresolved value dispute should therefore treat the appeal calendar and the payment calendar as running side by side.

What sets Henderson County apart from other Kentucky counties?

Henderson County sits in far western Kentucky on the Ohio River, facing Evansville, Indiana, and it is part of the Evansville, IN-KY metropolitan area. Its seat and largest city is Henderson, which grew from a riverside settlement called Red Banks. The county was carved out of Christian County in December 1798 and named for Richard Henderson of the Transylvania Company.

It measures 466 square miles, about 30 of which are water, and lies in the West Kentucky Coal Field. Corydon and Robards are the other incorporated cities, and Anthoston, Poole and Spottsville are census-designated places. Roughly 45 square miles called Green River Island lie on the Indiana bank yet belong to Henderson County, and Ellis Park Race Course occupies part of that ground.

Tobacco built the early town. Around 1880 Henderson counted 17 stemmeries and was the largest dark tobacco market in the world, and production fell through the twentieth century. The 2020 count of 44,793 residents was 3.2 percent below 2010.

Population density is 102.7 people per square mile, and 63.5 percent of residents lived in urban areas at the 2020 census. Hart County, by comparison, was 11.7 percent urban, so a Henderson seller is marketing in a far more urban county.

What local resources matter when you sell in Henderson County?

The county's links page lists the agencies a seller or buyer is likely to contact.

  • The Henderson City-County Planning Commission oversees public and private development inside both city and county limits.
  • Henderson GIS offers maps, data and information on the county.
  • Henderson County Schools and Henderson Community College anchor education.
  • The Henderson County Riverport and the Henderson City-County Airport, a general aviation field, serve industry and business users.
  • Audubon State Park, the Tourist Commission and the Downtown Henderson Partnership, begun in 1986 with Main Street program support, cover recreation and downtown life.
  • The Henderson Area Board of Realtors and the Housing Authority of Henderson are listed among community organizations.

If a buyer asks about zoning or development near your parcel, point them to the planning commission, and send questions about the tax bill itself to the sheriff or PVA.

How do Henderson County housing figures read?

The typical Henderson County home is valued above Hart County's $146,000 and below Henry County's $197,900. About 37 percent of occupied homes were rented at the 2020 census, which is a meaningful rental market next to the owner-occupied majority.

Henderson County at a glance, from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts estimates
ItemHenderson County
Residents, July 2025 estimate44,255
Housing units, 202520,295
Homes occupied by their owners64.9%

The county employed 16,375 people at 966 employer establishments in 2023. Retail sales in 2022 were about $763 million and health care and social assistance receipts about $312 million. Of adults 25 and over, 89.7 percent finished high school and 20.1 percent have a bachelor's degree. The poverty rate is 15.7 percent, and 7.2 percent of residents under 65 lack health insurance.

What happens after a Henderson County bill goes delinquent?

Interest and penalties begin, a lien attaches, and an outside buyer may purchase the debt. The county attorney's tax collection FAQ describes each stage.

  • The bill moves to the County Clerk's Office at 20 N Main Street, 2nd Floor, Henderson, where interest of 1 percent per month and penalties accumulate.
  • A lien stays on the property until payment in full.
  • Any individual or company qualified under KRS Chapter 134 may buy the bill at the clerk's tax sale. The clerk cannot predict or prevent that purchase.
  • The purchaser has 50 days to notify the owner. The owner then pays the purchaser, who sends a release to the clerk for recording.
  • A foreclosure suit by the purchaser becomes possible one year after the certificate of delinquency was created.

You can pay the clerk in person or mail a personal check, cashier's check, money order or certified check. Cards work for an added fee, and the clerk's number for details is 270-827-5753. American Express, Discover and MasterCard are taken, and Visa only as a debit.

Who can contest a Henderson County assessment, and how?

The owner starts with a conference at the PVA's office, a step KRS 133.120 places ahead of any formal appeal. The conference happens during or before the inspection window, and the Department of Revenue may allow up to 25 extra days.

If that fails, a written petition goes to the county clerk, and the appeals board holds a public hearing and fixes fair cash value. The county attorney speaks for the state and county there. Someone who loses may go on to the Board of Tax Appeals, but only after appearing before the county board.

Paid representatives must fall into listed categories such as attorney, accountant, tax consultant, owner's employee, broker or certified appraiser. They carry written authorization and disclose any contingency fee, although attorneys need not state its terms. The board can also raise a value, but it must first send the owner notice and a hearing date.

How should a seller handle taxes at a Henderson County closing?

Ownership on January 1 decides whose name goes on the year's bill, and under KRS 134.015 the debt is personal to that owner while a delinquency lien under KRS 134.420 outlasts any sale. Line up both numbers before the closing date: what the sheriff shows for the current year and what the clerk shows for earlier ones.

If a prior year sits with the clerk, the 1 percent monthly interest becomes part of the payoff, so ask for a fresh figure close to the signing. The title agent can pay the total out of your proceeds. For recording charges and the real estate transfer tax on the deed, see the Henderson County Clerk page, which lists the current fee schedule.

More questions about Henderson County, KY Property Tax Guide

When does Henderson County start taking property tax payments?

November 1. Notices go out in late October or early November, and the sheriff accepts payment beginning that day. A bill goes delinquent on the following January 1.

Where is a delinquent Henderson County bill paid?

At the County Clerk's Office, 20 N Main Street, 2nd Floor Offices, Henderson, KY 42420. Mailed payments must be a check, money order or other certified funds.

How much interest does the clerk charge on a delinquent bill?

One percent per month plus penalties. A buyer of the bill at the tax sale may add charges allowed under Kentucky law.

Can someone else buy my delinquent Henderson County tax bill?

Yes. Any person or company qualified under KRS Chapter 134 can buy it at the clerk's sale, and the clerk can neither predict nor stop the purchase.

How long before a bill buyer can foreclose?

One year after the certificate of delinquency is created. Some buyers wait longer while the property's equity covers the debt.

  • Sheriff: (502) 845-2909. This office sends and collects the current bill, and the PVA's website links to a bill search.

The PVA's site explains the January 1 rule in plain terms. Property is assessed on that date, and ownership for tax purposes is fixed on that date too. Buy a house in June and the state bill that year still goes out under the previous owner's name, with the new year bringing the change. The office tries to mail a copy to the new owner using the recorded deed, and a buyer who sees nothing can phone the sheriff.

Why do Louisville commuters look at Henry County?

Henry County is a farm and commuter county in north central Kentucky that has served as an exurb of the Louisville area since the 1990s, partly because land in neighboring Oldham County grew more expensive. The county was cut from Shelby County in 1798 and carries the name of a Virginia governor from the Revolutionary generation.

New Castle holds the courthouse, while Eminence is the largest city. Campbellsburg, Smithfield and Pleasureville (partly in Shelby County) complete the list of cities. The county covers 291 square miles, touches the Kentucky River, and is surrounded by Carroll, Owen, Franklin, Shelby, Oldham and Trimble counties. Every resident counted in 2020 lived in a rural area.

The population went from 15,678 in the 2020 census to an estimated 16,447 in 2025, up 4.9 percent. Two school systems serve the county, Henry County Schools and the Eminence Independent district, so check which one covers an address when you write a listing. The county keeps Eastern time, and the average trip to work lasts 30.5 minutes.

Outside the five cities, named communities include Bethlehem, Lockport, Pendleton, Port Royal, Sulphur and Turners Station. The county counted 15,416 people in 2010, so the 2025 estimate marks growth of about 1,000 residents over fifteen years.

Who lives in Henry County, and who is likely to buy?

The 2020 census put the median age at 42.0 years. Of residents, 22.8 percent were under 18 and 18.8 percent were 65 or older, and the QuickFacts estimate for 65 and over has since risen to 20.9 percent. That older group is the one the homestead deduction below is aimed at.

The same census counted 6,099 households and 6,600 housing units, of which 7.6 percent were vacant. Vacancy among owner-held homes was 1.4 percent and among rentals 5.0 percent. Households with a computer made up 88.5 percent of the total in 2020 to 2024, and 83.7 percent had broadband. Nine in ten residents (89.5 percent) had not moved within the previous year, and 941 are veterans.

Those numbers describe settled neighborhoods where few households move in any year, and a mean trip to work that already runs close to half an hour.

How does Henry County housing compare with nearby counties?

A typical Henry County home is worth more than the typical home in Hart County ($146,000) or Henderson County ($171,900), and three of every four homes here are lived in by their owners.

Henry County figures from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts estimates
ItemHenry County
Residents, July 2025 estimate16,447
Housing units, 20256,883
Homes occupied by their owners76.3%
Middle owner home value$197,900
Middle gross rent$895
Middle household income$63,347
Average commute30.5 minutes
New building permits, 202568

Households average 2.56 people, and 6,147 were counted for 2020 to 2024. Of adults 25 and over, 86.8 percent completed high school and 15.5 percent hold a bachelor's degree. Employers numbered 212 in 2023 with 1,707 jobs, down 3.4 percent from 2022. Retail sales reached about $259.6 million in 2022. The poverty rate is 15.1 percent.

Who can ask Henry County's appeals board to change an assessment?

Owners can, and so can local officials. KRS 133.120 allows the board of assessment appeals to revise a value when the county judge/executive, the mayor of a city using the county assessment, or a school superintendent recommends it in writing for a named parcel. The Department of Revenue can make the same recommendation.

An owner's route begins with a PVA conference, followed by a written petition at the county clerk's office no later than a workday after inspection ends. Hearings open 25 to 35 days after inspection closes (KRS 133.030), and the board usually wraps up inside five days.

  • Gather land and building details, insurance policies, construction cost, listings and loan papers.
  • Expect a notice and protest date if the board considers a higher value.
  • A taxpayer who listed their own parcel at fair cash value may ask the board to look at a neighbor's apparent under-assessment, in writing and with comparable sales or cost data.
  • Blanket reviews are not permitted.

Payment continues during an appeal. You pay on the value you claimed, and any difference is billed later with interest.

Does Henry County offer a homestead exemption?

The PVA's site says owners who are 65, or considered totally disabled, may qualify for an exemption on the primary residence. Revenue Department paperwork sets the 2025 and 2026 figure at $49,100.

On a house at the county's $197,900 Census median, the taxable base falls to $148,800. A birth certificate, license or passport proves age. Disability claims need a federal or retirement-system classification and are renewed yearly, except for service-connected veterans and holders of permanent Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems determinations.

How do I clear Henry County tax debt before selling?

Fold the debt into the sale plan. The tax is a personal obligation of the January 1 owner, and under KRS 134.420 a delinquency lien keeps running for eleven years even after title moves.

Ask the sheriff for a payoff on the current year. For any delinquent year, ask the Henry County Clerk, whose website has a delinquent taxes link. Once claims reach the clerk, KRS 134.119 stacks on the sheriff's fee: ten percent of the tax and ten percent of the penalty. Avoiding that starts with the calendar in KRS 134.015, where paying by November 1 saves 2 percent and each late stage after December 31 costs 5 and then 10 percent.

Deed recording also runs through the clerk, and the seller's transfer tax under KRS 142.050 is collected there. Call the office for current charges.

More questions about Henry County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Henry County, Kentucky?

The Henry County Sheriff, at (502) 845-2909. Delinquent bills go to the Henry County Clerk at (502) 845-5705.

Why does my Henry County bill name the previous owner?

Ownership is locked in on January 1. A purchase after that date leaves the bill under the former owner until the next calendar year.

What is the Henry County homestead amount?

It is $49,100 for assessment years 2025 and 2026, open to owners 65 or older or totally disabled through an application at the PVA.

Who besides the owner can seek a review of a Henry County value?

The county judge/executive, a city mayor, a school superintendent or the Department of Revenue, each by written recommendation naming the parcel.

Does an appeal stop my Henry County tax bill?

No. Pay tax on the value you claimed while the appeal runs, and expect a bill for any increase with interest.

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Knox County

  • Knox County Sheriff

Tax rate

Selling in Knox County?
We buy Knox County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which Knox County offices deal with a property tax bill?

Five phone numbers cover nearly every Knox County tax question, and each leads to the Barbourville courthouse complex at 401 Court Square. The PVA's office sets the value. The sheriff bills and collects. The clerk inherits what goes unpaid, and the county attorney pursues it from there.

Knox County contacts, from the Kentucky Department for Local Government county listing
OfficeUse it forPhone
Property valuation administrator (PVA)Value, exemptions, appeal conferences(606) 546-4113
SheriffPaying the current bill(606) 546-3181
County clerkDeeds, delinquent certificates, filing an appeal(606) 546-3568
County attorneyDelinquent bills and payment talks(606) 546-9515
Fiscal courtGeneral county government(606) 546-6192

Courthouse doors open weekdays from 8:30 until 4:00. Saturday mornings until noon, only the county clerk and circuit clerk offices stay open. To record a deed on a Knox County house, carry it to the clerk on the first floor.

What is Knox County like for a homeowner thinking of selling?

Knox County spreads over 388 square miles at Kentucky's southeastern edge and shares borders with Clay, Bell, Whitley and Laurel counties. Barbourville, the seat, stands where Richland Creek joins the Cumberland River. U.S. 25E links it with Corbin, 16 miles to the northwest, and Pineville, the same distance southeast. Most of Corbin lies in Whitley County. Artemus and Flat Lick are the other named communities.

Lincoln County gave up land to form Knox on December 19, 1799. The Wilderness Road crosses it, and the fiscal court's website calls the fight at Barbourville on September 19, 1861 the first Civil War battle in Kentucky. Dr. Thomas Walker State Park, inside the county, holds a replica of the first house built in Kentucky. The courthouse that stands today, finished in 1964, is the fifth one. Coal mining carried the economy for generations, and Knox kept more of its jobs and residents than most coalfield counties did. Today the largest employers are in health care, retail and schools. Groundwork has begun on a Keeneland racetrack at the north end of the county, according to the fiscal court, and the Appalachian Wildlife Center is taking shape to the south.

How does Knox County's housing market look in the Census data?

Knox County had 30,193 residents in the 2020 census and an estimated 29,532 by July 2025. That is a fall of 2.2 percent. The county holds 14,090 housing units, and the 2020 count found about one in eight of them empty. Census survey results covering 2020 through 2024 show a market with low prices and thin incomes:

  • Owners value a typical home they live in at $118,700.
  • Roughly two in three of the 11,711 households own their homes.
  • A typical monthly rent is $681.
  • A typical household takes in $32,527 a year, and 30.7 percent of residents live below the poverty line.
  • Three in four adults 25 and older finished high school.
  • Workers travel 24.4 minutes to their jobs on average.
  • The Bureau recorded no building permits for 2025.

When prices sit this low, a few thousand dollars of back tax takes a large bite out of a sale, so ask for payoff numbers before you list. Barbourville itself had 3,222 residents in 2020 and an estimated 3,081 in 2024.

Which school district covers a Knox County address?

Knox has three public school systems. Knox County Public Schools reaches every corner of the county. Barbourville Independent runs a single preschool-through-12 campus for the city. Corbin Independent serves Corbin, a district whose boundaries cross county lines. The county system operates schools named Central, Girdler, Flat Lick, Dewitt, Lynn Camp and Jesse D. Lay, among others.

A buyer comparing two houses a few blocks apart can find them in different systems. Give the parcel number to the PVA or the sheriff and ask which district applies before you quote a price or compare bills.

How does Knox County weather matter to a house?

NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals for Barbourville show about 54 inches of precipitation in an average year, falling on roughly 143 days. January lows average 24.6 degrees Fahrenheit and July highs reach 87. The record low is 22 below zero.

Steady moisture and hard freezes put roofs, gutters, crawlspaces and exposed plumbing at the top of an inspector's list. Sellers who keep receipts for recent repairs, or who tell a cash buyer plainly what needs work, shorten the back-and-forth. The same file supports an assessment conference if the PVA's value assumes a house in better shape than yours.

What if my Knox County assessment looks too high?

Ask the PVA for a conference first, because Kentucky bars an appeal until you have had one. After the May inspection window closes, the county clerk takes the appeal within a day, and a local board of fellow owners hears it a few weeks later.

Bring proof: photos, contractor bids, an appraisal or nearby sales. A board given nothing denies the appeal. The PVA's site says the office appraises everything at full market price, so recent nearby sales make the strongest argument.

When is the Knox County bill due, and what if it goes unpaid?

The year's property tax comes due at the end of December. The Department of Revenue notes that most sheriffs begin collecting in October or November. Discount and penalty steps differ across counties, so read the dates printed on your Knox County bill or call the sheriff at (606) 546-3181.

Anything still owed on April 15 goes to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency with a lien on the parcel. The clerk's website offers a delinquent tax lookup and says the clerk's own figure controls at the time of sale. The state's worked example grows a $1,000 bill to $1,254 at transfer and to $1,659.90 after a June advertisement. Interest adds one percent per month.

  • The county attorney mails a 30-day letter, then a 60-day letter.
  • A sale to a third-party buyer can follow, 90 to 135 days after the transfer.
  • That buyer takes over the lien, and the owner then pays the buyer.

Whoever held title on January 1 personally owes the bill, and under KRS 134.420 the lien lasts eleven years whoever holds the deed. A buyer inherits it with the house, so sellers clear it first.

Who gets the homestead exemption in Knox County?

Anyone past their 65th birthday, and anyone ruled totally disabled by a retirement system, can deduct $49,100 from the assessed value for 2025 and 2026 if the house is their residence on January 1. File with the PVA by the end of December. Heirs living elsewhere do not inherit the break automatically.

How are taxes divided when a Knox County house sells?

The bill carries the January 1 owner's name, so a March sale still leaves the seller as taxpayer of record. The closing agent splits the year on the settlement statement and pays the sheriff. KRS 382.135(1)(d) requires an in-care-of address on the deed for that year's bill, so supply the buyer's mailing address.

Heirs, owners who fell behind and landlords with an empty rental often ask whether a cash buyer can wrap up everything in one closing. It works when the payoffs are known first: the sheriff quotes the current-year amount and the clerk quotes any older certificate. Ask the county attorney's office as well whether a payment plan is on file, because the title agent will ask.

More questions about Knox County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which office takes Knox County property tax payments?

The sheriff, at (606) 546-3181, collects the current bill. After April 15 the clerk, at (606) 546-3568, handles it as a delinquent certificate.

How do I begin disputing a Knox County property value?

Schedule a conference with the PVA at (606) 546-4113. Filing with the clerk comes afterward, before the deadline that follows the roll inspection.

How much does the Knox County homestead exemption remove?

It removes $49,100 of assessed value for 2025 and 2026 for qualifying seniors and totally disabled owners living in the house. Applications go to the PVA before the year ends.

Do late Knox County bills pick up interest?

Yes. After the bill reaches the clerk as a certificate, interest runs at one percent per month, with commissions and fees on top.

Could I sell a Knox County home that has unpaid tax?

Yes. The lien stays attached to the parcel, so the payoff is deducted at closing. Get written amounts from the sheriff and the clerk before you pick a date.

Which Owen County offices touch a property tax bill?

Three offices in Owenton matter here: one collects the money, one decides the value, and one keeps records once a bill goes unpaid or an appeal is filed.

Owen County offices involved in property tax (Owen County government pages)
OfficeJobContact
SheriffTakes in state, county and school district tax103 W. Perry St.; 502-484-3363; Mon-Fri 8 a.m.-4 p.m.
Property Valuation AdministrationSets values and fields bill questions502-484-5172

On its own page the sheriff stresses that the office assigns no values, so a dispute over the amount begins with the PVA.

What is Owen County's size and history?

About 354 square miles of northern Kentucky belong to Owen County, with only 3.1 square miles of that under water. Owenton is the seat, Glencoe and Gratz are the lone other cities, and Carroll, Gallatin, Grant, Scott, Franklin and Henry counties surround it. Density is thin, at 32.1 residents per square mile in 2020.

Approved on February 6, 1819, the county took land from Franklin, Scott, Gallatin and Pendleton counties and honors Abraham Owen, a legislator killed at Tippecanoe. Hesler was the first seat, and in 1822 the court moved to the new town of Owenton. Settlers found numerous Native American burial mounds. Once locks and dams went onto the Kentucky River, regular packet boats between Frankfort and Louisville began stopping at Gratz and Monterey in 1844. The county is dry apart from a winery and limited sales inside Owenton.

How many people live in Owen County, and what do they pay for housing?

Owen County once held far more people than it does now, as the decennial census table on Wikipedia shows.

  • 2,031 people in 1820, climbing to a high of 17,676 in 1890.
  • A slide to 7,470 by 1970, the low point.
  • 10,547 in 2000, 11,278 in 2020 and an estimated 11,601 in mid-2025.

Recent survey figures point to an owner-dominated market with long drives to work.

  • Homes owned by their occupants carry a median value of $168,700, and 88.0 percent of the 4,252 households fall in that group.
  • Mortgage holders spend $1,385 a month at the median, and renters pay $830.
  • The typical household earns $61,134, and 13.9 percent of residents live in poverty.
  • Getting to work takes 41.9 minutes on average, the longest figure in the four-county Census table.
  • Only 17 building permits were issued in 2025.

The 2020 census adds that all of Owen County's residents lived in rural areas. Of 5,323 housing units, 18.3 percent stood vacant, a high share that includes seasonal and unsold property. The homeowner vacancy rate was 2.2 percent and the rental rate 6.3 percent. Median age was 41.9, and about 26.0 percent of households were one person living alone. Residents 65 or older made up 18.3 percent of that population, and children under 18 made up 24.3 percent.

Other Census measures round out the profile. Per capita income is $30,369, households average 2.64 people, and owners without a mortgage pay a median $434 a month. High school graduates are 86.5 percent of adults, 13.1 percent of people under 65 report a disability, and 3.2 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home.

What are the payment dates for an Owen County bill?

Sheriffs across Kentucky use the schedule in KRS 134.015. Owen County residents get a 2 percent break for paying by November 1, owe the stated amount until year end, and add 5 percent in January, then 10 percent from February.

April 15 ends the sheriff's collection season. What remains unpaid turns into a certificate of delinquency at the County Clerk, with a lien noted against the parcel.

How do Owen County owners contest a valuation?

A PVA appeal guide advises opening with a talk at the PVA office. Arrive with your own value figure and proof, such as nearby sales, an appraisal, damage photos or contractor quotes. Landlords add rent and expense records.

  1. Talk to the PVA while the roll is open for inspection each spring.
  2. Collect the appeal form from the clerk at 136 W. Bryan Street and return it by the next business day after inspection ends.
  3. Present your evidence to a local board of three residents.
  4. If the ruling stands and you disagree, send the state Board of Tax Appeals a letter within a month of the notice.

You may pay on your own claimed value while an appeal is pending, but a higher final figure produces a supplemental bill.

What happens to delinquent Owen County bills?

The clerk's website posts the delinquent list along with investor registration forms. The revenue department places a normal-schedule sale between July 14 and August 28, no sooner than 90 days after the bills reach the clerk.

  • Each month adds 1 percent interest.
  • The county attorney sends two letters, and the second names the sale date.
  • Newspaper notices run roughly a month to six weeks before the sale.
  • A certificate that sells to an investor can carry added fees.

If you are selling a listed parcel, ask the clerk (502-484-2213) for a written payoff.

Which breaks apply to Owen County property?

Homeowners who are 65 or older or totally disabled can shelter part of a home's assessed value through the homestead exemption. The amount is set by the state and reviewed every two years. A veteran with a total service-connected disability applies once, but a buyer starts fresh.

Working farm acreage is assessed at agricultural value, not market value, which can cut the taxable amount sharply. Before a farm is sold or split, ask the PVA whether the tract qualifies.

What charges follow an Owen County sale to the closing table?

The transfer tax is the seller's: half a dollar per $500 of value, with any partial block counted whole (KRS 142.050). Sold at the $168,700 median, a house spans 338 units and costs $169.00. The clerk wants proof of payment before taking the deed.

The deed itself must list the full price, both mailing addresses and a forwarding address for the next tax bill (KRS 382.135), or the clerk cannot file it.

Which economic facts matter to Owen County buyers and sellers?

Local spending is modest. Shops in the county sold $83.9 million of goods in 2022, about $7,426 for each resident, while health care and social assistance took in $24.6 million and lodging and restaurants $7.0 million. In 2023 the county had 133 employers, 969 jobs and a $39.9 million payroll, and employment slipped 1.5 percent from 2022. A further 764 nonemployer businesses were operating in 2024.

A bachelor's degree is held by 18.3 percent of adults, and 9.0 percent of people under 65 have no health coverage. About 90.4 percent of residents stayed in one house for a full year. Broadband reaches 80.4 percent of households, 89.3 percent have a computer, and 598 residents are veterans. Labor force participation is 58.0 percent.

More questions about Owen County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which office decides what my Owen County property is worth?

The Property Valuation Administration, 502-484-5172. Collection is the sheriff's job, valuation is not.

Where is the Owen County tax office?

In the sheriff's office at 103 W. Perry St., Owenton (502-484-3363), Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

What would the state transfer tax cost on a typical Owen County sale?

$169.00 for a $168,700 sale, counting 338 units of $500 at 50 cents each.

What if my bill is still open after April 15?

Phone the County Clerk, 502-484-2213. The bill has become a certificate of delinquency, with a lien and monthly interest of 1 percent.

Is a homestead exemption available in Owen County?

Yes, through the PVA, for residents who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Whoever buys the house applies separately.

Who to contact in Simpson County

What we confirmed on official pages

What is Simpson County, Kentucky, and where does Franklin fit?

Simpson County sits on Kentucky's southern edge in the Pennyroyal Plateau region, right against the Tennessee line. Allen, Logan and Warren counties gave up land to form it in 1819, and it honors Captain John Simpson, a militia officer killed at the Battle of River Raisin in 1812. Warren County borders it on the north, Allen on the east, Logan on the west, and Sumner and Robertson counties in Tennessee on the south.

Of its 236 square miles, 234 are land. Franklin is its lone city and its seat of government. Franklin received its charter from the state assembly on November 2, 1820, on a 62 acre tract bought from William Hudspeth, and carries the name of Benjamin Franklin. The 2020 census counted 10,176 people in Franklin and 19,594 in the county, so roughly half the county lives in town and the rest in farm and small community settings.

How do Simpson County home values and incomes compare in the Census data?

QuickFacts shows 20,788 residents for July 2025, up from 19,595 at the 2020 base, in 9,172 housing units and 8,025 households of about 2.44 people.

  • Households living in a home they own, 2020 to 2024: 66.7 percent.
  • Median value of owned homes: $229,400.
  • Monthly owner cost: $1,299 with a mortgage, $480 without.
  • Median rent: $1,012.
  • Median household income: $59,858, with 14.6 percent of residents under the poverty line and 18.8 percent of adults holding a four year degree.

Owners hold two thirds of the occupied homes, so most sales here involve a house that has had a long-term resident rather than a landlord.

What should a house seller know about Franklin?

Franklin's history includes a 1948 plane crash that sent a Kentucky Air National Guard pilot to his death while chasing an unidentified object, commemorated by a roadside historical marker at the tourism office, and the 1968 wedding of Johnny Cash and June Carter at Franklin First United Methodist Church. Kentucky Downs, a racetrack on the state border, hosts the Kentucky Cup Turf Festival.

  • Simpson County Schools runs Franklin, Lincoln and Simpson elementary schools, Franklin-Simpson Middle School, Franklin-Simpson High School and an alternative West Campus.
  • Franklin Mennonite Elementary and Faith Baptist Academy are private options, and Goodnight Memorial Library serves the town.
  • The city's Franklin Forward comprehensive plan covers land use, housing and community facilities, and the zoning map is posted on the city site.
  • Yearly precipitation averages about 50.5 inches, with only 4.3 inches of it as snow.

How does the Simpson County PVA value property?

The Property Valuation Administrator puts every parcel on the roll at fair cash value, using January 1 as the date, as Section 172 of the Kentucky Constitution requires. Setting rates and taking payments belong to other offices. The January 1 rule matters at a sale, because a buyer who closes later in the year may never see the bill. The PVA says to phone the Sheriff at 270-586-7425 if one does not arrive, and the PVA itself answers at 270-586-4261 on weekdays from 8 to 4.

Who sends and collects Simpson County property tax bills?

Three offices share the job. The County Clerk prepares and prints the bills and records deeds, the Sheriff collects the county and school portions, and the City of Franklin runs its own tax office at 117 W Cedar for city bills. Franklin's commission sets the city rates using a state formula, and the city office treats a postmark as proof of on-time payment.

City bills follow the deed records in the clerk's office on January 1. When a property sold afterward, the previous owner remains the city taxpayer, and the city office gives original bills only to the addressee. An escrow company that wants an electronic copy of the billing register pays $100, while substitute bills and master payment lists are taken at no charge.

What are the Simpson County payment deadlines and penalties?

KRS 134.015 supplies the schedule. A bill settled in full by November 1 earns 2 percent off. The printed amount carries no penalty through December 31, January adds 5 percent, and 10 percent applies after January ends. The city says its own issue, penalty and delinquent dates vary each year, so read the dates printed on each bill.

Anyone with an interest in the property, such as a tenant or a lender, may pay a delinquent bill without the owner's permission if the Sheriff is shown proof, and a payer can ask to be treated as a transferee (KRS 134.119). After the Sheriff files unpaid claims with the County Clerk, the clerk holds them as certificates of delinquency.

How does a Simpson County owner appeal an assessment?

An appeal begins with a conference at the PVA's office. KRS 133.045 keeps the real property roll open for inspection through 13 days from early May, six days a week, and the conference must be requested before that period closes. The 2026 period is over. Under the state process, an owner who still disagrees files with the County Clerk, and three local residents hear the case informally, with no attorney required.

The Franklin city site describes the local assessment board as a body with three year terms that meets once a year, with seats filled by the city, the Fiscal Court and the county judge. Bring comparable sales, a recent appraisal or photos of damage. A losing owner can carry the case to the state's tax appeals board.

Which Simpson County and Franklin rules can hold up a house sale?

Franklin applies the International Property Maintenance Code through its Code Enforcement department, which takes yard sale permits and public nuisance complaints through its citizen portal. The Planning and Zoning Commission follows KRS Chapter 100 and its own comprehensive plan, and its staff can be reached at 270-596-2756. The city also keeps a lienholder notification process listed among its services.

A home with a nuisance complaint, an unpaid city tax bill or a permit left open is harder to close. Ask city staff about open cases at an address before you list, and confirm county and city tax payoffs separately.

What does a Simpson County seller owe at closing?

Kentucky's deed transfer tax falls on the seller: 50 cents on each $500 of price, taken by the County Clerk at the recording counter (KRS 142.050). A sale at the county's typical $229,400 value owes $229.50. Add prorated property tax, any lien payoff and agent fees if you list. Owners who qualify for the homestead or disability exemption should confirm with the PVA that it is on file before the sale, since the PVA administers both. A cash offer avoids agent fees and repair demands, which can matter for an older farmhouse or a rental needing work, but the net after payoffs is the number to compare.

Simpson County and Franklin offices for tax questions
