Which Monroe County offices should you call or visit?

The county officials page gives these courthouse suites, all in Tompkinsville, KY 42167.

  • Sheriff: tax collection. 200 North Main Street, Suite E, phone (270) 487-6622.
  • PVA: assessments and exemptions. 200 North Main Street, Suite A, phone (270) 487-6401.
  • County Clerk: delinquent bills and liens. 200 North Main Street, Suite D, phone (270) 487-5471.
  • County Attorney: 215 North Main Street, phone (270) 487-6303.

Before paying anyone, learn from the clerk whether your certificate has been sold, because a buyer can attach costs of its own.

What is the Monroe County delinquent tax sale?

Right after April 15 the clerk issues a certificate of delinquency, a lien of record against the property. According to the clerk, that happens on or about April 16. Interest climbs monthly, so an early payment costs less.

The clerk scheduled the 2026 sale for September 23, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central, inside the clerk's office, and that date is behind us. A certificate unpaid at the sale may go to a private party who adds heavy administrative costs. The county attorney or a buyer may pursue foreclosure.

  • By mail: money orders only.
  • In person at the clerk's desk: check, cash or credit card, and card fees may apply.
  • Installments: the County Attorney's office offers them, though a sold bill no longer qualifies.

The clerk's page gives a phone number for learning whether a certificate was bought and by whom.

When are regular Monroe County bills due?

Through April 15 you pay the sheriff under the calendar in KRS 134.015. Fall brings the mailed bill, a 2 percent discount holds until November 1, and the printed amount can be paid up to December 31.

January costs an extra 5 percent, and later payments carry 10 percent. The state's property page gives a combined 21 percent penalty for February 1 through April 15. In its example a $1,000 bill becomes a $1,254 certificate, then totals $1,387.79 if the owner pays within five business days of the transfer.

How do you challenge a Monroe County value?

A PVA conference comes first, and the state requires it before anyone can file. The roll opens to the public on the first Monday of May for about two weeks, and the clerk's office accepts filings through the next workday after it closes.

The filing states your own opinion of value. Should bills go out before the appeal ends and the final figure beat your claim, a supplemental bill covers the gap. The board meets between 25 and 35 days after the window and may sit five days. Bring what the Department of Revenue lists as evidence: land and building details, insurance policies, construction costs and sales listings.

How are rural parcels valued in Monroe County?

Across 329 square miles and 34.4 people per square mile, many Monroe County sales come with land. The PVA must visit every parcel at least every four years and add new construction yearly, the Department of Revenue says. Farm land may be assessed at agricultural value instead of fair cash value, so ask the PVA how your acreage is classified before you list it.

Parcels near the Tennessee line, along the river or up in the hills can differ widely. If the roll shows a building that was torn down, or misses a barn you added, raise it at a PVA conference.

How does the homestead exemption work in Monroe County?

Anyone who owns and lives in a house and has turned 65, or carries a total disability classification, may claim it. Apply at the Monroe County PVA with proof, on the state's form.

KRS 132.810 sets one exemption per unit, even if the owner is both elderly and disabled, or several older residents share the unit. The amount follows a federal price index and is rechecked every two years. A sale or the owner's death must be reported to the PVA.

Can you sell a Monroe County house that owes tax?

Yes, and the usual route starts with a written payoff. The sheriff supplies it before April 15, and the clerk does afterward, when the figure rises monthly and carries the clerk and attorney fees.

Under KRS 134.015 the person who owned on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a lien can follow the property for 11 years. Houses in Monroe County that need work, or came to heirs, can change hands with a bill still open, so build the payoff into your numbers when you compare a listing with a cash sale.

More questions about Monroe County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who accepts Monroe County property tax payments?

The county sheriff, in Suite E at 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. Call (270) 487-6622.

When did the 2026 Monroe County tax sale take place?

Which Mount Vernon offices handle a Rockcastle County tax account?

The work is divided among three counters near the courthouse. The Property Valuation Administration values parcels and answers at (606) 256-4194, using P.O. Box 977, Mt. Vernon, KY 40456 as its mailing address. The sheriff bills and collects from 205 E. Main St., Box 2, at (606) 256-2032. The County Clerk, at (606) 256-2831 and Box 6 in that building, receives any bill that goes delinquent.

No one of the three sets a rate. The Rockcastle County Fiscal Court helps, meeting monthly on the second Tuesday at 1:00 p.m. inside the courthouse, and a resident who wishes to speak asks for a slot a day in advance. School and special districts choose their own levies, and the sheriff bills the total.

The county says every official record of its government is kept by the County Clerk, so a deed or lien search begins there. The Fiscal Court also runs an occupational tax office at (606) 256-8374 for employers, and the county health department, the dog warden and the solid waste office keep their own numbers for matters that sometimes come up when a house changes hands, such as trash service and animal control.

Which dates matter on a Rockcastle County tax bill?

KRS 134.015 makes December 31 the due date and names the sheriff as the collector. Barring a delayed mailing that shifts the calendar, the stages run in this order:

  • Through November 1: the whole bill paid at once is cut by 2 percent.
  • Early November through year end: only the printed figure is owed.
  • Throughout January: 5 percent is added.
  • From February: 10 percent is added, plus a sheriff's fee that Department of Revenue examples include.
  • Close of April 15: the sheriff stops collecting and passes the leftovers to the clerk, with a lien attached.

The shifted calendar gives a month for the discount, a month at face value and a month at 5 percent. The bill itself shows which one applies. Values are fixed as of January 1, so a late winter closing normally leaves the prior year's bill under the seller's name. Get the exact payoff from the sheriff before closing day.

What might a Rockcastle County home cost to carry?

Kentucky trimmed its 2025 real estate rate to 10.6 cents for every hundred dollars of assessment. Census QuickFacts puts a typical Rockcastle County house at $123,600, so the state's cut of that is about $131.02. School, county and district rates sit above it, and only the sheriff's bill for a given address shows the sum.

Older and disabled owners receive a deduction that shrinks the base. Take $49,100 away and $74,500 remains, which lowers the state cut to about $78.97. On a house this size the deduction removes a big share of the value, so a qualifying owner gains by filing at the PVA early.

A sale changes the picture. The bill follows whoever held the parcel when the year began, so the contract should assign the year in writing, and any open balance belongs at the closing table.

What steps does a Rockcastle County appeal follow?

Start at the PVA office, because no appeal can be filed until you have met with staff there. Staff must walk you through the law, the procedure and how your number was derived, and a written record captures your claim and the outcome.

  • Watch for the published inspection notice. The roll opens on May's first Monday and can be viewed for thirteen days.
  • Meet staff in that window, or sooner if an assessment notice has already arrived.
  • File the appeal with the clerk the next workday after viewing ends.
  • Attend the local board hearing, which convenes about a month after viewing.

The board weighs only evidence shown with both sides present. Insurance papers, construction costs, listings and property descriptions qualify as proof, and a case without them fails. If the board sets a number above yours after bills are out, a supplemental bill arrives.

Which Rockcastle County owners get a tax break?

Homeowners from age 65, along with owners whose total disability is recognized by a federal or retirement program, can take the homestead deduction on their residence. The figure is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. File with the PVA, along with a license, passport or similar proof of age.

An age claim stays in force while the first applicant keeps living there. Most disability claims must be refiled each year, but veterans with service-connected disability and people permanently disabled under Social Security or the state retirement system are excused. A couple counts as one claimant, and a purchaser files separately because the break travels with the person.

Churches, schools, charities and governments may be exempt altogether under sections 170 and 171 of the Kentucky Constitution, after an application to the PVA.

What do unpaid Rockcastle County taxes turn into?

Delinquency starts as April 15 ends. The sheriff forwards the list to the County Clerk, each bill turns into a certificate of delinquency, and the lien in KRS 134.420 survives eleven years, through any resale of the house.

Each month adds 1 percent, and commissions for the clerk and the county attorney follow. In the state's sample, a $1,000 bill grows to $1,254.00 on transfer and $1,611.30 once the attorney's first letter has gone out. The statute puts the sale between three and four and a half months after transfer, with a 30-day letter before it, a second letter if needed and newspaper advertising of at least 30 days.

Whoever buys a certificate can add costs. Paying the sheriff before the April deadline keeps the figure small.

How do Rockcastle County's housing figures look?

Rockcastle County was founded in 1810 and named for the Rockcastle River, whose own name comes from its rock cliffs. The seat, Mount Vernon, was founded in 1789 and is the largest city, and Brodhead and Livingston are the other towns. The county spans about 317 square miles of land, partly in the Daniel Boone National Forest, and sits inside the Richmond-Berea micropolitan area. Garrard, Madison, Lincoln, Jackson, Pulaski and Laurel counties are its neighbors.

Population, July 2025 estimate16,148 (0.7 percent above 2020)

The 2020 census counted 7,321 housing units, with 10.6 percent of them vacant, and 74.8 percent of occupied units were lived in by their owners. A renter vacancy rate of 6.3 percent was reported. Every resident counted as rural that year, and the middle age was 44.1. Workers commute 26.4 minutes on average, and 80 percent of households have a broadband plan. A house with pending repairs or an outstanding lien can be sold for cash as it stands, with the lien paid at closing.

More questions about Rockcastle County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where do I send a Rockcastle County tax payment?

To the sheriff's office at 205 E. Main St., Box 2, Mount Vernon, (606) 256-2032. The PVA at (606) 256-4194 only assesses and does not collect.

How much does early payment save in Rockcastle County?

Two percent of the bill when all of it arrives by November 1 on the regular schedule. Afterward only the printed amount is owed until year end, and penalties begin in January.

What is the older owner deduction in Rockcastle County?

It is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, deducted from the assessed value. Owners at 65 or beyond, or with a total disability, apply through the PVA.

When can I speak to the Rockcastle County Fiscal Court?

At its monthly meeting on the second Tuesday, 1:00 p.m., in the courthouse. Give 24 hours of notice to be placed on the agenda.

What if my Rockcastle County bill remains unpaid after April 15?

The County Clerk receives it as a certificate of delinquency with a lien. Interest starts at 1 percent a month, and the clerk and attorney commissions are added.

Where in Morehead do I handle a Rowan County tax bill?

The PVA and the sheriff both operate from the Rowan County Courthouse at 600 West Main Street, open weekdays from 8 AM to 4 PM. The PVA, at (606) 784-5512, assesses all taxable real and personal property, tracks changes of ownership, keeps parcel maps and processes exemptions. The sheriff, at (606) 784-5446, mails and collects the bills.

The county's property tax page says the sheriff takes cash, checks and money orders in person, and accepts cards through an outside vendor that charges 2.49 percent on amounts above $60 and a flat $1.50 below that. An online option also exists for anyone with a bill number ready.

When a bill goes delinquent, the County Clerk and the County Attorney step in, and the county's delinquent taxes page explains how they work alongside the sheriff.

What is Rowan County's own payment calendar?

Rowan County publishes a discount window that closes on November 30, later than the usual November 1 cutoff, and says bills first go out at the start of November.

A late mailing lets the Department of Revenue shift the calendar under KRS 134.015, so dates can move from one year to the next. Since the debt attaches to whoever held title on January 1, a spring seller should plan on settling the year's bill.

What would a median Rowan County house owe the state?

The state set 2025 at 10.6 cents for each hundred dollars of assessment. With QuickFacts listing a typical Rowan County home at $161,800, the state's share lands near $171.51. Other taxing bodies stack their rates on it, and the sheriff can quote a combined figure for any address.

Owners from age 65, and owners who are totally disabled, subtract $49,100 across 2025 and 2026. That leaves $112,700 taxable on the typical home and a state share near $119.46. Apply with the PVA at the courthouse, bringing a license or passport.

Only 61.5 percent of Rowan County homes are occupied by owners, so many parcels are rentals. A landlord who sells will be asked who covers the year's bill.

How does Rowan County pursue delinquent taxes?

After April 15 the bill rests with the County Clerk, and the county attorney follows a published timetable. Two letters go out on set dates, and the sale usually lands in mid August.

  • May 15: the County Attorney mails a 30-day notice.
  • June 15: a 60-day notice follows for bills still open.
  • Second week of August: the customary sale, where outside investors may buy a bill and add fees.
  • Each month: the delinquent amount climbs by 1 percent until it is paid.

The owner of record can sign a delinquent tax contract with the County Attorney's office up to three days before the sale. The county requires 10 percent of the bill that day and spreads the rest over monthly payments. A contract signed ahead of the clerk's sale keeps investors from buying the bill.

The County Attorney also presses the county's tax claim in foreclosure cases, where it holds priority.

How can a Rowan County owner contest a valuation?

The first step is a mandatory sit-down with the PVA or a deputy. Inspection of the roll runs thirteen days beginning May's first Monday, with the dates and appeal instructions advertised in the county's largest newspaper. At the sit-down the PVA explains how your figure was built and writes it up.

  • File the appeal with the clerk on the workday after viewing ends.
  • Prepare evidence: land and building descriptions, policies, construction costs, listings or sales. A case without any is rejected.
  • The hearing comes roughly a month after viewing, before a panel of local owners.
  • A hired agent must come from a statutory group, among them attorneys, CPAs and licensed appraisers.

Bills printed before a ruling use your claimed value, and a supplemental bill follows if the board lands higher.

Does selling a Rowan County house clear back taxes?

It does not. KRS 134.420 puts a lien on the parcel once taxes turn delinquent, and the lien lasts eleven years under any owner. A title search at the County Clerk reveals it, and it is normally paid off at closing.

A Department of Revenue example shows how fast debt grows after April 15. A $1,000 bill becomes $1,254.00 on transfer, about $1,387.79 inside five business days and $1,611.30 after the county attorney's first notice, before another month of interest. Paying the sheriff on time avoids that.

An owner who is behind has three routes before the August sale: pay the sheriff, pay the clerk, or sign a contract with the County Attorney. A direct cash sale is a fourth when repairs or inherited debts stand in the way, with the balance taken out of the proceeds.

What does a seller gain from knowing Rowan County's background?

Parts of Fleming and Morgan counties became Rowan County in 1856, in the Eastern Kentucky Coalfield, with about 280 square miles of land. Morehead is the seat and Lakeview Heights the other city. Morehead was incorporated in 1869, holds close to 7,000 people, and hosts Morehead State University, Cave Run Lake, Rowan County Senior High School and St. Claire Healthcare, which the city says employs 1,200. Lewis, Carter, Elliott, Morgan, Menifee, Bath and Fleming counties adjoin it, and part of the Daniel Boone National Forest falls inside the line.

The county's early story shapes today's map. Surveyors from Pennsylvania are believed to have explored the area in 1773, and the first settlement grew at Farmers, about ten miles west of Morehead. Clearfield came second and had the first sawmill in the county. Morehead, third in line, was founded in 1854 by a colonel who bought the land and named the town for a governor. A tax levied on Morehead in 1896 paid for hard-surfaced roads, and that road system reached Farmers by 1920.

Census QuickFacts supplies these housing figures:

  • July 2025 population estimate of 24,476, which is 0.7 percent under 2020.
  • Owners occupy 61.5 percent of homes, across 9,592 households averaging 2.25 people.
  • Typical home value $161,800; typical gross rent $825.
  • Household income at the midpoint is $54,321, and a quarter of adults (25.9 percent) have a bachelor's degree.
  • Eight building permits in 2025, and broadband in 93.4 percent of households.

The 2020 census measured a median age of 32.7 and counted 10,518 housing units, of which 13.2 percent stood vacant. Of the occupied units, 62.3 percent were owner-occupied and 37.7 percent rented, with 38 percent of residents in urban areas and 62 percent rural. New construction is thin, so most listings are existing houses.

When does the Rowan County discount end?

The county lists a 2 percent discount for bills paid before November 30. The printed amount is then due through December 31, and 5 percent is added in January.

Can I pay the Rowan County sheriff by card?

Yes: Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Discover, through a vendor that charges 2.49 percent above $60 or $1.50 below it. Cash, checks and money orders are welcome too.

Call (606) 784-5446 or visit 600 West Main Street in Morehead, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM.

Is a payment plan possible once a Rowan County bill is delinquent?

Yes, through the County Attorney's office: 10 percent of the bill is due on signing day and the remainder is split into monthly payments. Sign before the sale to keep investors out.

Who handles questions about a Rowan County valuation?

The Property Valuation Administrator, at (606) 784-5512. A conference there comes before any appeal at the County Clerk.

Shelby County by the numbers

Where is Shelby County, Kentucky, and which towns does it include?

Shelby County lies between Louisville and Frankfort and belongs to the Louisville metropolitan area. It was established in 1792 from land given up by Jefferson County, and its name honors Isaac Shelby, Kentucky's first governor. Shelbyville serves as the county seat. The other incorporated cities are Simpsonville and Pleasureville, and Pleasureville sits partly in Henry County.

The county covers 386 square miles, with 380 of them land. Its high point is Jeptha Knob at 1,188 feet, and Guist Creek Lake offers 325 acres of fishing water. Henry, Franklin, Anderson, Spencer, Jefferson and Oldham counties touch its borders. Besides Interstate 64, the main roads are U.S. 60, U.S. 421, KY 53 and KY 55, and Shelbyville itself sits on U.S. 60 about two miles north of the interstate, which was built in 1960.

Smaller places such as Bagdad, Finchville, Christianburg and Clay Village are unincorporated and fall under county government alone. Shelbyville calls itself the Saddlebred Capital of the World.

How do Shelby County incomes and home values look in the Census data?

QuickFacts lists 51,243 residents for July 2025, up from a base of 48,113 in April 2020, and 20,391 housing units. Most occupied homes are owned, which shapes both the tax roll and the typical sale.

  • Owner share of occupied homes for 2020 through 2024: 73.9 percent.
  • Median value of those homes: $304,800.
  • Monthly cost of ownership: $1,636 with a mortgage and $549 without.
  • Median rent: $1,033, across 18,484 households of about 2.58 people.
  • Median household income: $82,604, and 9.9 percent of residents living below the poverty line.

Louisville's metro area includes Shelby County, and Shelbyville has three industrial parks on its west side. Both shape who buys here and how far they commute.

What is the history and school picture behind a Shelby County address?

Shelbyville was established in October 1792 at the first meeting of the county court, after landowner William Shannon gave up 50 acres and one free acre for public buildings. The Louisville and Shelbyville Turnpike came in the 1830s, a rail line to Anchorage followed in 1870, and downtown was rebuilt after a large fire in 1909.

  • Shelby County Public Schools serves the county with elementary schools named Clear Creek, Heritage, Painted Stone, Simpsonville, Southside and Wright, plus Marnel C. Moorman School.
  • Middle schools are Shelby County East and Shelby County West.
  • High schools are Martha Layne Collins High School and Shelby County High School.
  • The county is classified wet, so package sales and restaurant drinks are legal under the conditions the state sets.

How does the Shelby County PVA assess real estate?

The Property Valuation Administrator runs a state office that works at county level. Each parcel is valued at its full fair cash value, the price a willing buyer and willing seller would agree on, using January 1 as the date. The PVA does not set rates or take payments. Your bill combines that assessed value with rates adopted by state, county and city governments, school boards and special districts.

Tax ownership is fixed on January 1 as well. A parcel bought after that date still produces a bill in the former owner's name until the next year, although the PVA tries to mail it to the new owner using the recorded deed. New owners who receive nothing should call the Sheriff. The county posts a reminder that a buyer's bill may have gone to the previous owner, and that a seller may still have an unpaid bill in their own name. The PVA can be reached at 502-633-4403.

When are Shelby County tax bills due, and what are the penalties?

One statewide schedule governs (KRS 134.015). Settling a bill in full by the first of November cuts it 2 percent. Between November 2 and December 31 the face amount is owed with no penalty. A January payment adds 5 percent, and a later one adds 10 percent.

The Sheriff collects the bills. The county's own notice says that after April 15 penalties are added and interest keeps accruing, because unpaid claims are then filed with the County Clerk, who keeps the delinquent tax records. A statutory collection fee is added to delinquent bills (KRS 134.119). The Sheriff's website has a Current Tax Bill Lookup, and the office number is 502-633-4324. Anyone paying someone else's bill, such as a tenant, a lender or a person holding an interest in the property, may do so under KRS 134.119 and can ask to be treated as a transferee.

How can a Shelby County owner appeal an assessment?

Start with the PVA. Under KRS 133.045 the real property roll stays open for inspection 13 days from early May, six days a week with one Saturday, and anyone planning an appeal must first ask for a PVA conference. The 2026 inspection period has ended, and the next arrives the following spring.

Bring evidence. Sales of comparable houses close by, a recent appraisal or repair estimates carry weight, and a request without paperwork rarely moves the number. If the conference leaves you unsatisfied, the published notice explains how to file with the local assessment appeals board, and a state level tax appeals board hears cases beyond that.

Which tax breaks can Shelby County homeowners claim?

All property is taxable unless the Kentucky Constitution exempts it, and the main relief for homeowners comes through the Homestead and Disability Exemptions. The PVA takes the formal application, and no exemption exists until one is on file. Ask that office for the current exemption amount and eligibility rules, because the rules can change from year to year.

How should property tax be handled when a Shelby County house sells?

Buyers and sellers commonly split the year's tax at closing, and any unpaid balance is cleared from what the buyer pays. Look up the bill on the Sheriff's website prior to signing, so you know whether an earlier year is still open. The Clerk handles deed recording and takes the seller's deed tax of $0.50 per $500 block (KRS 142.050). A deed at the county's typical $304,800 value owes $305.00, since 610 blocks are counted.

Table sources: Shelby County government pages and the Shelby County Sheriff's Office website.

How can a seller handle a Shelby County house with back taxes?

A listing, a sale on your own and a cash offer all work when taxes are owed, because the balance gets paid at the closing table. Each route starts with a current payoff figure from the Sheriff. A cash buyer can usually price in the amount owed and skip the lender's repair and appraisal steps.

More questions about Shelby County, KY Property Tax Guide

When are Shelby County property taxes due?

Settle everything by the first of November and the bill shrinks 2 percent; the printed amount holds through December 31. January adds 5 percent, and later payments add 10 percent. The county says penalties and interest build after April 15.

Who gets the bill if a Shelby County house changes hands mid-year?

It goes out in the name of the January 1 owner. A buyer who gets nothing should call the Sheriff at 502-633-4324 or use the online bill lookup.

Where can I check a Shelby County tax bill?

Use the Current Tax Bill Lookup on the Sheriff's website, or call the Sheriff's Office. The office is at 501 Main Street in Shelbyville and serves walk-ins on weekdays, 8:30 to 4:30, holidays excepted.

What does it take to claim a homestead exemption in Shelby County?

File a formal application with the Property Valuation Administrator. The county says no exemption can be granted without one. Call 502-633-4403 to learn the current age or disability requirements.

What deed tax does a Shelby County seller owe?

Fifty cents on each $500 of price, counting a partial block as a full one. A $304,800 sale owes $305.00, and the County Clerk takes the money at recording.

Typical monthly cost for a mortgaged owner$1,144
Households3,364
Average trip to work34.5 minutes
Typical household income$66,319

The 2020 count found 3,839 housing units, with 13.3 percent empty. Employers numbered 98 in 2023, and about 58.3 percent of residents 16 and older were in the labor force. Turnover is low: 95.7 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, the highest share of the four counties. The county counts 462 veterans, and broadband reaches 89.8 percent of households, and retail sales for 2022 totaled $29.6 million, or $3,506 per resident.

Who do I call about a Bracken County tax bill?

Valuing and collecting happen in separate offices that share the courthouse at 116 West Miami Street in Brooksville. The Property Valuation Administrator, 606-735-2228, owns the assessment, the property address, the name and mailing address on the bill, and exemptions. The Sheriff's Office (606-735-3233, second floor) only collects.

  • Address or name wrong: fix it on the return stub or call the PVA.
  • Disagree with the value: call the PVA before paying.
  • Bills from earlier years: County Clerk, 606-735-2952, on a separate check.

An online portal shows and takes payment for bills. Cards add a 2.50 percent charge that the cardholder pays and the sheriff does not keep. By mail, the check must cover the exact amount due.

When does the Bracken County discount end?

The sheriff gives the 2 percent discount period as October 1 through November 1. Bills go directly to owners. Later cutoffs and penalty steps are printed on the bill itself, and the sheriff's office can read them to you.

Escrow causes most of the grief. The sheriff mails to the owner and never to a mortgage company, so a borrower whose lender pays from escrow should pass the bill along as soon as it lands, or check that the lender has asked the sheriff for it. A check that bounces puts the bill back to unpaid, with the repayment schedule on the bill and a returned-check fee on top.

Why might a Bracken County bill carry the previous owner's name?

Ownership for tax purposes freezes on January 1. If a purchase closes after that, the bill for the year is addressed to the person who sold, and the PVA works from recorded deeds to find new owners. A buyer whose copy never turns up can ask the sheriff for one.

For a seller, that means a bill can show up at an address already left behind. The settlement agent normally divides the year by days of ownership and either pays the sheriff or credits whichever side will. Leave a forwarding address with the closing agent.

How does a Bracken County owner challenge an assessment?

Book a conference at the PVA first, since state rules require one before an appeal. The roll opens to inspection for thirteen days beginning with the first Monday of May, and appeals are filed with the clerk by the next workday after those days end.

If the PVA raises a value above what you listed, KRS 132.450(4) obliges the office to notify you. Anyone paid to speak for you must be an attorney, accountant, broker, appraiser or other qualified professional and must show your written authorization. Hearings may be recorded on audio.

What happens to an unpaid Bracken County bill after April 15?

The sheriff hands every unpaid bill to the County Clerk, who records a lien and files each as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk gives the Department of Revenue a list by May 15, and the Department publishes each county's list by June 1. On the normal schedule a tax sale can fall on any business day between July 14 and August 28.

Before that, the county attorney sends a 30-day letter and a second letter naming the sale date. The list is advertised in the paper with the biggest paid circulation between 30 and 45 days ahead and posted online at least 30 days ahead. An owner who still owes at the sale risks having the lien assigned to an outside buyer, who may add fees.

Interest accrues at 1 percent for every month or fraction. In the state's worked example, a $1,000 bill grows to $1,254 at transfer and to about $1,660 if paid after the June advertising.

Does Bracken County offer homestead relief?

Yes, to owners who turn 65 during the year or are permanently disabled. The Department of Revenue capped the exemption at $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026. The house must be your owned, occupied and maintained residence on January 1, and the application is due at the PVA by December 31.

The sheriff tells eligible owners to phone the PVA before paying a bill that lacks the exemption, because the exemption shrinks the bill. About 20.3 percent of Bracken residents are 65 or older.

How can I sell a Bracken County house that owes tax?

Treat the tax as a closing item. Get the present balance from the sheriff and any older balance from the clerk, and have the closing agent pay both from the proceeds. Inherited houses, houses with tenants and houses that need more work than a retail buyer will take on often sell to cash buyers who accept the property as it stands and pay the tax at the table.

More questions about Bracken County, KY Property Tax Guide

What is the Bracken County PVA's phone number?

606-735-2228, at the courthouse in Brooksville. The office handles assessments, mailing addresses on bills and homestead exemptions.

Where do I pay a Bracken County property tax bill?

At the sheriff's second-floor office in the courthouse, by mail, or through the sheriff's online portal. Card payments add 2.50 percent.

Does my mortgage company get my Bracken County tax bill?

No. The sheriff mails only to the owner. If your lender escrows taxes, forward the bill or ask the lender to request it.

Where do I pay a prior-year Bracken County bill?

At the County Clerk's office, 606-735-2952, with a separate check from the current year's payment.

Who owes tax on a Bracken County house sold in the spring?

The bill goes to whoever owned the house on January 1. Buyer and seller normally split the year at closing, and the agent pays the sheriff.

What should a Princeton seller know about how Caldwell County taxes a house?

The local Property Valuation Administrator values the house, the Caldwell County Sheriff collects the money, and anything unpaid after April 15 goes to the clerk. Values are fixed as of January 1, and the Department of Revenue says the PVA must walk every parcel at least once in four years, as described on its real property assessment page.

Princeton anchors a county of roughly 345 square miles of land. A Caldwell bill adds together several taxing districts, among them the state, the county and the schools, and each of those bodies picks its own rate. The assessor has no say over rates.

The county has long been farm country. Farmland is taxed on what it can produce rather than on market price. The sheriff's site says a parcel of ten or more acres used for livestock or crops, timber included, can qualify, so an owner with acreage should ask the PVA how the land is carried before listing.

Which dates and penalties apply to a Caldwell County tax bill?

The payment year runs on a fixed monthly ladder that starts on November 1 and ends on April 15. The sheriff's tax page lays out the steps, and the statewide framework behind them is KRS 134.015.

Collection for 2026 opened November 2, 2026, after bills were mailed October 30, and the sheriff replaced postcards with letter-style bills. Whatever the phase, a payment is credited if it is postmarked, handed over or dropped in the box before the next phase begins. The ladder looks like this:

  • All of November: the bill less 2%.
  • All of December: the bare face amount.
  • All of January: 5% extra.
  • February 1 through April 15: 21% extra.

The office is the first door to the right off Main Street inside the Princeton courthouse. It takes checks, money orders, cashier's checks, cash and, at the counter, cards with a processing surcharge. A drop box by the east courthouse door handles after-hours payments, with no cash allowed. Hours run 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays, and the sheriff posts a holiday closing list each season.

Which Caldwell County office answers which tax question?

Three numbers cover almost every question: 270-365-2088 for the sheriff, 270-365-7227 for the PVA and 270-365-6754 for the clerk. The PVA is on the courthouse's second floor at 100 East Market Street, and the sheriff takes mail at Room 25 of the same building.

  • Sheriff: mails bills, accepts payment until April 15, and runs a view-only bill search online.
  • PVA: sets values, takes homestead and disability forms, and holds the conference that must come before an appeal.
  • County clerk: takes over delinquent bills and records deeds.

The bill is addressed to whoever owned the parcel on January 1. A buyer whose bill went to the previous owner can print it from the sheriff's site, and the sheriff, who does not receive deed transfers, lists the new name in care-of form the first year.

How can a Princeton owner dispute a Caldwell County value?

Book a conference with the PVA first, then file at the clerk's office no later than the workday after public inspection ends. Inspection lasts 13 days from the first Monday in May, and the local appeals board sits up to five days beginning 25 to 35 days later, as the state property tax calendar explains.

Bring facts, not opinions. Useful evidence includes lot and building descriptions, insurance papers, what the house cost to build and listings of comparable sales. An appeal without that paper is denied. Skipping the local board also closes the door to later review. Because bills can print before a case ends, the value you claim is billed in the meantime, and a supplemental bill arrives if the board lands higher.

Whatever number survives is what a buyer's lender and title company will see. A Princeton owner whose house has gained a new roof or an addition should check that the PVA's record describes the house as it stands.

Which relief programs lower a Caldwell County bill?

Owner-occupants who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, can have part of the assessed value removed. The sheriff's page puts the maximum at $46,350 for 2024 and 2025, and KRS 132.810 resets it every two years, so the PVA can quote the current figure.

Applicants must live in the house they own, prove their age and claim no exemption elsewhere. The form is completed at the PVA office, which the sheriff says takes under five minutes. The benefit stays with the owner, so whoever buys from you files separately.

An older seller should confirm the exemption shows on the bill before closing. The sheriff asks owners to sort out a missing exemption with the PVA before paying.

What happens to the Caldwell County bill at closing?

The lien stays with the parcel while the closing agent splits the year between the two sides. According to the sheriff's FAQ, your agent or lender explains the split, since the sheriff is never told how a sale handled it.

Unpaid bills stay alive after a sale. Delinquent bills move to the clerk with penalties and 1% monthly interest, as the Department of Revenue's collection process page shows. A Princeton owner with back taxes should get the clerk's payoff figure before picking a closing date.

Where a lender escrows taxes, the bill still goes to the owner, and the sheriff says forwarding it is the owner's job. Checking in with the servicer now and then keeps a missed forward from becoming a penalty.

Who is buying and selling homes in Caldwell County?

Caldwell County has about 12,600 residents, and its typical owner-occupied home is valued at $118,500 for 2020 to 2024, far under Campbell County in northern Kentucky. Princeton, with 6,270 people in 2020, grew up around railroad junctions. It hosts a University of Kentucky research campus, factories such as Bremner provide jobs, and a December 2021 tornado hit the south side of town.

Caldwell County profile drawn from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page

Share lived in by owners70.2%
Typical home value$118,500

Roughly 30 percent of occupied homes here are rentals, and 93.4 percent of residents had not moved in the past year, so few houses change hands. Those that do often belong to estates, older owners or farm families, and an owner facing repairs or a tenant may prefer a direct cash sale to skip showings.

More questions about Caldwell County, KY Property Tax Guide

What dates matter for Caldwell County tax bills?

The bill opens for payment on November 1, and the 2% discount lasts through November 30. December is face value, January adds 5% and February 1 to April 15 adds 21%. Anything still open on April 15 goes to the county clerk.

Where can I pay a tax bill in Princeton?

Go to the sheriff's office in the courthouse, mail to 100 E. Market St., Room 25, or use the drop box at the east door. The website search only displays bills, and phone payments are not taken.

Is there a tax break for homeowners over 65 in Caldwell County?

Yes, the homestead exemption covers owners who live in the home and turn 65 during the year. Apply at the PVA office with proof of age. It trims the assessed value, and a new owner must apply again.

What if my Princeton house sells before the bill comes?

The bill is issued to the January 1 owner, so you may still get it. The closing agent prorates, and a buyer who never receives it can print a copy from the sheriff's site.

Do I need repairs before a cash sale in Caldwell County?

No. A cash buyer can take the house as-is. Back taxes and liens come out of your proceeds, so ask the sheriff and clerk for amounts early.

Which Johnson County offices handle property tax?

In Johnson County the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a number on your parcel, the sheriff takes your money, and the county clerk holds the liens and the appeal paperwork. Calling the wrong desk costs a day, so keep the split straight.

County offices cluster at 230 Court Street in Paintsville. The clerk sits in Suite 124 at (606) 789-2557 and is closed Saturdays. The sheriff's page gives (606) 789-3411, and both offices run on a weekday 8 to 4 clock.

Rates are not the PVA's call. The Fiscal Court sits on the second Monday of the month at 4:45 PM, and the county's two public school systems, Johnson County Schools and Paintsville Independent, are among the bodies that levy tax on a bill.

What are the key tax dates for a Johnson County parcel?

Value is struck on January 1, the roll opens for review on the first Monday of May, and bills arrive in the fall. Those dates come from Kentucky law, so they match every other county, but the offices that act on them are Johnson County's own.

The review window lasts 13 days and includes Saturdays. Anything you want changed has to be raised in that window, and the sheriff's discount for early payment ends November 1. Business equipment and other personal property is listed with the PVA through May 15. Ask the sheriff to confirm each year's collection dates, because the state sometimes shifts them.

What happens to an unpaid Johnson County bill?

On April 15 the sheriff hands any unpaid bill to the Johnson County Clerk. The clerk records a lien, and the bill can end up in the hands of a private buyer.

A tax sale cannot come sooner than 90 days after the handoff, under KRS 134.128, and interest of 1 percent a month runs in the meantime. The county attorney writes to the owner, and the clerk publishes the delinquent list before the sale. A county that also sells overdue oil and gas or unmined mineral bills gets 60 extra days, which suits a coalfield county where those interests are billed apart from the surface.

  • The lien rides with the land, so a buyer inherits it unless it is cleared.
  • Whoever buys the bill at the sale can add fees of their own.
  • Letters go to the address on file, so an outdated address means missed warnings.

What is the appeal route for a Johnson County value?

Ask the PVA for a conference in May. No filing with the board is allowed until that meeting has happened, and the PVA must explain how your number was built.

If the meeting settles nothing, file at the clerk's office in time for the following workday. A panel of local property owners hears the case. It must turn down any appeal that shows up without proof, for instance insurance policies, building costs or sales listings.

  • Ask which sales the PVA relied on for your house.
  • Get repair quotes if damage is missing from the record.
  • A paid representative must be an attorney, CPA, licensed appraiser or another category the state recognizes.

Past the local board, the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals is the last stop. With median values near $120,000, even a few thousand dollars off the value shifts a bill, so the call is worth making.

Who can claim a homestead or other exemption in Johnson County?

A homeowner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled under a federal or retirement plan, can take the homestead and disability deduction. One per household is the limit, and it travels with the owner, so a purchaser has to file fresh.

Kentucky resets the dollar amount every two years. A neighboring-region PVA posts $49,100 for 2025 to 2026, so confirm the Johnson County figure with the PVA. Service-connected totally disabled veterans and people ruled disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement file once, while those classed disabled by an out-of-state agency refile every year.

Churches, schools and charities apply on Revenue Form 62A023. Farmland is taxed on use value, a break the state says can be large where market prices run well above farm prices. Separately from property tax, the county charges an occupational tax of 0.5 percent on wages and net profit earned inside Johnson County.

How does Johnson County housing compare with other Kentucky counties?

Homes cost far less here than in the state's metro counties. Census survey figures for 2020 to 2024 put Johnson County's median home value at $120,200, a number that shapes how much any one assessment change matters to a bill.

Johnson County beside two metro-area Kentucky counties

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, 2020 to 2024.

Johnson County counted 22,680 people in 2020 and an estimated 22,051 in July 2025, a drop of 2.8 percent. Its population peaked at 25,771 in 1940. The 2020 census found 12.0 percent of the county's 10,493 housing units vacant, against 5.8 percent in Jessamine County and 6.9 percent in Kenton County.

Floodplain rules touch some parcels. Building in a Special Flood Hazard Area needs both a state and a local permit, and the county asks owners to call (606) 789-2550 before any development.

What does the Johnson County landscape look like?

Johnson County covers 264 square miles in the Eastern Coalfield and borders Lawrence, Martin, Floyd, Magoffin and Morgan counties. The highest point is Stuffley Knob at 1,496 feet, and the lowest is the Levisa Fork on the Lawrence County line at roughly 550 feet.

Paintsville is the only city and the seat. Van Lear and West Van Lear are census-designated places, and Paintsville Lake State Park, with a 1,140 acre lake, lies near Staffordsville. Big Sandy Community and Technical College runs two campuses in the county, at Mayo and Hager Hill.

On a rural parcel here, check the access road, the exact acreage and any flood zone before you set a price.

How did Johnson County's coal and oil history shape its parcels?

The railroad reached Paintsville in 1904 and opened the coal era, which lasted more than a century. Consolidation Coal and North East Coal built the towns of Van Lear and Thealka, and by the 1940s as many as 1,500 men worked the county's mines.

Oil and gas followed from 1917, and in 1922 the Johnson-Magoffin field produced over 2,000,000 barrels. Coal output peaked in 2008 at 2,713,196 tons. Wikipedia adds that many residents sold their mineral rights cheaply during the coal boom.

For a seller, that history is practical. Ask the title company whether minerals were severed from the surface on your parcel, and ask the sheriff whether a separately billed mineral or oil and gas tax bill is tied to it.

What should a Johnson County seller confirm before closing?

Three calls cover nearly every surprise: the sheriff for the bill and a payoff, the clerk for any certificate of delinquency, and the PVA for exemption status.

The county lists separate fire and rescue units for Paintsville, Van Lear, West Van Lear and others, and a Kentucky bill can stack school, city, county and fire levies. Ask the sheriff for a line-by-line breakdown. One Kentucky sheriff's FAQ explains that the seller's share is settled with the buyer at closing while the owner of record pays the full bill.

The Johnson County Sheriff, whose office lists (606) 789-3411.

Where is a Johnson County assessment appeal filed?

At the county clerk, 230 Court Street, Suite 124, Paintsville, once the PVA conference is done. The filing falls due the workday after the May review window shuts.

When does an unpaid Johnson County bill move to the clerk?

After April 15. The clerk then carries it as a certificate of delinquency with a lien on record.

Does a Johnson County homeowner get the 65 exemption automatically?

No. The owner applies through the PVA, and the home must be a primary residence.

Who decides Johnson County tax rates?

The taxing bodies on your bill, such as the Fiscal Court and the school districts. The PVA values property and the sheriff collects.

Who handles property tax for a McCreary County parcel?

Two offices share the work. One, the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), sets values; the other, the Sheriff, receives payment. McCreary County adds a twist: with no incorporated city anywhere inside its lines, there is no city hall tax office and no city levy. County government is the one local government covering every resident.

Mail for the PVA goes to PO Box 609, Whitley City, KY 42653, by phone at (606) 376-2514, and faxes go to (606) 376-4152. Dial (606) 376-2322 for the Sheriff and (606) 376-2411 for the County Clerk, who files deeds and later inherits any unpaid bill. The fiscal court works from 1 North Main Street in Whitley City and hears public business each second Thursday evening, starting at six.

When do penalties begin on a McCreary County bill?

The state schedule, KRS 134.015, measures value on January 1 and wants the bill settled before the year ends. The Sheriff keeps the window open through April 15, with higher costs at each step:

  • Pay it all by November 1 and 2 percent disappears.
  • November 2 to New Year's Eve: the printed total.
  • January: 5 percent more.
  • After that: 10 percent more.

The 2026 discount cutoff is history, which leaves the printed figure until December 31 and a penalty after it. The County Clerk inherits anything unpaid when April 15 ends. Two mailed warnings from the county attorney follow, then a sale scheduled three to four and a half months after the transfer. Whoever buys the certificate may add charges, so settle with the Sheriff first.

What does a McCreary County house cost in tax?

Very little, by Kentucky standards, because values here are low. A typical owned home here is worth $85,300 according to Census, compared with $188,100 in McCracken County. At the state's 2025 rate of 10.6 cents on every $100, Frankfort's share is about $90.42. The county, school board and special districts levy more, and the PVA can total them for one address.

McCreary County homes, rents and incomes in Census QuickFacts

With zero permits in 2025, the roll gains little from new building, and the market is existing houses. The Census Bureau's 2020 count, which Wikipedia reports, listed 6,892 housing units with one in eight empty, and 17.9 percent of residents now are 65 or older.

Does McCreary County offer a homestead deduction?

Yes, because the program is statewide. A homeowner who is 65 or older, or classed as totally disabled, has $49,100 removed from assessed value for the 2025 and 2026 years, ahead of the rates.

The subtraction bites hard in this county. At the $85,300 median, only $36,200 stays taxable, and the state's piece drops from about $90.42 to about $38.37. The application is made in person at the Whitley City PVA office, with a birth certificate, driver's license or passport as proof of age. Claims based on disability rest on a government or retirement-plan finding of total disability and are renewed every year. Service-connected veterans, and anyone already judged totally and permanently disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems, are spared the renewal.

What can a McCreary County owner do about an assessment?

Ask for a meeting with the PVA or a deputy before anything else, because Kentucky refuses appeals from owners who skipped it. Staff must explain how the number was produced. After that:

  • Review the roll during the 13 days after the first Monday in May.
  • Hand the appeal to the County Clerk no later than the first working day after the roll closes.
  • Attach evidence on land and structures: insurance records, build costs, comparable sales and photographs. A survey helps with rural tracts. Unsupported appeals fail.
  • Show up when the board of local property owners meets, about a month after the roll closes. It hears evidence only with both sides present.

Missing the hearing forfeits the next stage, the Kentucky Claims Commission. If bills have already printed and the board's value exceeds your claim, a supplemental bill makes up the difference.

What if McCreary County taxes are still owed when the house sells?

Unpaid tax stays attached to the house. The statute treats it as the owner's personal debt from January 1, and a KRS 134.420 lien can last 11 years whichever name is on the deed. Once the bill reaches the Clerk, monthly interest of 1 percent begins, with commissions for the Clerk and county attorney and a recording fee on top.

A title company will want a payoff figure before it releases funds. The Sheriff supplies it up to April 15, and the Clerk after that.

What is it like to sell a house in McCreary County?

The newest of Kentucky's 120 counties, McCreary was cut from Pulaski, Wayne and Whitley in 1912. Its 431 square miles lie along the western rim of the Cumberland Plateau, and no part of it lies inside an incorporated city, which no other Kentucky county can say. Whitley City is the seat, with Pine Knot and Stearns as the other census-designated places. Federal land dominates the map: the Daniel Boone National Forest holds roughly 43 percent and the Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area roughly 18 percent, so private acreage is a limited share.

Early livelihoods came from timber, coal and the Cincinnati Southern Railway, which arrived in 1880 and fed the Stearns company town. Cumberland Falls, a state park since 1930, and the Big South Fork Scenic Railway draw visitors now. Students all attend the McCreary County School District, and McCreary Central High School is its main campus. Clocks follow Eastern time, and the 2025 population of 17,124 is 1.4 percent above 2020.

The average worker needs 32.3 minutes to reach a job, and 80.1 percent of households subscribe to broadband. Pulaski, Laurel, Whitley and Wayne counties border it, along with two Tennessee counties. For an heir to a house here, or an owner behind on tax, a cash sale as-is skips repair bills. The sale price still has to clear the tax payoff, so get that number early.

Population peaked at 18,306 in 2010, and the 2020 count of 16,888 was a 7.7 percent drop. Census business data list 157 employer establishments with 1,522 jobs in 2023, a 4.3 percent decline from the year before, and retail sales near $110 million in 2022. Census lists 8.5 percent of adults with a four-year degree and 18.8 percent of residents under 65 with a disability. Pricing near the county's low median value matters in a market like that, and the Census median gross rent of $577 shows what nearby rental demand will support.

More questions about McCreary County, KY Property Tax Guide

Is there a city property tax in McCreary County?

No. McCreary is the only Kentucky county without an incorporated city, so no city levy exists. School and district levies still appear on the bill.

Whom do I pay for McCreary County property tax?

Hand it to the Sheriff, at (606) 376-2322, any time through April 15. The PVA at (606) 376-2514 sets values and receives exemption papers, never money.

What does the state collect on an $85,300 McCreary County house?

Roughly $90.42, at the state's 2025 rate of 10.6 cents per $100. Local rates add to that.

Can a 65-year-old in McCreary County shrink the taxable value?

Yes. Bring proof of age to the PVA office and $49,100 comes off assessed value for 2025 and 2026 under the homestead deduction.

What if my McCreary County bill moves to the County Clerk?

A lien is recorded and interest runs at 1 percent monthly. The certificate may be sold to an investor three to four and a half months after the move.

How does property tax work in Bell County, Kentucky?

Bell County is a small, low priced market in the southeast corner of Kentucky, and its tax bills move through the same chain of offices as any Kentucky county: the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets value, the sheriff bills and collects, and the county clerk takes appeals and unpaid bills.

The county touches Tennessee and Virginia at the Cumberland Gap, where the Wilderness Road ran in 1775. Pineville is the seat, Middlesboro is the largest city, and Arjay is a census designated place. The legislature formed the county in 1867 from parts of Knox and Harlan counties and first called it Josh Bell County, after a congressman, before shortening the name in 1873. Bell is the only Kentucky county holding both a state resort park, Pine Mountain, and a national park unit, Cumberland Gap National Historical Park. Steep ground and protected land govern where houses can go and how far a buyer must drive to reach one.

How has Bell County's population changed, and why does it matter to a sale?

Bell County lost about 5.3 percent of its people between the 2020 census count of 24,097 and the 2025 estimate of 22,829. Wikipedia's historical table shows 47,602 residents in 1950, so the county now holds roughly half the population it had seventy years ago.

That history shows in the housing stock. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates put the middle owned home at $89,000 and the middle household income at $31,354, with 31.8 percent of residents in poverty and rent at $592 a month. The 2020 census found 11,517 housing units with 13.8 percent vacant, and only 41 building permits were issued in 2025.

Bell County housing and income, Census QuickFacts

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts.

Work is scarce: 42.4 percent of adults 16 and over are in the civilian labor force, the lowest share among the four Kentucky counties in these Census tables, and 79.3 percent of households have broadband. At prices this low, a tax lien plus clerk fees and interest can swallow a bigger slice of a sale than in a high value county, so check the tax status first.

Which offices handle property tax in Bell County?

Three offices cover most questions, and a fourth takes over once a bill goes delinquent.

  • The Bell County PVA values real estate, takes age and disability exemption forms, and schedules appeal conferences.
  • The Bell County Sheriff sends the bills each fall and collects the money.
  • The Bell County Clerk, whose office keeps weekday hours, files deeds, mortgages and liens and takes in bills that go delinquent.
  • The county attorney mails the warning letters that follow a transfer and can set up payment plans.

The City of Pineville posts its own property tax page. The sheriff has collected Pineville's tax on the county bill since tax year 2020. The city's page shows 27.6 cents for each $100 of assessed real property value, but call city hall for the rate on your bill.

The clerk's recording room matters to sellers for another reason. The Bell County courthouse burned in 1914 and 1918, and a 1977 flood damaged it and destroyed stored documents. If an old deed or probate record looks incomplete, ask the clerk what the recorded chain shows.

When are Bell County property tax bills due?

KRS 134.015 sets the cycle. In a year when collection starts after November 1, the state grants 30 days per stage instead of the usual dates.

On the usual calendar, paying by November 1 saves 2 percent, the bill stands at face value through December, January adds 5 percent, and February 1 to April 15 carries a combined 21 percent. Payment is made to the sheriff.

The tax belongs to the person on title each January 1. A Bell County seller closing in spring therefore owes that year's bill unless the sales contract shifts it. If no bill reaches you, the sheriff can provide a duplicate.

How is a Bell County assessment challenged?

Phone the Bell County PVA and request a conference during the May inspection period. Kentucky requires that meeting before any filing, and the period lasts roughly two weeks.

If the two of you stay apart, the paperwork goes to the clerk on the next business day after inspection closes. Revenue's own example: an inspection ending May 20 means a May 21 filing. Write your claimed value on the form.

  • A three member local board hears the case roughly a month later.
  • Bring evidence: comparable sales, a contractor's estimate or an appraisal.
  • The PVA defends the assessed figure.
  • A certified letter reports the outcome and what to do next.

With typical values near $89,000, small gaps matter. A house with a failing roof or foundation can be valued like a sound neighbor unless you document the problem.

Which Bell County owners get a homestead break?

Yes. An owner who has reached 65, or who is totally disabled, can claim it on a residence. Apply at the Bell County PVA, and approval trims the assessed value by a fixed amount.

The figure began at $6,500 in 1972 and has been indexed to inflation since. Boone County's PVA lists $49,100 for 2026, and the Bell County PVA can confirm what your bill uses. A household receives a single exemption, even when both spouses qualify.

  • Approval carries forward as long as the applicant stays in the house.
  • A buyer starts over with a new application.
  • Disabled owners under 65 refile yearly, except veterans with a service rating and owners with a permanent finding.

After a death, an heir who sells should notify the PVA so the address loses the exemption.

How should a Bell County seller handle unpaid taxes?

A seller can pay ahead of closing or have the closing agent pay out of proceeds. Either way, ask the sheriff or clerk for a written payoff, since the total grows month by month after April 15.

After that the clerk holds a delinquency certificate and a lien. Interest grows at 1 percent a month, clerk and attorney commissions of 10 and 20 percent arrive, and a summer sale can pass the certificate to a private investor. KRS 134.015 lets the lien last 11 years even if the house changes hands.

Bell County has three public school districts: Bell County, Middlesboro Independent and Pineville Independent. The sheriff can say which school district and city rate appear on your parcel's bill. Heirs and owners of vacant houses who want to skip repairs and carrying costs may favor a cash sale, which clears liens at closing against a written payoff.

More questions about Bell County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who takes Bell County tax payments?

Pay the Bell County Sheriff. City of Pineville tax appears on the same bill as county tax, so one payment covers both.

How late can a Bell County appeal be filed?

File with the county clerk by the next business day after the May inspection period ends. A conference with the PVA must come first, and the period opens on the first Monday in May.

What does a typical Bell County house cost?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 data gives $89,000 for owned homes. Median household income for the same years is $31,354.

What do late Bell County payments cost?

On the usual calendar, 5 percent is added in January and a combined 21 percent applies from February 1 to April 15. After April 15 the clerk adds interest and fees.

Does a lien stop a Bell County sale?

Yes. The lien stays with the property until paid, so the payoff is usually taken from the seller's proceeds at closing. Get the figure in writing from the sheriff or clerk first.

Which Clay County offices deal with property tax?

Clay County splits the job three ways. The Property Valuation Administrator decides what a parcel is worth, the Sheriff prints and collects the bills, and the County Clerk takes appeal papers and later inherits any bill the sheriff could not collect. Knowing which desk owns which question saves a seller several wrong-number calls.

All three share one building, 102 Richmond Road in Manchester. The PVA sets no tax rate and accepts no payments. Its work ends at the number on the roll.

Clay County property tax contacts (source: Clay County Fiscal Court department pages and county clerk site)
OfficeHandlesReach it
Property Valuation AdministratorValuation, exemptions, ownership changesSuite 200, 606-598-3832, Monday to Friday, closing at 4:30
SheriffTax bills and collectionSuite 100, 606-598-3471
County ClerkAppeal filings, unpaid-bill certificates, deed recordingSuite 101, 606-598-2544

What is Clay County like for someone selling a house?

Clay County sprawls across 471 square miles of Appalachian hills with Manchester at its center. Kentucky created it in 1807 from land that belonged to Floyd, Knox and Madison, and named it for Green Clay. A fire took the courthouse in January 1936. Seven counties touch its borders: Owsley, Perry, Leslie, Bell, Knox, Laurel and Jackson. The Census Bureau groups Clay with the Corbin micropolitan area.

The 2020 count was 20,345 people. The July 2025 estimate is 19,465, which is 4.3 percent fewer, so a listing draws from a shrinking local pool. Census QuickFacts add this detail:

  • 7,288 households living in 8,781 housing units
  • 76.4 percent of households own their home
  • Typical home value: $90,700
  • Typical rent: $724 a month
  • Typical monthly owner cost: $978 with a mortgage, $367 without

A seller pricing near $90,700 will notice any unpaid tax in the final settlement figure.

How does the Clay County PVA decide what a house is worth?

Valuation is pegged to January 1. Kentucky wants fair cash value, which means the price a voluntary sale between informed parties would produce. Staff walk every parcel at least once in each four-year stretch, and new buildings join the roll every year.

A purchase can simplify things. When you bought in the previous year, the deed price may serve as next January's value, so long as nothing about the building changed. Frankfort values four categories itself: public service companies, bank shares, omitted tangible property and vehicles. Everything else, real and personal, belongs to the local PVA.

What else does the Clay County PVA keep track of?

Beyond the annual value, the office follows ownership changes, maintains parcel maps, updates building details and administers exemptions on real estate. A seller can ask the staff whether the map shows the correct acreage, whether the building record lists a finished basement or an outbuilding that no longer stands, and whether the exemption on file still matches the owner.

Errors in those records flow straight into the bill. Suppose a garage came down years ago but still sits on the record: it keeps lifting the value until someone asks for a correction. Visit during open hours, 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays, or write to the office at 102 Richmond Road, Suite 200, Manchester, KY 40962.

When does a Clay County tax bill come due?

Collection follows Kentucky's fall-to-spring pattern, and the sheriff runs it. The Sheriff's page on the Fiscal Court website carries a View Property Tax Bill button for parcel lookups. The sheriff's office, at 606-598-3471, can confirm the exact opening date, since the state lets a county use 30-day phases when a different calendar is needed.

The state's typical pattern:

  • October 1 to November 1: 2 percent off
  • November 2 to December 31: face amount
  • January: 5 percent added
  • February 1 to April 15: 21 percent added

Because value is fixed on January 1, a bill may carry a previous owner's name after a sale made later in the year.

What is the route for contesting a Clay County valuation?

The sequence is fixed, and missing one step closes the door.

  • Look for the notice the PVA mails after raising a value.
  • Request a conference with the PVA or a deputy while the tax roll is open for inspection. That window starts the first Monday of May and covers two weeks, Monday through Saturday.
  • If talks fail, file the appeal paper with the County Clerk by close of business the next workday after the window ends.
  • Attend the local board hearing, held 25 to 35 days after inspection. The board gets five sitting days unless the state grants more.
  • Bring proof: sales of similar houses, an appraisal, or building costs. With no facts, the board has to deny you.

Filing and then failing to appear forfeits the right to continue. A dissatisfied owner can carry the case to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

Does Clay County give a homestead exemption?

It does, to people who live in the house and are at least 65 or are classified as totally disabled. For assessment years 2025 and 2026 the amount is $49,100, taken off the valuation before tax is figured. A home worth the county's typical $90,700 would be taxed on $41,600.

Apply at the PVA office in Manchester, 606-598-3832. Age is shown with a driver's license, birth certificate or passport. A disability claim needs paperwork from the federal agency or retirement system that made the classification. Most disability claims renew annually. Exceptions cover veterans with a service-connected disability and owners ruled permanently disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

What happens to an unpaid Clay County bill?

When business closes on April 15, the sheriff hands the bill to the County Clerk. It becomes a certificate of delinquency and a lien on the parcel. Interest of 1 percent per month begins, and the clerk adds 10 percent while the county attorney adds 20 percent.

The county attorney writes to owners in May and, if necessary, June, and can arrange installments. From mid-July, certificates may be sold to outside buyers through late October. After a sale you owe the buyer, and more fees follow. The Clay County Clerk's website posts a delinquent tax page for each year.

Where can a Clay County seller look up records online?

The Fiscal Court website, claycountyky.com, has a page for each department with contact details and hours. The sheriff's page holds the bill lookup. The County Clerk's own site lists Recordings, Fees, Forms and an Open Records Request page, along with a delinquent tax page for each year, which is the place to check whether a parcel was advertised for sale.

How do I handle the tax bill when I sell in Clay County?

The closing agent normally pays the current bill out of your proceeds and splits it with the buyer. An open delinquency has to be settled first, because the lien stays with the parcel. Get a payoff amount from the sheriff before signing a contract, and ask the PVA whether an exemption on the parcel ends when ownership changes.

The deed adds a separate charge. Kentucky taxes the seller $0.50 for every $500 slice of the price, and a partial slice counts in full. The clerk takes it at the recording counter. A $90,700 price makes 182 slices, so the charge is $91. Foreclosure deeds, divorce transfers, correction deeds and nominal gifts between parent and child fall outside the tax.

More questions about Clay County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who mails the Clay County tax bill?

The Sheriff does. If nothing arrives, call 606-598-3471 or use the bill lookup on the sheriff's page of the Fiscal Court site.

Can a Clay County owner contest a value in summer?

Generally no. Both the conference and the clerk filing must land in the May inspection window, with the filing due the next workday after it ends. Phone the PVA at 606-598-3832 in spring.

Does the Clay County PVA take tax payments?

No. That office only values property and processes exemptions. Money goes to the sheriff, then to the County Clerk after mid-April.

Is transfer tax owed on a Clay County sale?

Usually yes. The seller owes $0.50 per $500 of price, and the clerk collects it before recording. Foreclosure deeds, divorce transfers and correction deeds are exempt.

Can a Clay County house with a delinquent bill still be sold?

Yes. The delinquency gets paid at or before closing. Ask the County Clerk for the total with interest and fees so the title company can build it into the payoff.

Who do Fleming County owners deal with on property tax?

Two courthouse-square offices carry most of the load, and a third takes over when a bill goes bad. The PVA answers value questions at 606-845-1401, and the county's PVA page lists weekday opening from 8 until 4:30. The sheriff bills and collects at 201 Court Square in Flemingsburg, with phones answered at 606-845-4701 (press 1) from 8 until 4:30 Monday to Friday. Once a bill is delinquent, the county clerk handles it.

It helps to know what the PVA will not do. By its own description, the office appraises property at fair cash value, maintains tax maps and ownership records and processes exemptions, but it neither writes laws nor sets rates. Rates come from the fiscal court, city councils, the school board and other districts. The fiscal court itself meets at the courthouse, 100 Court Square, on the second Tuesday of every month at 9 a.m. Eastern.

A PVA or deputy walks each property at least once in four years and may measure the outside of a building whether or not the owner is in. Send the PVA any new mailing address in writing so notices do not go astray.

What does the Fleming County tax year look like?

Fleming runs the standard Kentucky calendar, which opens October 1. Statements usually leave the sheriff's office near the end of September. A missing bill changes nothing about the debt, so owners without one phone 606-845-4701 and ask for the balance, or use the sheriff's online tax record search.
