Which Lyon County offices send, value and collect the bill?

The Lyon County Sheriff collects, the county's valuation administrator (the PVA) sets values, and the County Clerk takes over when a bill goes stale after April 15. The Sheriff's own page cites KRS 134.140 and 160.500 as the basis for collecting state, county, school and district tax on real, tangible and intangible property, and says the office handles about seven million dollars a year.

Find the Sheriff at 500 West Dale Avenue, Suite 100, Eddyville. Its mailing box is PO Box 126, Eddyville, KY 42038. The PVA operates from 500 B West Dale Avenue and answers at 270-388-7271. For prior-year delinquent bills, the Sheriff directs taxpayers to the County Clerk at 270-388-2331.

Both the Sheriff and the PVA work on West Dale Avenue, so one visit can answer two questions. Call before you go: the Sheriff cannot accept money until bills arrive from the clerk around the end of September.

Why is Lyon County unlike most Kentucky counties?

Water covers a sixth of the county. Lyon County totals 257 square miles, 43 of them water, with Lake Barkley on the Cumberland River along its south side. Eddyville, the seat, had 2,375 residents in 2020 and neighboring Kuttawa had 629. Both towns were relocated to higher ground when Barkley Dam backed up the lake. The new Eddyville plat was filed on August 13, 1959, and owners of land in the two doomed towns were offered a free lot in the new one.

Interstates 24 and 69 cross at Eddyville, with U.S. 62 and 641 running through the center. Mineral Mound State Park sits on a Lake Barkley peninsula, the Kentucky State Penitentiary stands on the shore south of town, and Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area faces Kuttawa across the water. A single district, Lyon County Schools, serves everyone and enrolled 884 students in 2024 to 2025.

Storms have left marks on the housing stock. An EF4 tornado tore through Eddyville and the county on December 10 and 11, 2021, damaging or destroying hundreds of homes and businesses, and an EF3 touched down near Eddyville on May 26, 2024. If your house was repaired or rebuilt, tell the PVA, because the January 1 value follows the property's condition.

Lyon County snapshot from the Census Bureau (2020 to 2024 surveys and 2025 estimates)
ItemLyon County
Residents, 2025 estimate9,123
Share aged 65 and above26.6%
Housing units, 20254,889
Owner-occupied share of homes80.4%
Typical home value$189,500
Typical monthly rent$747
Typical household income$65,066

What do the Lyon County numbers suggest about selling?

The market is small and mostly owner-held. Owners occupy four of every five occupied homes, and over a quarter of residents are in the retirement-age group. The 2020 census found 4,780 housing units, with 30.4 percent of them vacant.

New building adds little to the roll: the Census Bureau logged just five building permits for 2025. Typical household income in Lyon County runs higher than in Logan County, and so does the typical home value. A seller here often prices against lake access as well as square footage.

What is the Lyon County payment calendar?

Your payment counts if it is received or postmarked by the date shown. The Sheriff gets bills from the clerk late in September, so statements normally land in mailboxes during early October.

  • October 1 through November 1: pay 2 percent less.
  • November 2 to year end: pay the stated amount.
  • January: add a 5 percent penalty.
  • February 1 until April 15 closes: add a 21 percent penalty.
  • Past April 15: the clerk holds the bill, and further penalties may apply.

No bill by October 10? The Sheriff will send a duplicate. The tax year is the calendar year, so the bill covers January through December of the year printed on it.

The office accepts checks, money orders and cards, with the card processor charging a fee, and the same options are online. Partial payments are refused, though a single payment can cover several bills. For owners who find the lump sum hard, the Sheriff suggests checking for exemptions and asking a lender about escrow.

Who is on the hook for the bill when a Lyon County house sells?

Kentucky addresses the bill to the January 1 owner, even if the house has since changed hands. The Sheriff says a closing agent or attorney usually works out each side's share of the year. Some agents then pay the Sheriff directly, and in other deals one party receives a credit and pays later.

  • Prorated payments are refused. Someone must cover the full bill.
  • Mortgage companies do not automatically get the statement. Lenders can pull data from the PVA roll, yet the owner must make sure the lender actually has the bill.
  • If a bill arrives in your name after a sale, send it on to the new owner at your former address.

Get the closing agent to confirm in writing who pays the Sheriff and by when, and keep the receipt.

How can a Lyon County owner contest an assessment?

Confer with the PVA first, then lodge the appeal at the clerk's office. State rules give you until the end of the workday after the roll's public viewing period closes, and that period opens in early May and runs about two weeks.

A local panel then takes up the matter about a month after viewing ends. It wants facts: photographs, an appraisal, insurance policies, construction costs or listings. A written decision explains any change and describes the next step to the state tax appeals board.

Call the PVA at 270-388-7271 each spring for the exact dates, since the window can be shifted and the change is advertised locally.

Which exemptions shrink a Lyon County bill?

Start with the homestead and disability exemptions. A senior, or an owner classed as totally disabled, who occupies the home can deduct $49,100 for the 2025 to 2026 assessment years. For a house at the county's typical $189,500 value, the taxable base then falls to $140,400.

The Sheriff sends people who struggle to pay toward these exemptions and refers questions about them to the PVA at 270-388-7271. File with the PVA, not the Sheriff or clerk. Disability claimants normally reapply annually, except service-connected veterans and people whom Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems has ruled permanently and totally disabled.

What is the best way to sell a Lyon County house with tax owed?

Get the payoff in writing from the correct office and let the closing agent pay it out of your proceeds. This year's balance comes from the Sheriff, and earlier years come from the County Clerk.

Delinquent bills get advertised before any sale, and the county attorney sends notices, so early action avoids added fees. Interest builds at one percent monthly once the clerk takes the bill, with clerk and attorney commissions on top. Have the closing agent pay any recorded lien from the sale proceeds so the house passes to the buyer with a clean tax record.

More questions about Lyon County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where does Lyon County send its property tax payments?

Payments go to the Lyon County Sheriff at 500 West Dale Avenue, Suite 100, Eddyville, or by post to Box 126 in Eddyville (KY 42038). An online link on the Sheriff's tax page also works. Past April 15, pay the County Clerk.

How large is the Lyon County early-payment discount?

It is 2 percent, for money received or postmarked between October 1 and November 1. The stated amount applies through year end, and a 5 percent penalty begins in January.

Will the Lyon County Sheriff take a partial payment?

No. Partial payments are refused. A single payment may cover several bills, and the Sheriff suggests checking exemptions or lender escrow if the full amount is hard to meet.

If I sell my Lyon County home in June, who pays that year's tax?

The January 1 owner is billed, and the closing agent usually prorates each side's share at the table. The Sheriff needs the whole bill paid, so confirm in writing who sends the payment.

How much is the Lyon County homestead exemption?

The deduction is $49,100 for seniors and totally disabled owners living in their homes, set for the 2025 to 2026 assessment years. Apply through the PVA at 270-388-7271.

Where can Nicholas County owners get answers on property tax?

Everything runs through the courthouse at 125 East Main Street, Carlisle. The PVA works from the basement, answers at 859-289-3735 and keeps hours from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays. The Sheriff's Office, at 859-289-3740, collects what is owed.

Mail to the PVA goes to P.O. Box 2, Carlisle, KY 40311. Its website carries the certified tax roll, a tax estimator, forms and a fee schedule, and the office says its goal is to help owners understand how assessments are built. The county's own sheriff page describes the job as public safety plus tax collection. Because the sheriff only collects, a dispute about a figure starts with the PVA.

How rural is Nicholas County for a homeowner?

Nicholas is among Kentucky's smallest and most rural counties. Carlisle is the seat and the only incorporated community, and the 2020 Census classed every resident as rural. Bourbon and Mason counties supplied the land in 1799, and 195 square miles of it are dry ground, with Bluegrass-style farms, wooded hollows and small villages.

History is close at hand. Forest Retreat, built in 1814, is a historic district on the National Register. A marker on U.S. 68 identifies the cabin Daniel Boone built in 1795 as his last Kentucky home. Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park, 148 acres shared with Robertson County near Mount Olivet, marks an August 1782 fight often called the last battle of the Revolution.

Jobs lie mostly elsewhere. Workers average 35.6 minutes to reach work, longer than in Montgomery, Muhlenberg or Nelson County. Only 82 employer establishments operate inside the county, with total employment of 415 in 2023, and retail sales for 2022 were $23,532 thousand, or $3,022 per resident. A buyer here is rarely tied to a local employer.

What does Census data show about Nicholas County housing?

The estimate for July 2025 is 7,949 people, up 5.5% from the 2020 base. In so small a county, a few sales can move the averages.

  • 3,355 housing units in 2025, and only 3 building permits that year.
  • Owners occupy 74.5% of homes in 2020 to 2024.
  • The Census midpoint for an owned house is $123,000.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,143 with a mortgage and $426 without.
  • Gross rent has a midpoint of $728.
  • Household income has a midpoint of $59,531, with 16.2% of people in poverty.

Only 9.8% of adults past 25 have a four-year degree, and 10.3% of people under 65 have no health insurance. About 92.6% of residents stayed in place last year, the highest share of the four counties in the Census comparison used for this guide.

Who lives in Nicholas County households?

The county has 2,776 households averaging 2.74 people, larger than in the other three counties compared here. Children under 18 make up 24.9% of residents and people 65 and over 18.2%. Census Bureau data show 237 veterans, 17.1% of residents under 65 with a disability and 81.6% of households with a broadband subscription.

Self-employment matters. The Census Bureau lists 611 nonemployer establishments for 2024, many times the count of employer firms, so a seller may be dealing with a farm, a trade or a home-based business that shares the property. Horse farming also shapes the landscape: the 1954 Kentucky Derby winner Determine was bred on Forest Retreat Farm in the county. A seller with acreage should ask the PVA how land, barns and the house are classed on the roll before comparing values.

What does Nicholas County charge by date paid?

The PVA site announced that 2026 bills would be mailed on or about October 1, 2026. Payment steps follow KRS 134.015.

Nicholas County bill totals under the state due-date statute
Date paidConsequence
No later than November 1Two percent off the total
November 2 through year endThe total printed on the bill
During JanuaryFive percent added
Past January 31Ten percent added

The statute stops at 10%, though the Montgomery, Muhlenberg and Nelson County sheriffs each post 21% for the stretch between February and mid-April. Call 859-289-3740 for the figure that applies on your payment date.

Take an $800 bill. It costs $784 with the discount, $800 through December and $840 in January. At a 21% penalty it would be $968. The same statute describes the tax, fees, penalties and interest as a personal debt of the taxpayer from the assessment date until paid.

What steps lead to an assessment appeal in Nicholas County?

Ask the Nicholas County PVA or a deputy for a conference. KRS 133.120 requires it first, before or during the inspection window or any extension. The PVA must explain the constitutional and statutory rules and how the value was reached, and the office logs what was discussed.

KRS 133.045 keeps the tax roll open 13 days beginning the first Monday that falls in May. An owner who stays dissatisfied delivers a letter or petition to the County Clerk with the parcel, the reasons and an opinion of fair cash value, by the workday after the window closes. At the county hearing, an owner may record the audio. Filing never postpones payment. You pay on your stated value, and the final value decides what else is owed, with interest.

What homestead relief can Nicholas County seniors claim?

Owners aged 65 and up, and owners classified as totally disabled by a federal agency or a retirement system, may claim the state deduction of $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026. Applied to the county midpoint of $123,000, it leaves $73,900 to be taxed. The PVA takes the application in the courthouse basement. Disability claims renew yearly, except for service-connected veterans and for owners found permanently and totally disabled by the federal Social Security Administration or the state retirement system.

Who receives the bill after a Nicholas County purchase?

According to the PVA, both value and ownership are pinned to the first day of January. A house bought afterward is billed to the previous owner until the next calendar year. The PVA tries to mail a copy to the buyer using information from a tax agreement signed by buyer or seller. A buyer who receives none can get a copy from the sheriff at 859-289-3740.

  • Seller: confirm the current bill is paid and keep the receipt.
  • Buyer: have a mailing address entered on the deed, as KRS 382.135 requires.
  • Both: put the year's tax split into the contract.
  • Estate sales: the executor lists heirs and estimated values in an affidavit at the County Clerk's office.

Unpaid tax can outlast a sale. KRS 134.015 says the lien from a delinquent bill runs up to eleven years under KRS 134.420, whoever holds title. A seller who suspects an old year is open should ask the sheriff before listing, and a buyer's title agent will want the answer anyway. With only three building permits issued in 2025, most buyers here are weighing older houses, so a clean tax record is one less thing to negotiate.

More questions about Nicholas County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where does Nicholas County keep its PVA?

The PVA works from the courthouse basement at 125 East Main Street in Carlisle, with weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30 and a phone at 859-289-3735.

Who gets a Nicholas County bill after the house sells?

The previous owner is billed until the next calendar year, and the PVA tries to mail a copy to the buyer. A buyer with none can call the sheriff at 859-289-3740.

How much does paying early save in Nicholas County?

Two percent, if the whole bill is paid by November 1. After that the printed total is due through December 31.

What penalty follows January in Nicholas County?

KRS 134.015 sets 5% for January and 10% after January 31. Ask the sheriff for the exact payoff, since sheriffs elsewhere in Kentucky post 21% for the late winter and spring stretch.

What does the homestead exemption remove in Nicholas County?

The state takes $49,100 off assessed value once a qualifying owner applies at the PVA. Qualifying means 65 or over, or totally disabled, and the figure covers tax years 2025 and 2026.

Who to contact in Powell County

  • PVA Dustin Billings, 525 Washington Street, P.O. Box 277, Stanton KY 40380; (606) 663-4184; hours Mon-Fri 8:00-4:00, closed 12-12:30

Which offices in Stanton deal with a Powell County tax account?

Three counters in Stanton cover nearly every question a Powell County owner will have. The PVA puts a value on each parcel. The sheriff collects the money. The county clerk holds deeds and the lien paperwork. Rates are voted elsewhere, by the fiscal court, the school board and the library, extension and health districts that appear on a bill.

Powell County, KY: who to call about a tax account

Sheriff(606) 663-2226Bills and payments through April 15
County Clerk(606) 663-6444Delinquent bills, deeds, lien records

The PVA sits at 525 Washington Street, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 277, Stanton, KY 40380, and a fax line at (606) 663-0947. The county publishes the details on its PVA page. Call before visiting, since hours at the sheriff's office and the clerk's office vary by weekday.

How does the PVA arrive at a figure for a Powell County house?

The office appraises each parcel at fair market value for January 1 and states openly that it never decides what you owe, since the bill multiplies that value by rates other bodies adopt. Cars and trucks get the same January 1 treatment. Staff start from NADA guides and can lower a figure for high mileage or for two written repair estimates from licensed body shops.

Owners are not obliged to relist land each spring when last year's roll described it correctly and nothing major changed. After a purchase, the price on the deed can serve as the listed value the following January 1. For Powell County buyers that means a recent sale price often becomes the next assessment.

Business equipment and other personal property goes on a list filed with the PVA between January 1 and May 15, and anything missed by May 15 is treated as omitted and billed later.

What dates govern Powell County bill payment?

KRS 134.015 sets the usual calendar for the whole state, and the sheriff collects:

  • Settle everything by November 1 and 2 percent comes off.
  • From November 2 into December, the printed amount applies.
  • January adds 5 percent.
  • February and later add 10 percent, and the Department of Revenue's examples show a sheriff's fee on top.

When mailing slips, the Department can switch to a shifted calendar that gives each stage one month from the mailing date. Which version applies in a given year is printed on the bill, and the sheriff at (606) 663-2226 can confirm it. Once April 15 passes, the sheriff hands whatever remains to the clerk, who records a lien.

What might a Powell County owner actually pay?

For 2025 the state rate fell to 10.6 cents per hundred dollars of assessment, a drop from 10.9 cents in 2024. Census QuickFacts reports a typical Powell County home at $141,100, and the state's slice of that is close to $149.57. County, school and district levies come on top, so only the address-specific bill gives the final total.

Older and disabled owners who qualify for the homestead deduction are taxed on less. Removing $49,100 from $141,100 leaves $92,000, and the state slice shrinks to about $97.52. Early payment trims a further 2 percent.

At a sale, the bill follows the person who held title when the year began. Put the split of the year's bill into the contract, and ask the sheriff for a payoff number ahead of closing.

Can a Powell County owner push back on a value?

Yes, but the sequence matters. Meet the PVA or a deputy first, because the board turns away any case that skipped that step. The tax roll lies open for inspection for thirteen days starting on May's first Monday, Saturdays included, and a higher assessment must come with written notice under KRS 132.450.

  • At the meeting the PVA explains the method and writes down your claimed number.
  • The written appeal goes to the clerk on the workday right after the inspection window shuts.
  • Hearings begin about a month after inspection and can run up to five days.
  • Bring proof: building and land details, insurance policies, construction cost, sales listings. No proof means a denial.

A paid advocate must belong to a listed profession, such as lawyer, CPA, licensed broker or certified appraiser, and carry your signed authorization. Should the board land above your claim after bills are printed, a supplemental bill covers the gap.

Who gets the older owner deduction in Powell County?

The state fixed the deduction at $49,100 for assessments in 2025 and 2026. Seniors from age 65 and people classed as totally disabled receive it on the house they occupy. File at the PVA office on Washington Street and bring a document that proves your age.

A couple gets one deduction, and either spouse turning 65 is enough. After approval, an age-based claim rolls forward while the same person lives there. Disability claims are renewed every year, with exceptions for veterans whose disability is service-connected and for people with a permanent finding from a federal or state retirement program.

The benefit belongs to the person, so a buyer must file again after a sale.

What if taxes on a Powell County house are never paid?

Transferring the deed does not erase them. Under Kentucky law the tax is a personal debt of the owner from the assessment date, and the lien described in KRS 134.420 lasts eleven years whoever takes title next. A title search will find it.

After April 15, 1 percent a month starts, and the state's worked example shows a $1,000 bill turning into $1,254 at transfer, then $1,387.79 inside five business days and $1,611.30 after the first county attorney notice. A clerk's sale follows roughly three to four and a half months after transfer, and whoever buys the certificate gains a lien carrying its own interest and costs. A payment to the sheriff ahead of mid April sidesteps every one of these costs.

How does Powell County's housing market look to a seller?

Carved in 1852 from Clark, Estill and Montgomery land, Powell County has Stanton as its seat and Clay City as its only other town. About 179 square miles of foothills, rising from 580 to 1,440 feet, hold part of the Daniel Boone National Forest. Natural Bridge State Resort Park, the Red River Gorge and the Nada Tunnel bring walkers and climbers, and the county advertises quick access to two interstate highways.

Census QuickFacts supplies the numbers behind the market:

  • July 2025 population estimate of 12,812, which is 2.4 percent below the 2020 base.
  • Owners occupy 68.2 percent of housing units, spread over 4,790 households with 2.65 residents each.
  • Typical home value $141,100, typical rent $747.
  • Household income of $40,309 at the midpoint, with 20.8 percent below the poverty line.
  • Five building permits in 2025, so nearly all sales involve existing houses.

Montgomery, Menifee, Wolfe, Lee, Estill and Clark counties border it. Workers commute 26.6 minutes on average. A house that needs work or carries back tax can still move quickly through a direct cash purchase, with the bill paid at the closing table.

More questions about Powell County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where does a Powell County tax payment go?

The sheriff, reachable at (606) 663-2226. The PVA, at (606) 663-4184, only assigns values and neither bills nor collects.

What does early payment save on a Powell County bill?

Two percent when the whole amount arrives by November 1 on the regular calendar. A shifted calendar gives one month from the mailing date.

How much is the older homeowner deduction in Powell County?

$49,100 for assessments in 2025 and 2026, subtracted from the home's value for owners at 65 and up or those totally disabled. The PVA supplies the form.

Can I go straight to the appeals board?

No. A meeting at the PVA office must come first. The appeal is then filed with the county clerk on the workday after inspection ends.

If I sell, do old Powell County taxes transfer to the buyer?

Delinquent amounts can. A lien lasting up to eleven years stays on the parcel, so the closing statement should pay off whatever is open.

Who handles property tax inside the Todd County courthouse?

Todd County puts its tax work in one building: the courthouse at 202 East Washington Street in Elkton. All three offices answer through the county switchboard at (270) 265-9966, each on its own extension.

  • Sheriff, ext. 208: takes payment of property tax bills. The sheriff's website lets owners view their bills online and says payment cannot be made there, so ask the office which payment methods it accepts.
  • Property Valuation Administration (PVA), ext. 504: the county's answer for the value of a property and for disputing that value.
  • County clerk, ext. 501: registers vehicles and, after April 15, runs the delinquent-tax process.

The City of Elkton keeps a separate property tax payment link on its own website. If your address is inside the city, ask the city whether a city bill exists in addition to the county bill.

What sets Todd County apart from the counties around it?

Todd County spans 377 square miles and almost none of it is water, 2.6 square miles in all. The legislature created it on April 1, 1820, from parts of Christian and Logan counties, after residents petitioned for a seat of government closer than the two existing ones. It was named for Colonel John Todd, killed at the Battle of Blue Licks in 1782.

Historically the county divides into a northern high country of steep sandstone slopes with oak, walnut and poplar, and a southern low country of rolling limestone flatlands. The lowlands, with Pembroke soil, are known for strong crop yields, and farming is a long-standing local tradition. In the early 1800s a stagecoach hub at what is now Guthrie sent routes out to larger cities. Elkton took its name from the elk that watered at a spring near the center of town, and its courthouse square was laid out as a trapezoid rather than a square, so buildings on both sides catch sunlight longer.

Early settlers came while the area still belonged to Virginia, which set aside southern Kentucky land for Revolutionary War veterans, and the Cherokee had hunted these lands long before. The cities are Elkton, Guthrie and Trenton, with Allensville and Fairview (mostly in Christian County) as census-designated places. Muhlenberg, Logan and Christian counties border Todd, as do Robertson and Montgomery counties in Tennessee. Todd County runs on Central time and has a single public school district, the Todd County School District, with Todd County Central High School.

What do the Census figures say about Todd County homes?

Todd County is estimated at 12,972 residents in July 2025, a 5.9 percent rise since 2020, after a small slide during the 2010s. The housing figures matter most to a seller:

  • The middle of the market is a $166,700 owner-occupied home, the lowest value among the four counties.
  • Owners occupy 76.0 percent of homes, spread across 4,559 households.
  • Typical gross rent is $851, above Taylor and Trigg.
  • 5,313 housing units stood in the county in 2025, and 40 building permits were issued.
  • Household income sits at $61,103, and the trip to work averages 27.8 minutes.

In 2020, 10.8 percent of housing units were vacant and 30.0 percent of occupied homes were rented. Retail sales for 2022 came to $150.3 million. Todd also has the youngest population of the four, with 27.2 percent of residents under 18 and 7.6 percent under 5. About 82.4 percent of adults finished high school, 16.5 percent hold a four-year degree, and 13.9 percent of people under 65 have no health insurance.

How has Todd County's population moved over time?

The headcount peaked around the start of the twentieth century and has hovered near 12,000 for decades. The county has not grown steadily the way Spencer has.

Employment tells a quieter story. Todd County had 208 employer establishments in 2023 with 1,794 jobs, 3.4 percent more than the year before, and a total payroll of $84.5 million. Another 1,118 businesses had no employees at all.

When do Todd County property tax bills go delinquent?

The sheriff's file closes at the end of the day on April 15. Whatever is unpaid moves to the clerk's office, where a recorded lien attaches and the bill is renamed a certificate of delinquency. Until then the state schedule sets the price: 2 percent off if you pay by November 1, the bare amount through year end, a 5 percent surcharge in January and 10 percent afterward, with the sheriff's add-on fee on top.

Once the bill reaches the clerk, monthly interest of one percent runs, and commissions for the clerk and the county attorney follow. In the Revenue Department's sample, a $1,000 bill arrives at the clerk as $1,254, costs $1,387.79 to settle within five business days, and costs a third-party purchaser $1,704.21 at the sale. Waiting adds money fast, and the attorney's commission is waived only during that first five-day window.

When does the Todd County tax sale happen?

Under KRS 134.128 the sale falls 90 to 135 days after the sheriff hands bills to the clerk, a window the Department of Revenue puts at July 14 to August 28 on a regular schedule. Each year the clerk lists the sequence in order: a half-page notice, the published list, the deadline for outside buyers to register, and the sale itself, which begins at 9 AM.

A buyer of up to three bills registers with the county, while anyone wanting more than three registers with the state. The clerk's page points out that a buyer of a bill gets a lien, not the house. Afterward the owner settles with that buyer, who may pile on costs. The county attorney mails notices to owners beforehand, and the list runs in the newspaper roughly a month before the sale.

How do I dispute a Todd County assessment?

The county FAQ sends valuation questions to the PVA in the courthouse, extension 504. A conference there is mandatory. File the appeal at the clerk's office on the workday after the May viewing period ends. A panel of area owners then holds hearings a few weeks later.

The panel wants evidence: nearby sales, an appraisal, construction costs or insurance records. An owner who skips the local step or the hearing cannot continue to the Kentucky Claims Commission. Paid representatives must be professionals such as attorneys, accountants, brokers or appraisers and must hold written authorization.

What does the homestead exemption mean for a Todd County sale?

For 2025 and 2026 the state lets an owner past 65, or totally disabled, subtract $49,100 from the assessed value of a home they live in. The Todd County PVA takes applications through December 31. The benefit stays with the owner, so a buyer files again.

Before closing, get the sheriff's payoff and ask the clerk about older certificates. Delinquent tax is the personal debt of the January 1 owner, and its lien can last eleven years, so a title agent will want a clean record before releasing funds.

Where is a Todd County property tax bill paid?

At the sheriff's office inside the courthouse at 202 East Washington Street, extension 208 of (270) 265-9966. The sheriff's website lets you view bills, and the office can tell you which payment methods it takes.

Who reviews a Todd County assessment I disagree with?

The PVA, at extension 504. Ask for a conference first, because the local board hears only owners who have had one.

What is the Todd County homestead deduction?

The amount is $49,100 through the 2026 tax period, available to owners past 65 or totally disabled. Applications go to the PVA before the year ends.

Can an investor buy my delinquent Todd County bill?

Yes. After April 15 the bill sits at the clerk's office, and an outside purchaser can buy it at the yearly sale and then collect from you.

Can a Todd County house with unpaid tax be sold?

Yes. The balance comes out of the sale price. Get written payoffs from the sheriff and clerk so the buyer's closing agent sees no surprises.

What makes Carroll County, Kentucky, different for a house seller?

Carroll County is a small river county where the Kentucky River meets the Ohio, and its seat, Carrollton, sits at that confluence. At 128.68 square miles of land it is the third-smallest county in Kentucky by area, and the 2020 Census counted 10,810 residents. Carrollton lies about 54 miles from Cincinnati and 55 from Louisville along U.S. 42, with Interstate 71 about four miles south of town.

That location shapes who buys here. The county's own website lists employers such as North American Stainless, CertainTeed and Kentucky Utilities, and describes General Butler State Resort Park, a 791-acre park, as a local draw. Jefferson Community College serves the county. A house in Carrollton is often sold to a worker commuting along the river or I-71 corridor, and Carrollton itself was laid out in 1792 under the name Port William.

The city itself is compact, about two square miles with 3,890 residents in 2020. Prestonville lies across the Kentucky River to the west, and Switzerland County, Indiana, sits across the Ohio to the north. The county's own site adds that the Kentucky Veterans Memorial is in Carrollton and that boats launch from Point Park.

Carrollton's worst recorded flood was the Ohio River flood of 1937, with a crest of 79.9 feet, according to Wikipedia. Sellers of low-lying homes near the river should ask the city planning office for floodplain information.

Which Carroll County office does what with a tax bill?

A parcel is valued by the PVA, billed by the Sheriff's Office, and handed to the County Clerk if it goes delinquent. The county's clerk page lists those delinquent collections beside recording deeds and mortgages and filing wills and probate orders.

  • Sheriff: first floor of the courthouse at 440 Main Street, (502) 732-7010, with online tax lookup and payment through the sheriff's page.
  • County Clerk: same building, (502) 732-7005, for delinquent taxes and deeds.
  • County administration: (502) 732-5448, the office that edits or exonerates county tax amounts when a bill looks wrong.

Carroll's FAQ puts the annual due date at December 31 and expects bills in October or November. An owner who has seen nothing should look the bill up on the sheriff's page. In the state's description, most counties begin collecting on October 1 or November 1. The exact discount cutoff is printed on the bill, and the sheriff's office can confirm it.

Can Carroll County owners split payments or get a late fee waived?

Neither. The county FAQ rules out a payment plan and requires the whole bill in one transaction. It also says that a bill that never arrived is not a permitted ground for waiving late fees under the state's administrative regulations.

Mixing tender is fine, such as part check and part cash or card. The penalty ladder comes from KRS 134.015:

  • On or before the discount date: 2% off.
  • Until December 31: the printed amount.
  • During January: 5% on the unpaid tax.
  • Past January 31: 10%.

The debt also becomes a lien. A Carrollton house with a past-due bill will be flagged by the buyer's title company, so line up the clerk's payoff figure early.

How does a Carroll County tax sale work?

After April 15 the sheriff hands unpaid bills to the County Clerk, and a sale comes at least 90 days afterward. KRS 134.128, summarized on the state's collection page, puts the sale 90 to 135 days after the transfer, with notices to the owner at 30 and 60 days.

The clerk sold Carroll's 2025 delinquent taxes on July 24, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. on the courthouse's second floor, with third-party purchasers registering by July 14, 2026. Questions go to the clerk at (502) 732-7005. A buyer who purchases a certificate may add substantial fees, which is why owners fare better paying before the sale.

In the state's first example, a $1,000 bill paid within five business days of reaching the clerk costs about $1,388 once interest, a clerk commission and a recording fee are added. Waiting brings in the county attorney's commission, postage and advertising costs.

How can a Carrollton owner appeal a value?

Ask the PVA for a conference, then file with the clerk once the roll closes. The roll stays open 13 days after the first Monday in May, and an appeal is valid only after a conference with the PVA or a deputy, as the state calendar sets out.

The PVA must send notice whenever it assesses above the value you listed. A deed price can also serve as the listed value for the next January 1 if the property has not changed. For a Carroll County seller who bought recently, that means the purchase price may be the PVA's starting point, so keep your closing statement.

The local board owes a written explanation for any increase or decrease, and you may record the hearing. Do not skip it, since not filing or not appearing ends your right to further review.

Which exemptions are open to Carroll County homeowners?

The homestead exemption is available on a primary residence to owners aged 65 or more and to owners who are totally disabled. One state form, 62A350, covers both, and the PVA keeps it on file.

It deducts a set dollar amount from the assessed value, not the entire value, and the amount is reset every two years. A buyer cannot inherit it. Veterans with a total service-connected disability file once, as do owners found disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement System.

Ask the PVA for the current dollar amount, because the dollar figure published on the state's page covers a past assessment period. A seller who is 65 should confirm the exemption was applied before closing.

What do the numbers say about Carroll County homes?

A typical owner-occupied house in Carroll County is valued at $140,900 for 2020 to 2024, between Caldwell's $118,500 and Calloway's $183,200. Owners live in 65.7 percent of homes, the second-lowest share of the four counties, and the 2025 estimate of 11,141 residents is 3.1 percent above 2020.

The Census counted a single building permit in Carroll County in 2025, so most buyers are choosing among existing homes. Employers in Carroll County reported 6,600 jobs in 2023, with total payroll near $497 million, and employment rose 4.7 percent from 2022. Only 11.4 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, and 17.3 percent of residents live in poverty, figures that sit beside the county's $140,900 median home value. Sellers who cannot wait for financing, or who are managing an estate or a rental with tenants, can sell as-is for cash and pay the tax payoff from the proceeds.

What is the Carroll County tax deadline?

December 31 is the annual due date, with a discount for bills paid by the early cutoff printed on your bill. January adds 5% and anything later adds 10%.

Does Carroll County allow a payment plan?

No. The county requires the full amount in a single transaction, though check, cash and card can be combined.

Whom do I call about delinquent Carroll County taxes?

The County Clerk, at (502) 732-7005, collects delinquent real estate taxes and runs the sale.

Is a late fee waived if my bill never came?

No. The county FAQ lists a missing bill as an impermissible reason for a waiver. Look the bill up on the sheriff's page each fall.

Can a Carrollton house with back taxes be sold?

Yes. A buyer can take it as-is and the payoff is paid from your proceeds at closing. Get the figure from the County Clerk before you sign.

What shapes the housing market in Harlan County, Kentucky?

Harlan County lies in southeastern Kentucky against the Virginia line. Harlan is the county seat, Cumberland is the largest city, and Benham, Evarts, Loyall and Lynch complete the six incorporated places. Black Mountain, east of Lynch, rises 4,145 feet and is the state's highest point. Three streams, Poor Fork, Clover Fork and Martins Fork, meet at Baxter to start the Cumberland River. It dates to 1819 and carries the name of Silas Harlan, a frontier soldier.

Coal built the economy. The first coal left by rail in 1911, and the population rose from 10,566 in 1910 to 75,275 in 1940. Every count since 1980 has been lower, down to 26,831 in 2020 and an estimated 24,725 in July 2025. Mining jobs dropped from 13,619 in 1950 to 764 by June 2016.

A seller here is entering a market that has shrunk for decades. That affects the price more than it affects the tax bill, but it decides how much cushion a house has when unpaid taxes or repairs come out of the proceeds.

How low are Harlan County home values?

The 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey figures from Census put the typical owned home at $73,700, roughly half of Hancock County's figure and a third of Hardin County's. Owners live in 71.6 percent of the housing, typical rent is $678 a month, typical household income is $41,693, and 29.4 percent of residents live below the poverty line.

The county has 13,136 housing units against 10,731 households, which is about 2,400 more units than households, and the Census recorded zero building permits for 2025. Around one resident in five is past 65, and 21.4 percent of residents under 65 report a disability. Both groups are the ones the Kentucky homestead exemption is written for.

On a $73,700 house the yearly tax bill is small in dollars. The real risk is a string of unpaid years in which interest and fees grow faster than the home's value.

Which Harlan County offices do I deal with?

Each office keeps its own schedule, so call before you drive in.

  • Sheriff: collects the bill. The sheriff's website links to an online public tax lookup. Call for the discount and penalty dates printed on your bill.
  • Property Valuation Administrator: write to P.O. Box 209 in Harlan (ZIP 40831) or call (606) 573-1990 between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.
  • County Clerk: phone (606) 573-3636. Monday it stays open until 6 p.m.; Tuesday through Friday it closes at 4:30; and on the last Saturday of the month, holiday weekends excepted, it opens 9 a.m. to noon.

The clerk's website has a delinquent taxes page and a third party purchaser application. The PVA's website carries the tax roll and a property search showing assessments and owners. Harlan County's fiscal court is led by the county judge executive and five magistrates, one for each of five districts that run from Bledsoe and Pine Mountain to Pathfork.

What is the real estate tax calendar in Harlan County?

The PVA's website posts the state's cycle in a single chart.

How the Kentucky tax year runs for real estate, from the Harlan County PVA chart
StepWhen
Assessment dateJanuary 1
Listing periodJanuary 1 through March 1
Tax roll open for review, conferences with the PVA13 days beginning on the first Monday of May
Appeals board hearingsFive days, beginning 25 to 35 days after review closes
Bills delivered to the sheriffNo later than September 15
Discount paymentsBy November 1
Payments at face valueNovember 2 through December 31
Bills turn delinquentJanuary 1, with 5 percent through January 31
10 percent penalty and 10 percent sheriff add onAfter January 31
Sheriff passes bills to clerkApril 15
Clerk's certificate salesJuly 14 through August 28

A state ordered delay can move a county to a slower plan with 30 days for each stage, so the dates on your own bill control.

How do I question a Harlan County assessment?

Start with the PVA. A conference in the May inspection window is mandatory, and when it produces agreement the new value flows into the fall bill.

Without agreement you have until one workday after the window shuts to file at the clerk's office. A three member local board, appointed by the largest city's mayor, the fiscal court and the county judge executive, meets about five weeks after inspection. It must reject a claim that comes with no facts, so gather sales of similar houses and repair estimates beforehand.

At these values an appeal pays off mostly when the PVA's record is wrong about something concrete, such as a bedroom count, a shed that no longer exists, or a fire damaged building still carried at full value.

Does the buyer get the Harlan County bill after closing?

Not automatically. The bill for a year goes to the January 1 owner, so a later sale leaves it in the seller's name for that year. According to the PVA, staff read the recorded deed and mail the bill to the new owner when they can. A buyer without a copy should call the sheriff.

List a mailing address the buyer will check in the deed, since the clerk cannot take a deed without an in care of address for that year's bill. A seller on the homestead exemption should also tell the PVA, since the exemption does not go to the buyer.

What does a Harlan County bill cost once it is delinquent?

A bill still open when April 15 closes passes to the County Clerk, and a monthly 1 percent interest charge starts. The Department of Revenue's example uses a $1,000 bill.

  • On transfer, with the penalty, sheriff add on and an assumed commission: $1,254.00.
  • Paid within five business days: $1,387.79.
  • Paid after the county attorney's first notice: $1,611.30.
  • Paid after the June advertisement: $1,659.90.

Notices come by mail, and installment plans can be requested before a certificate is sold. If a third party buys it, the owner pays that buyer, who can add substantial fees.

An owner with unpaid years can still sell. The closing agent gets the payoff from the clerk and pays it from the proceeds. A cash offer on an older house can be weighed against a listing by comparing what is left after the payoff.

Which schools and nearby places affect a Harlan County sale?

Two public districts operate here. Harlan Independent Schools serves the city of Harlan, and Harlan County Public Schools covers the rest, with Harlan County High School in the Rosspoint area east of Harlan. Southeast Kentucky Community and Technical College has its main campus in Cumberland.

Part of Cumberland Gap National Historical Park and the Blanton Forest preserve lie in the county, so a house near them may draw outdoor minded buyers. School district boundaries, city limits and fire protection can change the taxes on a bill, so ask the sheriff which districts appear on yours.

More questions about Harlan County, KY Property Tax Guide

What is the last day for the Harlan County discount?

November 1. After that, the chart lists face value through the end of December and a 5 percent penalty in January.

How much extra does a February payment cost in Harlan County?

Ten percent in penalty plus a 10 percent sheriff add on, both of which start once January ends. The state describes the total as 21 percent.

Who answers questions about my Harlan County assessed value?

The PVA at (606) 573-1990 handles the conference that must come before any appeal.

Where do I check for delinquent Harlan County taxes?

The County Clerk's website has a delinquent taxes page, and the clerk's office answers at (606) 573-3636. The sheriff hands over bills after April 15.

Can a Harlan County owner under 65 get the homestead exemption?

Yes, if totally disabled. The statute, KRS 132.810, opens the exemption to age 65 and up, or total disability, for owners living in the home, filed with the PVA.

Who handles a property tax bill in Lawrence County?

Four offices in Louisa handle the tax year between them, and the PVA and the sheriff list the same Main Cross Street address. Each covers its own step.

  • Property Valuation Administrator (PVA): 122 Main Cross Street, Louisa, KY 41230. The PVA sets the assessed value and takes homestead applications.
  • Sheriff: 122 Main Cross Street, Louisa. Phone (606) 638-4368. The sheriff takes payment.
  • County Clerk: runs the appeals board paperwork and, after April, the sale of unpaid bills. The clerk's site posts the current delinquent list.
  • County Attorney: mails the warning letters to owners whose bills have moved to the clerk.

Taxing districts set different rates, so the sheriff's bill and the PVA's assessment for your own parcel are the figures that count.

What should a Lawrence County owner know about the place?

Lawrence County was formed in 1821 from parts of Floyd and Greenup counties and has had four courthouses over the years. Louisa is the lone city and holds the courthouse. In the east, a quarter-mile concrete T-bridge links Louisa to Fort Gay, West Virginia, across the point where the Levisa Fork and the Tug River join to form the Big Sandy River. Yatesville Lake covers about 2,300 acres, opened in 1992 and is run by the Army Corps of Engineers for flood control and recreation. Alcohol sales are limited to Louisa city limits.

  • People: an estimated 15,765 in July 2025, compared with 16,293 counted in 2020 and 15,860 in 2010. About 416 square miles of land works out to 39 residents per square mile.
  • Housing: 7,737 units and 6,342 households, with 77.8 percent owned by their occupants.
  • Middle home value: $111,700. Typical owner costs are $1,216 a month for mortgaged homes and $386 for paid-off ones, while typical rent is $760.
  • Income: $46,772 for the median household, with 23.4 percent of people in poverty.
  • Work: 207 employer establishments with 2,950 jobs in 2023, a 5.9 percent rise over 2022, and a 30.1 minute average commute.
  • Broadband reaches 83.7 percent of households, and 81.7 percent of adults over 25 hold a diploma.

What is the payment deadline in Lawrence County, and what happens after it?

KRS 134.015 sets the year-end deadline at December 31 and gives a 2 percent discount to anyone who clears the whole bill by November 1. January costs 5 percent extra, and February onward costs 10 percent. The state's sample for a $1,000 bill makes the late cost concrete: a $100 penalty plus a $110 sheriff add-on fee, so the bill is about 21 percent higher from February 1, before any commission.

Late-mailed bills fall under a state alternative schedule that allows 30 days per stage. Oil and gas bills also exist in Lawrence County. The clerk's delinquent tax page says its sale leaves out the 2023 oil and gas bills, so ask the sheriff whether one is attached to your parcel.

How does a Lawrence County owner fight a high valuation?

The sequence runs in order. Step one is a sit-down with the PVA's staff. Step two is the May viewing window for the roll. Step three is the written appeal, which the clerk must have by the next workday after viewing ends. Step four is a hearing before the local board about a month later. Only evidence counts at the hearing, so bring proof such as a description of the lot and buildings, insurance papers, construction costs and listings of nearby sales.

Written reasons follow any change the board makes. Hearings may be recorded, and a paid representative has to fit the categories in KRS 133.120. Skipping the board closes off the Kentucky Claims Commission.

Who can claim the Lawrence County homestead exemption?

Eligible owners are those who have turned 65 and those classified as fully disabled. The 2025-26 deduction is $49,100, which means a $150,000 assessment is taxed as $100,900. Locally, 19.9 percent of people are past 65, and 17.5 percent of those younger report a disability.

The PVA's courthouse office takes the form. A claim built on disability has to be renewed each year. Two groups are excused from renewing: veterans whose disability is service-connected, and people Social Security or a state retirement system has ruled permanently and totally disabled.

How has Lawrence County's head count changed over time?

The count was 20,067 in 1910, fell to 10,726 by 1970, recovered to 14,121 in 1980, and since then has ranged from roughly 14,000 to 16,300. The 2020 census counted 16,293 residents. July 2025 is estimated at 15,765, about 3 percent below the 2020 base.

The same Census tables show 6,342 households, 612 veterans, and a labor force participation rate of 46.7 percent. In 2022 retail sales reached about $209 million and health care receipts about $81 million. A seller who needs to confirm the exact bill, the exemption status or a possible lien will find that the offices above can answer in a single visit to Louisa.

How does the Lawrence County Clerk sell unpaid tax bills?

Anything the sheriff has not collected by April 15 becomes a certificate of delinquency at the clerk's office, with interest of 1 percent a month. Letters from the county attorney go out, and the clerk publishes the list before the sale date. At the sale a registered outside buyer can buy the lien, and from then on the owner pays that buyer. The Lawrence County Clerk's website lays out how its draft-style sale works, which also tells an owner how much the buyer may be paying.

Lawrence County Clerk delinquent tax sale rules (lawrencekyclerk.com, delinquent taxes page)
ItemRule
RegistrationAt least 10 business days before the sale
Deposit$10 per bill, capped at $250, not refundable
Prior year certificatesSeparate list due 10 business days before the sale
Bidders per entityOne potential purchaser
Order of purchaseRandom drawing, lowest number picks first, in rounds
PaymentCash, certified check, money order or company check
RefundsNone after the sale

The lien on the land from delinquent taxes lasts eleven years under KRS 134.015, no matter who owns the property.

What should a Lawrence County seller handle before listing?

  • Ask the sheriff at (606) 638-4368 for the current bill and any earlier unpaid year.
  • Look through the clerk's delinquent list for any certificate tied to the parcel.
  • If you have the homestead exemption, find out from the PVA what becomes of it after a sale.
  • Compare your assessment with the sales of similar houses before the May inspection window opens, in case a dispute is worth filing.
  • Agree on the split of the current bill in the sales contract.
  • Because the PVA and the sheriff list the same Main Cross Street address, one trip to Louisa can settle both the assessment question and the bill itself.
  • Ask whether any oil and gas bill is attached to the parcel, since the clerk's sale notice mentions them by name.

Owners who want no repairs or showings can request a direct offer. Any tax still due is paid from the sale money at closing regardless of buyer.

More questions about Lawrence County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where is the Lawrence County tax bill paid?

The Lawrence County Sheriff collects it at 122 Main Cross Street in Louisa. Call (606) 638-4368 to confirm the amount and the payment methods before you go.

How much does paying early save in Lawrence County?

Two percent comes off a bill paid in full by November 1, and the full printed amount is owed from November 2 to December 31 under KRS 134.015.

What comes first when disputing a value here?

A conference at the PVA's office. Without it the board that reviews assessments will not take the appeal.

How big is the homestead exemption?

It is $49,100 for 2025-26. The owner has to be at least 65 or classified as fully disabled, and the form goes to the PVA.

Can an outside buyer purchase an unpaid bill here?

Yes, when the certificate stays unpaid until the clerk's sale. A registered purchaser can buy the lien, and the owner then settles with that purchaser.

Which offices value, bill and collect Letcher County property tax?

Letcher County runs its tax through a valuation office, the sheriff and the clerk. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets each parcel's value. The Letcher County Sheriff sends out the bill and receives the payment. The Letcher County Clerk inherits anything still unpaid in mid-April.

The PVA sits at 156 Main Street, Suite 105, in Whitesburg, with a phone line at 606-633-2182 and a fax at 606-633-3995. Its page on the statewide PVA portal explains that ownership, like value, is fixed on January 1, so a house bought in March still shows the seller on that year's bill. A new owner who never sees a copy can phone the sheriff at 606-633-2293.

The county government site gives the sheriff's weekday hours as 8:30 to 4 and links to a web page for paying the bill. The clerk, at 606-633-2432, keeps the same hours and runs a delinquent tax section. Phone the clerk to learn when the current year's tax sale is scheduled.

What kind of place is Letcher County for a seller?

It is a mountain county where the land shapes everything, including how a house is priced and how long it sits. Letcher County is tucked into Kentucky's southeastern tip. Pine Mountain stretches 125 miles and runs down the county's center, Black Mountain tops out near 3,700 feet along the Virginia line, and national forest covers a big slice of the acreage.

The first permanent settlement dates to 1803, at the mouth of Pert Creek where Whitesburg now stands. Lawmakers created it in 1842 from pieces of three older counties, Harlan, Perry and Pike, and gave it the name of the sitting governor. Courthouse history tells the story in miniature: a log building finished in 1844, a brick one in 1898, a modern one dedicated in 1965 and remodeled in 1998. Whitesburg is the seat, Jenkins is the biggest city, and Fleming-Neon makes three. Blackey, Mayking, McRoberts, Millstone and Payne Gap are unincorporated.

Coal drove the boom. Before mining the county never topped 10,000 people, and by 1940 it had passed 40,000. The Scotia mine explosions of March 1976 killed 26 miners and led to the federal mine safety act the next year. More recently the July and August 2022 floods killed three people here and left others homeless. If a building was damaged, ask the PVA how that damage shows up in the assessment.

  • Letcher County Public Schools covers most addresses, with its high school in Whitesburg.
  • Jenkins Independent Schools covers the Jenkins area, with an elementary school in Burdine and a combined middle and high school.
  • US 119 climbs Pine Mountain between Jenkins and Whitesburg, and US 23 skirts the eastern edge.
  • Fishpond Lake near Jenkins, the Pioneer Horse Trail and the recreation center draw weekend visitors, and the Mountain Heritage Festival has run since 1983.

How inexpensive are Letcher County homes, by the federal numbers?

Homes here are inexpensive, mostly owner-occupied and rarely new. The federal QuickFacts table for the county shows a population that has slid while households stay fairly stable.

Letcher County snapshot from the federal QuickFacts table
ItemFigure
People counted in 202021,548
People estimated for July 202519,952 (down 7.4% from the 2020 base)
Households, 2020-20248,463
Share of homes occupied by owners74.1%
Typical value of an owned home$67,400
Middle monthly rent$669
Residents 65 or older21.9%
Building permits in 20251
Land area337.93 square miles

With so few permits, nearly every sale is a resale, and buyers compare each house against a small set of older homes. A tax bill on a $67,400 home is small in dollars, which is why a few years of neglect can feel manageable until the penalties compound.

When is the Letcher County bill due, and what happens after the deadline?

Kentucky's collection statute, KRS 134.015, sets one calendar for every county, and the sheriff here follows it. Anyone who settles the full amount by November 1 gets 2 percent off. Between early November and year end the bill is payable at face value. January adds 5 percent, and February onward adds 10 percent plus the sheriff's fee. If the state delays a county's bills, it can swap in a schedule that allows a month per stage.

Closing time on April 15 is the cliff. The sheriff passes the unpaid list along, every item turns into a certificate of delinquency, and a lien goes on record against the house. Monthly interest of one percent starts, and the clerk and county attorney each earn commissions that climb as notices go out.

The Revenue Department's own sample shows the pace of growth. A $1,000 bill reaches the clerk at $1,254 once the penalty, fee and commission are added. If it is still open after the June newspaper ad, the sample total is $1,659.90. Investors can then buy the debt at a public sale three to four and a half months after the handoff, and the lien can last eleven years whoever owns the house.

How can I appeal a Letcher County assessment?

Begin with a sit-down at the PVA's office. The appeals panel refuses any case that skipped that meeting, and the meeting must happen before or during the viewing window.

The roll opens for public viewing on May's first Monday and stays open thirteen days. Once you have held your conference, you must file with the Letcher County Clerk by the end of the workday that follows the window. The local appeals panel then sits in Whitesburg, the county seat, roughly a month later, within 25 to 35 days of the window closing.

  • Bring proof: building and land details, insurance policies, what construction cost, and listings of similar houses. An appeal with no evidence is denied.
  • A paid advocate has to be a lawyer, accountant, consultant, broker, appraiser, your own employee or a holder of a state-recognized designation, and needs your authorization in writing.
  • Audio recording is allowed, and the panel must explain any change in writing.
  • If bills were printed before the ruling and the value rises, a supplemental bill follows.

Can a Letcher County senior or disabled owner cut the tax bill?

Yes, through the homestead exemption. For assessment years 2025 and 2026 the deduction is $49,100 off a home's taxable value. A house assessed at $120,000 would be taxed as though it were worth $70,900.

The home must be the applicant's residence, and the applicant must either reach 65 during the tax year or hold a total disability rating from a federal program or a retirement system. About 22 percent of residents are past 65, so plenty of owners may qualify. Apply at the Letcher County PVA. Disabled owners under 65 generally renew every year, except service-connected veterans and people ruled permanently disabled by the Social Security Administration or the state retirement system, who document it once. A buyer cannot inherit the break, since the exemption belongs to the person.

What does a Letcher County seller owe at closing?

The bill follows the January 1 titleholder, and the settlement statement decides who reimburses whom. A common Kentucky practice is for the seller to credit the buyer for the months of ownership, with the buyer paying the full bill when it arrives.

Kentucky also charges a transfer tax under KRS 142.050: a rate of $0.50 on every $500, or fraction, of the price stated in the deed, billed to the grantor and collected by the clerk at recording. Foreclosure transfers, spouses splitting in a divorce and nominal parent-child transfers are exempt. Because delinquent tax is a lien, closing agents insist on paying it out of the proceeds. Request a payoff figure from the sheriff before closing, and ask the clerk whether any parcel has been certified as delinquent.

More questions about Letcher County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who gets the Letcher County tax payment?

Send it to the Letcher County Sheriff, who answers at 606-633-2293 on weekdays from 8:30 to 4. The county website also links to an online payment page. Anything unpaid after April 15 shifts to the county clerk.

Is there an early-payment discount in Letcher County?

Yes. Paying the whole bill by November 1 of the tax year takes 2 percent off. After that the printed amount is due until December 31, and penalties of 5 and then 10 percent follow.

I bought in Letcher County and no bill came. What now?

Phone the sheriff at 606-633-2293 and ask for a copy. The bill is written to whoever owned the parcel at the start of the year, so it may carry the seller's name, and a missing bill leaves the debt in place.

Who hears a property tax appeal in Letcher County?

A local board of assessment appeals hears it in Whitesburg, after you have met with the PVA at 156 Main Street, Suite 105 and filed with the clerk. The filing deadline is the workday after the thirteen-day roll inspection ends.

Who pays the year's tax when a Letcher County house changes hands?

The settlement statement decides. The sheriff bills the January 1 owner, and sellers commonly credit the buyer for their months of ownership. Delinquent amounts are a lien that has to be cleared for the title to pass clean.

Which Smithland offices deal with Livingston County property tax?

Livingston County splits the job three ways, and every office is in or near the courthouse square in Smithland. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) fixes each parcel's value. The Livingston County Sheriff, who also handles court security and civil papers, collects the bill. The Livingston County Clerk steps in once a bill is certified as delinquent.

The sheriff's office is at 321 Court Street (PO Box 340, Smithland, KY 42081), answers at 270-928-2122, and opens its doors from 8 to 4 on weekdays. The clerk, at the same street address with a separate box (PO Box 400), takes calls at 270-928-2162 and runs a slightly longer Monday, 8 to 5, and 8 to 4 Tuesday through Friday. The PVA mails from PO Box 77 and lists 270-928-2524 in the state's directory of valuation offices.

Because the PVA does not set rates or take payments, each question has a natural first call. Dispute a value or ask about an exemption with the PVA. Ask about the amount owed or a payoff with the sheriff. Ask about a recorded lien or a tax sale with the clerk.

How do the Census numbers describe a Livingston County house?

Livingston is a small rural market with settled households. The federal QuickFacts table reports the following for 2020-2024 unless noted.

  • The middle owner-occupied home is worth $125,600, and owners live in 81.2 percent of the county's homes.
  • Median gross rent is $926, and median household income is $58,984.
  • One resident in four, 25.1 percent, is 65 or older.
  • The 2020 census counted 8,888 people, and the July 2025 estimate of 8,863 is almost flat.
  • Few people move in a given year, since 93.8 percent stayed at the same address.

Stability like that means listings are few, and buyers often come from nearby Paducah. The county is part of the Paducah metropolitan area, and the Ledbetter community sits directly across the Tennessee River from that city.

What is Livingston County's setting, and how did Smithland start?

The county touches rivers on almost every side. The Ohio River forms its border with Illinois, and the county seat of Smithland sits at the confluence of the Ohio and Cumberland, which is why water covers 8.5 percent of the total area of 342 square miles. Kentucky formed the county in 1798 from Christian County and named it for Robert R. Livingston, a member of the committee that drafted the Declaration of Independence. The county keeps Central time.

Smithland takes its name from John Smith, sent in the late 1790s to scout the river junction for a land company. A plat laid out in 1805 was not recorded until 1837, and the county says that same plat still locates lots in town. The earthquake of December 16, 1811 along the New Madrid Fault shook the river town, and the county's own history page recounts how residents fled into the streets as chimneys fell.

Livingston County communities and what the county government says about them
CommunityStatusPopulation noted

CarrsvilleSixth-class city on the Ohio River50 in 2010
Grand RiversCity between the Cumberland and Tennessee riversNot listed
LedbetterCensus-designated place, largest community1,683 in 2010
BurnaUnincorporated, home to North Livingston Elementary and the middle schoolNot listed

Grand Rivers is the one place in the county that voted to allow alcohol sales, in 2016. The rest of Livingston County is dry.

When is the Livingston County tax bill due?

State law gives owners until December 31 of the assessment year, with a discount for early birds. The discount is 2 percent for a full payment made by the first of November. The next two months carry the plain amount, January adds 5 percent, and 10 percent applies after that. If the state approves a late schedule for a county, each stage lasts about a month instead.

The sheriff turns over what remains on April 15. At that point the clerk records the lien, and the debt picks up 1 percent monthly interest. The Department of Revenue's walk-through of a $1,000 bill shows $1,254 at the handoff. Pay in May after a second month of interest and the sample reaches $1,627.61. A buyer at the clerk's sale pays $1,704.21 in the same example, and that figure becomes the base on which the buyer later charges interest and fees.

Before any sale the clerk must run the delinquent list in a newspaper and on a county-sponsored site, and the county attorney mails a 30-day warning to each owner, with a second warning if needed. Ask the Livingston County Clerk for the date of the current sale and for the list of bills certified as delinquent.

How does the PVA arrive at a value, and can a farm owner pay less?

Kentucky recognizes three main methods. For homes the PVA leans on the sales comparison approach, adjusting nearby sales up or down for differences such as a basement. Barns, fences and commercial buildings are valued at replacement cost minus depreciation. Rental properties are valued by the income they produce.

Rural parcels get special treatment. Under Section 172A of the Kentucky Constitution, farmland is assessed at agricultural value, not market value, so the state's own example taxes an acre that would sell for $50,000 on an agricultural value of $750. The Revenue Department builds per-acre values for cropland, pasture, woodland and waste ground. Ask the PVA whether a parcel is classed as farm use before assuming a market-based figure.

  • Federal, state, county and city property is exempt, as are schools run by nonprofits and religious institutions' buildings and personal property.
  • A nonprofit or religious group applies on Revenue Form 62A023 through the PVA, and a denial can go to the local board.
  • Every parcel gets a physical look from the PVA's staff at least every four years.

How can I appeal a Livingston County assessment?

You have to talk to the PVA first, and the talk has to happen before the inspection period ends. Public viewing of the roll starts the first Monday of May and lasts thirteen days. After your conference, the clerk needs the paperwork by the end of the next workday. The board then sits at the county seat, Smithland, 25 to 35 days later.

Evidence wins or loses these cases. The board considers only what is presented while both sides are in the room, and it denies an appeal that arrives without documents. Photographs of the building, its construction cost, insurance policies, nearby listings and sales all help. A paid representative must hold one of the credentials Kentucky lists, such as attorney, accountant, broker or appraiser, and present your written authorization. If the board changes a value, it must explain why in writing, and a value that rises after bills have printed produces a supplemental bill.

Can Livingston County seniors cut their bill, and what happens at a sale?

Yes. With a quarter of residents past 65, the homestead exemption matters here. For assessment years 2025 and 2026 it removes $49,100 from the assessed value of the owner's home, so a house assessed at $175,000 is taxed on $125,900. Apply through the PVA, bringing a license, birth certificate or passport that proves your age. A buyer cannot inherit the exemption and must file separately.

The year's bill belongs to the person who held title when January 1 arrived, and the closing statement divides the cost. The seller also owes Kentucky's transfer tax under KRS 142.050, $0.50 on each $500 of price, which is collected as the deed is filed in Smithland. Foreclosure transfers and transfers between divorcing spouses are among the exemptions. A delinquent amount stays attached to the property as a lien for up to eleven years, so expect the title agent to want it paid first.

More questions about Livingston County, KY Property Tax Guide

Where is the Livingston County sheriff's tax office?

Find it at 321 Court Street in Smithland; mail goes to PO Box 340. Call 270-928-2122 on a weekday between 8 and 4.

What phone number reaches the Livingston County PVA?

The state directory lists 270-928-2524 for the Livingston County PVA, whose mailing address is PO Box 77, Smithland, KY 42081. Call it about values, exemptions and ownership records.

Does Livingston County give a discount for paying early?

Yes. Pay the full bill by November 1 and it drops by 2 percent. Past that date you owe the printed amount until year end, and then penalties begin.

What happens to a Livingston County tax bill I never pay?

The sheriff sends it to the clerk after April 15, and a lien goes on record with interest and commissions piling up. Investors may buy the debt at a sale a few months later.

Is farmland taxed differently in Livingston County?

Yes. Kentucky assesses farmland at agricultural value rather than market value, using per-acre figures for cropland, pasture and woodland. Ask the PVA whether your acreage qualifies as farm use.

Who handles property tax for a Menifee County house?

Three Frenchburg offices share the chores here. An elected appraiser, known as the PVA, values each house. The sheriff mails and takes in the bill. The clerk receives whatever remains unpaid when April 15 closes. Match your question to the right desk and a payoff figure or a corrected value comes faster.

The PVA, clerk and county attorney all list 12 Main Street on the county website, while the sheriff keeps a post office box of its own.

What is Menifee County like for someone selling a house?

Menifee is mountain country, with roughly 204 square miles of land carved out on May 29, 1869 from Bath, Montgomery, Morgan, Powell and Wolfe counties. Frenchburg is both seat and sole city, and its charter dates to 1871 according to the county. Cave Run Lake and the Red River Gorge flank the county, and Lexington is under 70 miles away via the Mountain Parkway.

National forest land takes up much of Menifee, and cultivated farms cover about a tenth of it. Sellers here mostly offer hillside lots, small tracts and cabins. The county website names tourism, forestry, small business, farming and public service as the economy. Menifee belongs to the Mount Sterling micropolitan area, and the school district office is on Wynn Flat Road in Frenchburg.

A March 2, 2012 EF3 tornado cut through Menifee and neighboring counties, and three people were killed in the region. A lender may ask about storm repairs on an older house, so keep permits and receipts together.

What do Census figures say about Menifee County housing?

Menifee counted 6,113 residents in 2020, a dip from 6,306 a decade earlier, and a mid-2025 estimate of 6,430 would be a 5.2 percent bounce. The 2020 count tallied 3,277 housing units, 24.3 percent of them empty, and classed the entire county as rural.

The five year survey adds these points:

  • Owners live in 75.5 percent of the homes.
  • Monthly owner costs run $996 with a mortgage and $299 without one.
  • Broadband reaches 81.2 percent of households, so ask what internet a remote address can get.
  • A worker's average trip to the job takes 29.8 minutes.
  • Per capita income is $25,879, and covered employment was just 454 jobs in 2023, up 3.9 percent from a year earlier.
